The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:55:54 GMT

This video can not be played

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.

It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.

Should it have been a red card though?

Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?

Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

1 of 5

Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.

Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.

Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.

Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.

There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:

distance between the offence and the goal

general direction of play

likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball

location and number of defenders and attackers

As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.

The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".

The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.

The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.

The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.

If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.

It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.

Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.

Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.

Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.

"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.

"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."

But for Liverpool boss Iraola the decision is not up for debate.

"I think he's the last man, no?" he said. "It's a clear foul and a red card, yes?

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes felt it should not have been a red card and said the decision had a detrimental impact on the game.

"It's one that needs to be looked at," Fernandes told Sky Sports.

"We have far too many meetings with the referees for this to happen to us again. The last one against Chelsea [when Lisandro Martinez was sent off], you can give it as a red card and it was probably a second yellow also. Today, you can't give a red card.

"It's very clear they show us if the player is not in control of the ball, it's never a red card.

"Isak kicks the ball forward, the ball goes into the hands of Senne. Isak has got no control of the ball, he has no chance to get on the ball. He puts his leg across to try to get some advantage from Leny. I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card.

"There are too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR taking so long to see to make a mistake like this that can change the game.

"It's not because of them we conceded the goal from the free-kick, but it changes the game completely."

Pochettino, meanwhile, was frustrated by what he perceived as inconsistency in the decision-making of the officials.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss felt his new team should have been awarded a penalty moments before Yoro was sent off, after Jeremy Jacquet went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo.

"It's difficult to accept that because it was a foul under my view and for me was a penalty," Pochettino told Match of the Day.

"Look how everything changes if that action was a red card and a foul, I think we need to review. When I played football that situation is normal. The action against Mbeumo, if that [Yoro foul on Isak] was a red card then that was a penalty."

There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.

Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.

The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

Sounds quite similar.

Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.

Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.

Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.

It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.

That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.

Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:18:26 GMT

A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

Russell Brand's wife says she'll honour prison rules after message row

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 16:51:57 GMT

The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.

She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.

Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.

"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."

In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".

Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised.

His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.

Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking".

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".

She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat plane, air chief says

Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".

His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.

The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.

Writing in the Telegraph, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.

He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."

Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.

The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.

According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.

Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.

In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

Centrica boss 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 13:50:21 GMT

The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.

Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.

The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.

The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.

But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.

Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.

"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."

The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.

"Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said.

"Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."

Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.

When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 09:49:15 GMT

The Las Vegas Grand Prix featured 'yo-yo racing' throughout the field with regular overtaking

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.

The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.

The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.

And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.

Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.

But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.

The key stories of an engrossing race were:

Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstances

Another dip in a dreadful season for Russell

More controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other

Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Verstappen's superb racecraft & Russell's costly mistake - driver ratings

"How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s.

"Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.

Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.

If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.

The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.

As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.

Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.

At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".

They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.

In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.

Challengers came and went but Max Verstappen was never without the lead for long in Las Vegas

That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.

Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.

Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier, but a ninth-place finish was not what he was expecting.

The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."

Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.

But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.

But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.

Antonelli had lifted off the throttle because he wanted to stay behind Verstappen and attack him later, but in so doing had triggered a setting in the engine defined by the rules that left him without battery power.

It deprived him of the chance to deploy what Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff said was a "secret" deployment strategy on the final lap that he felt would have kept Antonelli ahead through the final corners after passing Verstappen down the Strip.

Instead, it gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.

Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 09:20:45 GMT

South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

Widow fears losing home built by husband after support payments end

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 07:14:14 GMT

Every room in Lauren's family home reminds her of her late husband.

A self-employed builder, Andy carried out much of the work on the property himself, helping create the house where the couple raised their four children.

Now, more than two years after his death from cancer, Lauren fears she may struggle to keep it.

The financial support that helped her cover mortgage payments and household bills has ended, leaving her facing uncertainty as she prepares to remortgage the property.

"I don't want to uproot my children," she said. "They've already been through too much the last two and a half years."

Lauren, from Redditch, lost her husband in May 2024, just five months after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer at the age of 42.

The family's income fell by about 80% after his death.

She says bereavement support payments provided a lifeline while she adapted to life as the sole provider for her children.

Now those payments have ended, she faces an uncertain future.

"Will I get a mortgage? I don't know," she said.

Lauren said Andy had first begun suffering stomach complaints in December 2023, around the same time the family were looking into life insurance.

"By the time we really needed it, it was too late... he now had something that was pre-existing," she said.

Although doctors initially gave Andy a prognosis of 16 months, his condition deteriorated rapidly.

"He died a very scared man," Lauren said. "His biggest worry was how I was going to cope financially."

As well as a lump sum payment of £3,500, the government provides financial support of up to £350 a month to bereaved spouses, though it is time-limited.

For recipients of Universal Credit like Lauren, the payments only last a year.

Before 2017, support known as Widowed Parent's Allowance was available until children reached the age of 18, but it was replaced by Bereavement Support Payment.

Lauren said the payments had helped cover mortgage costs, food and household bills after her husband's death.

Without them, she says she is struggling to bridge the gap.

"I just can't find that money," she said. "I can't work any more hours than I'm working."

She believes bereavement support should last longer, rise in line with inflation and be promoted more clearly.

"It feels like a secret benefit," she said.

Lauren's experience has led her to join campaign group Widows Fight, which is calling for changes to the system.

Its petition, which attracted nearly 109,000 signatures, is due to be debated by MPs on Monday.

Campaigners want support to better reflect the financial pressures facing bereaved families, particularly those with dependent children.

For Lauren, however, the issue is less about politics than the practical reality of providing for her family while trying to preserve what her husband left behind.

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: "Losing a loved one is devastating and we understand the financial impact it can have on families.

"Bereavement Support Payment provides short-term financial support, with higher amounts paid for those with children.

"Further help with everyday living costs may be available through benefits such as Universal Credit which provide targeted, means-tested support to those in greatest need."

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 06:01:49 GMT

"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Burnham promised a "brainstorm" on stage in Brussels yesterday, so what's his plan?

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."

Then of course, there is the politics at home. When cornered on this subject the prime minister and his cabinet often say the "British people will be the boss" - going on to cite polling that clearly displays disappointment with Brexit and a discernible interest in going back in.

But that's not the same as polling suggesting the public is demanding the government puts it at the top of the list.

As one senior Labour figure puts it, there has "certainly been a shift - and an openness to have the conversation" about rejoining, but the PM "has to be really careful about locking himself into a manifesto commitment that alienates a lot of people" alongside plenty of voters who might welcome a move.

What of May's warnings about getting tangled up in EU talks at the exclusion of all else?

One government insider from the time asks: "Can you even remember anything else that happened between 2017 and 2020? It's extremely naïve to think he can do all the other things that are extremely pressing, like defence, or Neets, while trying to play out a future with the EU - it won't happen."

It's worth noting, as some ministers do privately, that Burnham himself was not working in Westminster during the most intense struggles over leaving the EU - an advantage perhaps, that he doesn't carry that baggage, or a gap in his experience of how bad it was.

And yet, the prime minister - who, crucially, is confident in his ability to communicate with the public - is plainly resolved on exploring going back into the European Union, and choosing to take that argument on.

After what the government considers to have been a successful summit, that adventure looks more tempting to the many in Labour's tribe who think he is right to do exactly that.

After the last 72 hours, opportunity is knocking - but the warnings from prime ministers past ring out too.

Under May, Brexit affected nearly everyone and everything - trying to go back in under Burnham could perhaps affect everyone and everything too.

The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI characters

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 05:00:38 GMT

Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.

But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.

From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.

Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.

Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.

"A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.

Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.

BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.

The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.

But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.

"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.

In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.

Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money.

"What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.

Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.

And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."

Dozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission.

"I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress.

"I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered."

"I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.

Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.

American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people.

"And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.

Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.

But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.

Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says.

"It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."

Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.

Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".

But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:09:58 GMT

Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".

"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.

But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.

They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.

Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.

Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.

During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".

Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.

While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.

She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.

Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.

But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door.

"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"

The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.

He remains behind bars awaiting trial.

A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."

"She's doing great for what she's gone through."

They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.

"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:04:07 GMT

Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.

Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.

And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.

But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.

Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.

"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.

The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.

But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?

Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

"If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is."

There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.

Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.

"Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on."

Why Nicola Coughlan's new drama might leave viewers uncomfortable

BBC News Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:01:27 GMT

This article contains spoilers for I Am Helen

If you want to unwind on the sofa after a long day, I Am Helen probably isn't the show for you.

The Channel 4 drama starring Bridgerton star Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole from Peaky Blinders has been called a must-watch by critics - but the cast don't want viewers sitting comfortably.

"There's going to be a few awkward sofas," Cole, who plays Helen's partner Steve, says.

"There's going to be people up and down the country that will be able to relate to this in varying degrees.

"And if we can put that in their living rooms and open up a debate, open up a conversation - and maybe help people be better - then we've done our job."

I Am Helen is the latest project in director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationships.

The two fully-improvised episodes, devised in collaboration with Coughlan, follow a relationship spiralling after Steve tries to choke Helen during sex without consent.

"We never realised how incredibly timely it would be," Coughlan tells BBC Newsbeat.

"We filmed this over a year ago.

"It feels incredibly relevant right now, and specifically right now, because pornography that includes strangulation has just been outlawed in the UK."

Earlier this month, the government made it illegal for anyone to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation.

That decision followed a review last year that found choking was "rife" on porn sites and had become normalised, particularly among younger people.

Coughlan and Cole say they were keen to make everything about their characters and the setting as relatable as possible to emphasise the shocking fallout.

"We needed one inciting incident that felt like something that could really plausibly happen between a couple, that it just goes slightly too far without consent, and it just blows everything up," Coughlan says.

"It's really important we see Steve's perspective in it because it makes him a normal guy.

"He's not this evil guy who's attacking Helen. He does bad things, but he's complicated. And hopefully you see them both as real people."

Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.

"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.

She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.

Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.

"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.

"It's a lot to keep going."

Cole agrees that "it was tough".

"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.

For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.

But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.

"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.

"I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."

Cole researched the manosphere online while developing his role and says he could see how people like Steve "quickly become lost in this quite simple ideology".

"The more interesting thing was the lower level, the kind of 'bro influencer' type people, who a lot of what they say is actually quite good," he says.

"You know, 'go to the gym, be healthy, look your best'.

"But occasionally they veer into comments on male and female societal roles and how a woman should stay at home."

For someone like Steve, who Cole says wants a traditional relationship and a family, those ideas left him "completely lost".

The characters quickly "get caught in a cycle", he says, as they find it harder and harder to understand each other.

"It starts off as a question, which becomes a debate, which becomes an argument, which becomes a huge bust-up, which becomes forgiveness, an apology, tears."

Coughlan says viewers have told her they expected the series to end with serious violence, perhaps even with Steve killing Helen.

But she was determined to avoid a shock factor so the characters didn't tip into being unrelatable.

"There's some very extreme moments in this, but some of them are not extreme," she says.

"It's better that he didn't [kill Helen] because as a viewer, you don't want people to go, 'well, if he does X, then that's the moment to leave'.

"From my perspective, you watch it and you go, 'you don't need to hit a threshold'.

"If you feel scared and uncomfortable, that's enough reason to get out of a situation."

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

New Scientist November 20, 2026

If the past year was the “mathpocalypse”, a claim that AI has helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis is its most stunning horseman yet. Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic says he has used AI to solve this problem, which has sat at the heart of mathematics for nearly 200 years. This is not just the latest in the series of famed mathematics problems to fall to AI, but could be the biggest mathematical result of the century. Accordingly, mathematicians have received the news with a combination of exhilaration, bewilderment and caution.

“If true, it would, in my opinion be the greatest achievement yet by AI, and one of the greatest proofs in the history of mathematics,” says Thomas Bloom at the University of Manchester in the UK. “The Riemann hypothesis has represented a major barrier in our current understanding of the way numbers behave – if the AI proof has correctly solved it, this would represent a huge leap in what we know.”

Rainer Dietmann at Royal Holloway University of London is similarly in awe. “If it turns out to be correct, this is not only huge, it’s the biggest result in pure mathematics ever… It’s like having found the Holy Grail,” he says.

Advertisement

Dating back to the 1800s, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers. Because they cannot be factored into any smaller whole numbers, primes are like the atoms of numbers – they are the simplest units out of which any other number can be made. However, predicting when a prime will show up in a list of numbers is notoriously difficult. In 1859, Bernhard Reimann hypothesised a formula that would stunningly reduce that difficulty, but didn’t finish a proof before he died. Mathematicians have been trying to wrangle it ever since. After years of approximate results, including an AI-generated proof released by Open AI in October, Alpöge’s work may have finally confirmed Reimann’s centuries’ old intuition.

“It has captured the imagination, presumably because it is about something that we can all understand – the prime numbers – and because it has resisted the efforts of so many for so long. And it is important to mathematicians because it is so useful for other problems: a lot of theorems begin, “assume the Riemann hypothesis…” says Chris Daw at the University of Reading in the UK.

The new proof has not been formally reviewed by other mathematicians, which would be required for publication in an academic journal, and Alpöge hasn’t released the full proof, which he described in a public statement as being over 250,000 pages long. Instead, he has released the version of the proof that has been adapted for verification in the proof-checking software Lean, which is 17 million lines long. Anthropic and Alpöge did not respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

Michael Levitin at the University of Reading says hundreds of thousands of pages of Lean output won’t be easily checked. “In proportion to the magnitude of this claim, we should be appropriately sceptical,” says Bloom. “Even after the Lean formalisation has been independently checked, it remains possible that the AI might be taking advantage of some subtle undiscovered bug in the code. I’d feel more confident once we have a combination of the Lean compiling correctly, with no bugs found, and also human experts [having] had a chance to discuss the ‘big picture’ of the proof and whether it seems plausible.”

“Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to understand the proof themselves. And that will of course take time, since we only move at biological speeds,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. It is here that this new result, with its prospect of incredible historical significance, exemplifies the trouble mathematicians have had with AI over the past year, as it has been used to check one problem after another off their most coveted list of open questions.

Put simply, AI-assisted work benefits tremendously from prior work by human mathematicians, yet its end result isn’t immediately understandable to them. Coming to terms with the new proof will almost certainly take a long time, and it brings to the fore big questions about the future of mathematics. “Pretty much every mathematician will need time to process this. If AI can do this, what can it not do – in mathematics, at least?” says Daw. Many mathematicians already feel a sense of grief and anguish over how quickly AI tools have been solving problems that would have previously consumed a human mathematician’s whole career, and Dietmann says this new proof could have a similarly negative effect.

“What looked impossible one year ago has become reality. Many other problems in mathematics, computer science and related fields will fall as well, and it will become increasingly difficult for humans even to follow and understand,” he says. “While this progress is tremendous, it will massively amplify the despair by many in the mathematical community.”

Some mathematicians are more optimistic. “This is a very exciting time for pure mathematicians, and we are needed more than ever,” says Alex Bartel at the University of Glasgow in the UK. “AI is capable of spitting out proofs at a much faster pace than we are used to, but our task remains that of properly understanding what is going on… and that work is as fulfilling as ever, but there is now a lot more of it. The announcement of a very long proof of the Riemann hypothesis only reinforces my view.”

Mere hours after Alpöge’s announcement, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, wrote in a blog post that mathematician Alessandro Masullo has also put forward a proof of a generalised version of the Riemann hypothesis. This proof was completed without the use of AI, and it is 940 pages long. It has also not yet been checked by other mathematicians nor confirmed using Lean.

This day will be remembered as a shocking one, and the aftershocks may continue. “I can only compare this achievement to the aliens with a vastly superior intelligence coming to the Earth and explaining to us all the sacred mysteries we ever dreamed of,” says Alexei Skorobogatov at Imperial College London. “Humanity managed to create an amazingly powerful yet completely alien form of intelligence. The only event in history I can compare it to is the discovery of a nuclear bomb. Hopefully, AI will be put to better use!”

Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity

New Scientist November 20, 2026

Flying in the face of Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, quantum physics could turn the famous force repulsive instead of attractive – and we could soon test the idea in the lab.

A hallmark of gravity as we know it is that it pulls objects with mass together: gravity explains why the moon orbits Earth, and why an apple falls to the ground after detaching from the tree. While this is well established, there is still no agreement on how gravity works at scales dominated by quantum effects, and what quantum properties it may have.

Now, two research teams have independently found that quantum effects can make gravity act repulsively, pushing objects apart instead of pulling them together.

Advertisement

Could gravity produce quantum entanglement if it’s not fully quantum?

“Gravity is always attractive – this has been the cornerstone of gravity from Newton to Einstein,” says Pablo Saldanha at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Brazil, who worked on one of the studies with Vlatko Vedral and Chiara Marletto, both at the University of Oxford. “Anti-gravity or repulsion: no one has seen that before,” says Sougato Bose at University College London, who co-authored the other study with Lev Vaidman at Tel Aviv University in Israel.

A key concept for both studies was that of a quantum superposition state. Consider a car driving down a city street. When it arrives at an intersection where one road forks into two, it can take either the left or the right branch. But a quantum car would have another option: to enter a superposition of taking the left road and also the right one, assuming a state where it is impossible to tell where the car is exactly without disturbing it.

Another quantum object, called a “probe”, moving along a path parallel to both the left and right road branches, would be gravitationally attracted to the car. In both new studies, the researchers mathematically modelled an analogous setup and used equations to show that this gravitational interaction would make the car and the probe inextricably connected through the link of quantum entanglement.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The two teams mathematically examined a scenario equivalent to the two roads – left and right – merging some time after they had split apart. At this point, a measurement taken by the probe can reveal how each of the paths shaped the superposed car’s quantum state.

Quantum mechanics is probabilistic. This means that if this experiment is repeated many times, the final state of the car won’t always be the same, but will follow some distribution of states instead, reflecting its capacity to follow a combination of the left and right branches. The researchers in both experiments found that if all but some specific states were then discarded after the measurement – a technique called post-selection, partly pioneered by Vaidman – then the probe should theoretically experience gravitational repulsion and be pushed away from the car in the experiment. “That repulsion, that going away [from the superposed object], is created at the time of the measurement,” says Bose.

Even Einstein’s theory of general relativity, which has for over a century proven to be an incredibly accurate description of gravity, doesn’t predict this kind of gravitational repulsion. “There is a measurement that will somehow conditionally give you repulsive gravitational force,” says Vedral. Confirmation that such a repulsive force occurs would demonstrate the quantum nature of gravity.

If gravity is a truly quantum entity, something as simple as measuring the strength of an object’s gravitational field should change its quantum state

Because this measurement effect is inherently quantum, just like the possibility of a superposition state is, the scenario the two teams explored doesn’t have any non-quantum analogues. But it could still be tested in experiments.

Objects that can stay in a superposition state for the duration of an experiment would have to be very small, says Bose, and yet also still massive enough for gravity to make a difference to their behaviour. Bacterium-sized objects should do the trick. He and Vaidman calculated that the probe object at this scale would experience acceleration roughly smaller than a quadrillionth of gravitational acceleration on Earth. Vedral says that he and his colleagues are already working with experimentalists who specialise in unusually large quantum objects.

Tomasz Paterek at the University of Gdańsk in Poland says that the new idea is “brilliant”. Past studies explored making the force between electrons attractive, even though it is usually repulsive, through post-selection. But this is the first time that the same process has been shown to potentially reverse gravity’s character too, he says. In Paterek’s view, lab experiments that use gravity to quantum entangle objects could be achievable in the near future – but he cautions they will be really difficult to perform.
