Fonterra seeks permission to dump millions of litres of raw milk

New Zealand Herald November 22, 2026

Fonterra’s conservative scenario would send 60% of surplus milk to Clandeboye. Photo / 123rf

By Keiller MacDuff of RNZ

Fonterra has alarmed environmentalists with a proposal to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury – the equivalent of almost nine Olympic-sized swimming pools.

The dairy giant said the move was necessary to manage a potential surplus caused by production constraints across the South Island. The company would not be drawn on what the production constraints were.

Federated Farmers welcomed the proposal, calling it a sign of prudent risk management.

Fonterra’s applications to vary the conditions of seven resource consents were filed with the Canterbury Regional Council on October 2. They relate to wastewater discharges at its Clandeboye, Darfield and Studholme sites in Canterbury.

The variations were sought as a contingency response to surplus raw milk that Fonterra anticipated during the peak milk period in the 2027 and 2028 financial years, but, if granted, would apply for the duration of the original consents, which range from 2027 to 2045.

In its technical memorandum to the council, Fonterra said it anticipated “surplus raw milk will require disposal during the peak period of FY27 due to processing constraints that may occur across the South Island”, and estimated the volume would be about 22,340cu m (22 million litres) over the current season.

A Fonterra spokesperson said the consent variations would allow the co-operative to dispose of milk when events “out of its control” prevented it from being processed.

“We deal with a perishable product that needs to be processed within 24-36 hours,” they said.

The spokesperson said Fonterra had similar provisions in other consents across the country.

The company had not needed to dispose of milk this season and was already through the peak processing season (late October to mid-November), nor did it foresee having to dispose of milk next season, the spokesperson said.

“Work done across our network during winter this year has helped to ensure that we have enough capacity to efficiently process all our milk,” they said.

If needed, Fonterra could shift processing to the North Island or adjust the products it made, the spokesperson said.

“With 24 manufacturing sites across the country, we have considerable flexibility to manage our farmers’ milk. If those options were exhausted, we have contingency arrangements for the safe and appropriate disposal of milk, including on farm, where necessary,” they said.

New Zealand’s milk production set a new record in the 2025/2026 season, processing 2.02 billion kilograms of milksolids, a 4.5% increase on the previous season, from 21.8 billion litres of milk.

DairyNZ’s latest figures showed the South Island had higher average milksolid production per cow and per hectare compared to the North Island, while North and South Canterbury had the biggest average herd sizes and stocking rates in the country.

Infometrics puts the average number of cows in the Canterbury region at just over 970,000 in the year to May, an increase of 2.1% over the year, double the nationwide increase of 1%.

The Canterbury Regional Council has granted effluent consents allowing for up to 57,000 more cows since a temporary freeze on dairy conversions expired in January last year.

Fonterra’s application stated the surplus raw milk would be incorporated into existing wastewater systems or applied directly to land. Either way, the milk would end up on farmland after being mixed into the wastewater streams and irrigated on to pasture, or loaded straight into tankers and spread on to or injected into soil.

Raw milk contained the same substances as the consented wastewater, including organic matter, fats, protein, nitrogen and phosphorus but at “significantly higher concentrations”, the application stated.

The company advised any environmental effects were considered to be “no more than minor”.

Milk dumping would also have “positive effects” by adding extra capacity for surplus milk and “allow beneficial re-use of nutrients and organic matter”, contributing to soil fertility and supporting pasture and crop growth, the application said.

The variations were consistent with the regional council’s objectives and policies, including the Canterbury Land and Water Regional Plan, and neither public nor limited notification of the consent variations was required, Fonterra argued.

The Environmental Law Initiative (ELI) called on the regional council to reject the application.

Senior researcher Anna Sintenie said the group was concerned by a “vast” change in activity from the original consents and the scale of the proposal.

“We’re looking at beforehand discharging wastewater related to processing of trucks and plant facilities’ wash down. What’s been proposed here is a completely different substance of raw milk and the scale of that is huge,” she said.

“Twenty-two million litres is more than four litres of milk for every person in New Zealand. That’s an extraordinary volume of food to waste, especially with so many households experiencing cost-of-living pressures.

“It also comes at a significant environmental cost, including greenhouse gas emissions, heavy freshwater use and nutrient pollution.”

The council should require Fonterra to submit new consent applications, which had higher notification and analysis requirements than variations, Sintenie said.

“Fonterra is trying to shoehorn a major discharge of raw milk into existing wastewater consents through a variation. In our view, that’s not acceptable. A discharge of this kind should require a full, new consent application and proper public scrutiny,” she said.

ELI was also concerned about regional council dairy conversion approvals that had green-lit consents associated with tens of thousands of additional cows in the past year, Sintenie said.

“That raises a fundamental question: why is the region continuing to expand dairy production when Fonterra is seeking permission to dispose of surplus milk because production is likely to exceed its processing capacity?”

The environmental footprint of 22.3 million litres of milk included about 20,000 tonnes of emissions, about 6.5 billion litres of freshwater (mostly for irrigation and stock water) as well as many billions of litres more to dilute nitrate pollution, she said.

Sintenie said the application also requested the definition of wastewater be amended to include raw milk.

“By applying for this, it would open the door to that happening in these consents into the future. It’s concerning that it could set a real precedent about how we think about incorporating this hugely valuable and nutrient-rich food product into wastewater,” she said.

Canterbury Regional Council general manager of regulatory implementation Paul Hulse said the council became aware of Fonterra’s processing constraints in late September.

He said the council “do not and cannot take business constraints into account” when assessing consent applications.

Hulse said it was not for the council to say whether the application should have been lodged as new consent rather than a variation.

“Fonterra is entitled to submit the applications in the form it considers appropriate. Our role as regulator is to determine whether the proposed changes fall within the scope of the existing consents,” he said.

Asked what effect large amounts of raw milk could have on the environment, Hulse said the council’s water and land science team would “assist consents planners in evaluating an assessment of environmental effects for the proposed activity”.

Federated Farmers national dairy chair Karl Dean said he was not aware of similar attempts to allow milk dumping but welcomed the move, calling it “good, prudent business practice”.

He said there were a number of scenarios that could require milk to be disposed of, such as following an earthquake.

“It was a matter of making sure the appropriate systems and risk mitigations are in place so that if something bad did happen, the options are there - even if they never get used - that those options are available,” he said.

“I think what this highlights to me in doing some research is it’s a bit concerning that some of the other milk processors don’t have that ability in their consents.”

“Obviously, I would expect the cooperative to be ... wanting to utilise every drop of milk which I’m sure they will. I think this is more of a case of making sure that good risk management is in place so that should the absolute worst happen, that there’s allowance to do something.”

Dean also supported Fonterra’s attempt to have the definition of wastewater changed to include raw milk, which he said would be beneficial for the entire industry.

Federated Farmers understood most South Island production constraints had already been mitigated, with significant upgrades to several sites in the South Island over the last year.

“As a farmer, I haven’t been impacted this year the same way I was impacted last year when there was some issues, so I’d say that those mitigations have obviously worked,” he said.

In September, Fonterra announced it would spend $1 billion over three years on its South Island manufacturing network.

Greenpeace freshwater campaigner Rhiannon Mackie said dumping raw milk could have harmful environmental impacts.

“Canterbury has highly porous soil, which means it’s really easy for fluids to get through the soil and into water tables like we see with the cow urine and synthetic fertiliser that causes nitrate contamination,” she said.

“In lakes and rivers in particular you can see increases in toxic algal blooms, which are already an issue in Canterbury, and have a really negative impact on the health of the freshwater ecosystems,” she said.

“Not only are New Zealanders subsidising the dairy industry through the pollution of drinking water and lakes and rivers, we’re also paying huge amounts of money at the supermarket for dairy products and meanwhile Fonterra is talking about dumping these raw milk products because they’ve just got so much of it,” she said.

According to Fonterra’s “conservative assessment scenario”, the co-operative would send the bulk of the surplus milk (60%) to the Clandeboye site, near Temuka – an indicative volume of 13,404cu m (13 million litres per season or 600,000 litres per day) – although it noted actual volumes could vary depending on milk supply, processing capacity and operational requirements.

The next largest amount (37% of the total) would go to Darfield in the Selwyn district – 500,000 litres per day – while 3% (25,000 litres per day) would be disposed of at Studholme near Waimate.

A recent Journal of Dairy Research paper quantified dairy food loss in New Zealand for the first time, finding the industry routinely lost 1.8% of dairy food on farm and 5.5% at the processor.

The study said the loss was “not a sizable issue” but equated to the annual milk production of about 86,000 cows on farm and 264,000 cows at the processor.

Victoria University research fellow Dr Mike Joy said even the routine dairy losses had a big impact.

“You can call that minor if you like, but that’s equivalent to 350,000 cows worth of milk that’s just discarded. To me, that’s criminal, that’s not minor, that’s a massive impact.”

Research led by Joy in 2022 concluded each litre of milk produced required up to 11,110 litres of water to dilute nitrogen leached from Canterbury dairy farms.

He dismissed Fonterra’s stance the effects of the dumping on the environment or to neighbours, residents and groundwater users would be “less than minor”.

“Every application claims the impacts are less than minor but the cumulative effects of a whole heap of less than minors is major,” he said.

Most people know my suburb for one giant building, but I see a community full of heart

Sydney Morning Herald November 23, 2026

Three years ago, when I moved back to Australia with my family after spending a decade in New Zealand, living in Slacks Creek wasn’t even on our radar. We wanted to stay close to our families in Underwood and Eight Mile Plains, while also finding a good neighbourhood to call home.

Slacks Creek didn’t exactly stand out, based on the stories I had heard. People told me it was rough. Others described it as one big industrial area. And then, of course, there was the so-called “Logan reputation”. Looking back now, it’s funny how quickly assumptions can take hold when you’ve never actually experienced a place for yourself.

When we started looking for houses, Slacks Creek offered something we thought might remain a dream: a solid family home with a backyard my eight-year-old could play in. The best part was it was affordable and still close to my parents and extended family, which was very important to us.

Living nearby means more family dinners, more celebrations, and more opportunities to spend time together without needing to plan weeks in advance. As anyone with young children knows, having family close by is priceless.

What’s it really like to live in Slacks Creek, I often get asked? Nearly three years later, I can confidently say that almost everything we heard about the suburb was wrong. What we’ve found instead is a community full of friendly and welcoming neighbours where we’re building great friendships, creating memories, and feeling genuinely connected to the people around us.

I still remember last year when we were on our way home and received a notification on our phone that our house alarm had been triggered. When we arrived, we found several neighbours standing out the front of our property keeping watch, while others had walked around the yard to make sure everything was OK. Nothing was wrong, but seeing our neighbours rally around like that meant a lot to us.

When I tell someone who isn’t from Logan that I live in Slacks Creek, I’m often met with a blank look. Then I say, “You know, where IKEA is,” and suddenly they know exactly where I’m talking about. The flatpack furniture giant has become Slacks Creek’s unofficial town centre.

Certainly, having IKEA and the adjacent Logan Supercentre nearby was a lifesaver when we first moved because we didn’t have any furniture! We could quickly go home and check measurements before making a purchase, or come back and grab missing dowels or Allen keys.

It’s funny to think that long before people knew Slacks Creek as the place with IKEA, it was known for cattle. The suburb was named in 1971 after the Slack family, who settled in the area during the mid-1800s. (The creek’s Aboriginal name is Mungaree.) John Slack grazed cattle here, and son William ran a slaughter yard between Paradise Road and the Loganlea Road interchange.

These days, it’s a well-connected and convenient place to live. Having easy access to both the M1 and Logan Motorway makes commuting incredibly simple. You can be heading to Brisbane one minute, the Gold Coast the next, or travelling west via the Logan Motorway.

The suburb’s biggest claim to fame is possibly as the place where Darren Hayes grew up, escaping from physical and emotional abuse into dreams of music and movies before going on to form Savage Garden (with another Logan resident, Daniel Jones) and selling 35 million records. There was a time when Truly Madly Deeply was my favourite song – I listened to it on my Sony Walkman so many times.

Another thing we love about living in Slacks Creek is the food. From amazing sandwiches at Janus Deli to banh mi at TNT Banh Mi – as well as the growing number of local food trucks on Kingston Road on Friday and Saturday nights – every meal feels like a celebration of the suburb’s diverse community.

One of the best things about living in Slacks Creek is being close to family-friendly attractions. We love visiting the Daisy Hill Koala Centre with our daughter, and a trip to the Global Food Markets at Woodridge, where locals sell produce grown across Logan, is a regular part of our routine.

Looking back, buying our home in Slacks Creek was one of the best decisions our family has ever made. What started as a practical choice – somewhere affordable, close to family and within reach – became so much more.

When people ask me about Slacks Creek now, I don’t think about reputations or stereotypes, I think about the hidden local eateries tucked behind industrial buildings. I think about neighbours gathering for barbecues and arriving with a plate to share. I think about our relatives living just down the road, children growing up together, and the convenience of having everything we need within easy reach.

For our family, Slacks Creek has become a place we love: truly, madly and deeply.

The accidental leader who negotiates with the Premier and nude toddlers

Sydney Morning Herald November 23, 2026

Melbourne is never a safe seat, says Ellen Sandell, the country kid who holds it. But the leader of the Greens thinks she can win it – and expand the party’s presence even further.

Ellen Sandell is easy to spot at the school drop-off on Monday morning.

In her green woollen jacket and triangle Greens earrings, the party’s Victorian leader is sometimes asked by people where she gets all her clothes from. The answer is, as you might expect, from secondhand clothing apps like Depop.

“Green’s not often in fashion,” she explains. “Green clothes can be hard to find.”

Sandell is hoping that on November 28, the Greens themselves will be in fashion, and that they can extend their presence in Victoria’s lower house beyond the three seats they currently hold.

Right now, however, the member for Melbourne is focused on her immediate responsibility: leading the “walking bus” to school drop-off.

Sandell has three children aged four, seven and nine. This morning, they were almost delayed by the last-minute emergence of her youngest son, completely nude and carrying a plastic sword.

“Chaos,” she says of the ensuing battle to get him dressed.

Things calm down nearby at Local Folk, one of Sandell’s favourite neighbourhood cafes in Kensington, where she’s on a first-name basis with the staff and recommends the banana bread with a pot of tea.

The 41-year-old portrays herself as someone who found themselves leader almost by accident. Mid-way through her third term in parliament, she says it was a “total surprise” when the party’s then-leader Samantha Ratnam stepped down, and colleagues chose Sandell to take over.

“I was very hesitant to start with,” Sandell says. “It’s a lot of work running a marginal seat. Melbourne is always going to be a marginal seat, particularly with the CBD. There’s so much turnover. It’s never going to be a safe seat. You have to work for it every single time. And I had little kids.”

It has indeed been a juggle. Her weakness, she says, is trying to take on too much at times.

“My eyes are bigger than my stomach,” Sandell says.

Sometimes, after a long day, she will get home and decide to make a huge meal for her family, only for her husband, Lloyd Davies, to try to dissuade her.

“He’ll say: ‘You’re an idiot. Why are you doing that?’” she says.

Davies’ preferred solution: “Just give them tomatoes on toast. It’s good enough.”

1:06

A rapid-fire round with Ellen Sandell

The Greens leader reveals her dream dinner guest and her most important policy.

But Sandell is the sort of parent who spends hours baking her birthday cakes and devising elaborate Harry Potter-themed parties. Doing the bare minimum doesn’t come naturally to her.

Saturday’s state election will be her first as the Greens leader, and she is quietly confident about her party’s prospects.

“It looks like a shocker for Labor,” Sandell says, drawing on conventional wisdom that a bad election for Labor means a good election for the Greens.

She thinks the major parties are lacking vision, and the Liberals are “just hoping Labor will fall over, and they’ll do a bit of a Steven Bradbury and get the reins”.

The Greens, in her telling, are offering transformative and bold policies, and a real alternative for voters.

These policies include cutting stamp duty, building public housing, freezing and capping rent increases, free public transport, ending coal and gas, building renewables, a moratorium on data centres, and stronger protection for forests.

“We’re polling higher, 50 per cent higher than we ever have,” Sandell says, referring to the party’s primary vote climb from 10 per cent to 15 per cent. “We’re in with the chance of winning more seats than we ever have.”

When she took the reins in 2024, Sandell said seats such as Prahran, Albert Park, Footscray and Northcote were potentially winnable in 2026.

With polling day now in sight, she stands by this, but says the Greens are also in genuine contention in seats further out from the CBD, such as Pascoe Vale.

“I’ve tried to have a focus in the party of shifting us from just being a senate or upper house party to genuinely contesting power in the lower house,” she says.

Bob Brown, the former federal Greens leader and a mentor to Sandell, says he is not sure how polling will translate into seats. But he thinks the Greens will be a “formidable political force” in both houses after the election, led by an MP whom he praises as “a very positive intelligent young woman”.

The wild card in this election, of course, is One Nation. Ironically for Sandell, the rise of Pauline Hanson’s populist party at a state level also means that for the first time, the Greens were invited to participate in a leaders debate.

“When push got to shove, of course, they couldn’t have One Nation in without having the Greens,” Brown says.

Sandell brightly took up the chance at the debate to take swings at Premier Ben Carroll, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, and One Nation’s Warren Pickering. But she is concerned about the impact the right-wing party is having.

“I am worried about One Nation and the state and what happens to our politics and divisive misinformation,” she says.

In Prahran, which is an unusual contest between the Liberals and the Greens, Labor is running an open ticket, a position on preferences that is expected to work against Sandell’s party. She believes this is unconscionable.

“It really confirms everything that I think about the Labor Party at the moment, which is that they are much more closely aligned with the Liberals and the One Nation than they are with the Greens,” she says.

Do Victorians feel the same way? Sandell is hoping they do, and will turn to the Greens because Labor has moved away from its traditional values.

One Nation’s emergence is far from the only challenge Sandell has had to weather since she took over. Most recently, and most painfully, was the death of Tim Read – the party’s MP for Brunswick – from cancer. He had been a powerful advocate of reforms to the state’s integrity laws that finally passed after his death.

“He was such a good conscience in our party room and such a wise head,” Sandell says. “So many times I just want to call him and ask his opinion on things.”

She also had to deal with the departure of her co-deputy leader Sam Hibbins from the party, after he admitted to a consensual relationship with a staffer.

“It was such a shock because none of us had any idea that this had been going on,” Sandell says. “To have to go and confront someone that you have been working so closely with, they’ve been such a close ally and friend. It felt like a real betrayal.”

Hibbins is critical of how Sandell handled the situation, and says she “jumped the gun” by issuing what he describes as a highly inflammatory public statement before the facts were established.

“I was completely blindsided,” he says. “Her comments undermined due process and resulted in harmful public speculation.”

Hibbins ultimately resigned. It was a difficult time, Sandell says, given she had worked closely with Hibbins throughout her time in parliament and relied on him.

Hibbins says what began as a strictly confidential workplace process overseen by parliament ended up with the vandalism of his parliamentary office, which targeted his family.

“Whilst we are continuing to move on with life, I am pursuing these matters with the Victorian Parliament through formal means,” he says.

Sandell grew up in Alice Springs and Mildura. Her dad was a forester turned environmental scientist and firefighter, and her mum a pharmacist.

“I definitely got my values from both my parents,” Sandell says. “They both cared a lot about the environment. We spent a lot of time out bush as kids.”

Her childhood memories are punctuated by family camping trips and community sport, before she won a scholarship to study science at the University of Melbourne, where she lived at Queens College and met her husband.

“We had lots of political conversations, but I wouldn’t say I was politically active, even at uni,” Sandell says.

Her scientific background shines through in the measured and careful way Sandell considers and answers questions.

She started to get involved in environmental campaigning, participating in forest blockades in the central highlands and East Gippsland, and protests at Hazelwood Power Station in the Latrobe Valley.

“I was never arrested, but I was involved in lots of actions,” Sandell says.

Upon graduating, she worked as a scientific researcher at the CSIRO, and then under Labor premiers Steve Bracks and John Brumby in the Department of Premier and Cabinet in the newly formed Office Of Climate Change.

One of her projects was putting solar panels on every Victorian school. But on the first day of the school year, on a day of extreme heat, Brumby was inundated by talkback radio callers wanting air conditioning in schools instead.

“The premier pretty much changed his mind and said: ‘OK, instead of putting solar in schools, let’s look at how we could put air conditioners in schools instead’. I’d been working on that project and I was like, ‘Wow, that’s an interesting case study of how quickly politicians’ minds can change based on public opinion’.”

Sandell later ran GetUp founder Simon Sheikh’s Senate campaign in the ACT. When that was unsuccessful, she moved back to Victoria with Davies to figure out what to do.

“Someone in the Greens kind of tapped me on the shoulder and said, ‘Have you thought about running? We need a candidate for Melbourne in 2014’,” Sandell says. “For various reasons I put my hand up.”

One of those was the proposed East West Link, which united in opposition groups including the Greens, public housing residents, the Friends of Royal Park, and the Seeing Eye Dogs.

“It was a huge community campaign,” Sandell says. “Labor was so scared they reversed their position … and cancelled it.”

It was also a lesson for the rookie politician in the power of community.

“I always say politics isn’t just what happens in the parliament, it happens in the streets and in the community,” she says. “You have to build power and have unlikely alliances.”

Those skills are set to be tested in this campaign. The Greens have to battle to get reporters to show up to their press conferences, compared to the major parties, which have branded buses to drive the media pack to and from events.

Only one television camera turns up to a press conference on housing which Sandell holds with federal senator Barbara Pocock. Another media event on empty shops in the Docklands is cancelled due to a lack of interest.

Sandell is sanguine about the downsides of leading a minor party.

“We try to be creative where we can,” she says. “We did a press conference submerged in the Yarra River to try to get some attention to our policies.”

These challenges occupy her late at night, when the lines between her family life and work blur. Her husband says it is a constant juggle between being the leader and being a mum.

“She’s negotiating with this four-year-old about their underwear, and the kid’s refusing to put his underwear on,” Davies says. “She’s doing that, and then she picks up the phone, and the premier’s on the line. That’s a massive pivot.”

Should the Greens win the seats Sandell has her sights on this Saturday, she’ll have plenty more negotiating ahead of her.

Russian ship hit in Benghazi by suspected Ukrainian drone attack, say Libyan officials

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 18:50:56 GMT

No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said. Several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press.

The officials were affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

Authorities in divided Libya’s east said in a statement that the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries.

In a separate attack, another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi on Sunday evening, Libyan military sources told Reuters. Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible. “The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News also identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it was almost certainly destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Initial reports and footage suggest the Merkury was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.

Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port, which has a growing importance since it lost bases in Syria, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 18:45:30 GMT

Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Twenty-seven of those trusts are in such dire financial straits that they have rated lack of money as the biggest threat they face. Six have given that danger a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. A much-larger number of trusts have launched cost-cutting programmes to save as much as £106m each this year by limiting the services they provide and shrinking their workforces, despite understaffing being widespread across the NHS.

The six include King’s College hospital NHS trust in London, which is seeking to save £85m this year, and the St George’s, Epsom and St Helier hospital group, also in the capital, which has a savings target of £91m. The others are the North Midlands, Gloucestershire, and Doncaster and Bassetlaw acute trusts, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trust.

Trust bosses say their finances are in a “precarious” and “severe” state. They blame rising drug prices, strikes and the cost of covering pay rises, the extra demand caused by this summer’s heatwaves, and the introduction of electronic health records. Privately they accuse NHS England of forcing them to adopt unreasonable savings targets in order to help the health service as a whole balance its books, because hospitals have been told to stop overspending.

In an illustration of the impact that savings drives can have, in August people in Kent with cancer had to wait up to a month for appointments before they could start chemotherapy; this was because the cancer unit had fewer nurses on duty than usual after the East Kent trust cut rates of pay to work extra “bank” shifts as part of a cost-cutting plan, which led to understaffing.

The trust admitted in a paper, which its board discussed, that it was seeing “increasing waits for new patient appointments and pre-chemo appointments … due to lack of take-up of bank shifts due to [pay] rate changes”.

In September, York and Scarborough trust said it would shut a 28-bed ward at Bridlington community hospital, a “step-down” facility that looks after people recently discharged from hospital before they go home, to help it save £1m. It did so despite the risk this will add to pressures on beds at its two acute hospitals.

The trust also looked into withdrawing the maternity and radiology services it provided at Whitby community hospital as another of its “opportunities for efficiencies”, to save an estimated £200,000. However, those plans were “no longer being considered”, it said. It is also considering cutting the opening hours of the three urgent treatment centres it runs in York, Scarborough and Malton, to save a further £200,000, even though such services are intended to prevent overcrowding of A&E units. The trust refused to answer questions the Guardian asked about that.

Harrogate and district trust has decided to stop providing out-of-hours GP care in Hambleton and Richmond, covering a large swathe of rural North Yorkshire, after 15 years because it can no longer afford to do so. It is unclear who will offer patients that service in the future.

Sherwood Forest trust’s plan to close a hydrotherapy pool at King’s Mill hospital in Sutton-in-Ashfield, to save £150,000 to £200,000, has provoked an outcry. The pool is used to help rehabilitate about 1,500 patients a year, including those with long-term health conditions or those recovering from car crashes or a hip replacement, said the local Labour MP, Steve Yemm.

Sara Hazzard, of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy, said: “The proposed closing of this pool is deeply concerning and risks depriving vulnerable patients of vital specialist rehabilitation. For people with chronic long-term conditions, aquatic physiotherapy is a clinical lifeline. The warmth and buoyancy of the water help people to manage pain, exercise and maintain mobility when land-based rehabilitation may not be suitable.”

Sherwood Forest also recently admitted in a paper discussed by its board that “financial restraints, including the need to reduce bank and agency spend, may lead to impacts on ability to maintain patient care and safety”.

Torbay and South Devon trust is axing 199 non-clinical posts and charging staff more for parking and food to help it meet its £54.4m “cost improvement plan” target. It has an underlying deficit of £100m.

In a paper submitted to its 5 November board meeting, it said it would “assess all available options to close the forecast risk gap and deliver financial plan, including ‘unpalatable’ and high-risk options”. NHS England has told its leaders to break even this year or risk having their performance being reviewed, which could lead to them being replaced.

The NHS is so short of cash that it cannot afford to have the number of beds it needs to help hospitals cope this winter, Emma Rowland, NHS England’s executive director for performance and recovery, told MPs earlier this month.

One trust boss said: “I have been a [trust] chief executive for more than 10 years and the NHS’s finances are as tough as they have ever been. Many trusts are forecasting deficits larger than recent years. Balancing the books often means breakeven. Very few trusts will break even and many will miss their financial plan for this year.”

Trusts are also cutting jobs in a desperate effort to save money. For example, Nottingham university hospitals trust plans to shrink its workforce by 1,279 to help it meet its £106m savings target for 2026-27. It admits that a third of its identified savings are “high risk”.

Similarly, Barts health trust in London aims to axe 1,100 posts to save money.

Dr Tony O’Sullivan, a co-chair of the campaign group Keep Our NHS Public, said: “This financial straitjacket on the NHS is deeply irresponsible and the consequences are devastating. Years of underinvestment have left trusts being asked to make huge savings while demand and costs keep rising.

“AI can’t staff a ward, and another reorganisation won’t reopen a single bed. Closing step-down beds means some patients will spend longer in hospital waiting for somewhere safe to go. That leaves fewer beds for people waiting in A&E and makes it harder to carry out planned operations.”

O’Sullivan added that Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, should ask the chancellor for emergency funding for the NHS to help it cope with the pressure it is under. The Department of Health and Social Care’s total spending for 2025-26 was £217bn, most of which went to the NHS.

NHS England did not respond directly to a request for comment over the widespread cost-cutting. A spokesperson said: “The NHS did an amazing job last year to bring its finances in within budget for the first time in more than a decade, while also delivering record levels of treatments and operations to patients.

“This has been another challenging year, and NHS boards are rightly being transparent about financial risks and taking action to mitigate them. Across the NHS, organisations are working hard to improve productivity, live within their means and make the best use of taxpayers’ money, while continuing to deliver the care people need.”

Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 18:42:34 GMT

Harlequins 21-48 Bristol

Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club

As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope and she was dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her Bristol debut. The full-back did it under significant pressure too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener.

The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old, and if her debut is anything to go by he will be proved right. The World Cup winner not only scored two tries but was also a linchpin in Bristol’s attack. Her gamechanging reputation was felt among her former teammates as she drew multiple defenders to her whenever she had the ball, meaning the wings on her outside had a lot more joy. The back three looked formidable with both wings, Reneeqa Bonner and Millie David, also scoring two tries apiece.

Lawson was “reluctant to single out individuals” because of a “strong team performance” but he said on Kildunne and the back three: “Ellie joined us in the summer and there were a lot of headlines around that, but for us it is about getting a happy squad that wants to work hard. You saw that out there today.

“The firepower we have and have now got is there for people to see. The pleasing thing for me was you name that team and everyone thinks: ‘What an explosive back three, what a great front five,’ and they fronted up and delivered.”

Kildunne’s move was not the highest profile signing of the off-season with Ruby Tui joining Ealing Trailfinders, who won the PWR Cup and claimed the first league win of the season when they beat Loughborough in the PWR curtain raiser on Friday night. The England full-back’s return to the Stoop, though, is up there with the biggest stories of the opening weekend with Sale’s first victory over three-time PWR winners Gloucester-Hartpury and Saracens racking up 100 points against Leicester also among the top headlines.

Walking out on to the pitch in west London, the England internationals Lark Atkin-Davies and Abbie Ward, who returned to the pitch during the PWR Cup after giving birth in June and July respectively, were carrying their daughters. Both World Cup winners looked as if they had never been away from the game, with the scrum a particular highlight for Bristol and the prop Hannah Botterman’s performance was also impressive.

The hosts struggled defensively but their captain, Marlie Packer, who joined from Saracens in the summer, had a good debut. Packer, who is a new mother again too after her partner, Rosie Galligan, gave birth last month, asterisked the result by saying: “It’s the first game of the season.”

She added: “I think we need to make better decisions. We were really confrontational at times and other times we let it off. For me, I think there are learnings, and roll on next week.”

After a scrappy start from both sides it was Quins who were first over, through Maja Mueller. Bristol hit back with Bonner muscling her way through and Kildunne was next to score, though the former World Rugby player of the year withheld any celebration at her old stamping ground.

Bonner added her second, as did Kildunne, to put Bristol 22-14 up at the break, but three missed conversions from the fly-half Meryl Smith gave Quins hope of a comeback.

Bristol extended their lead as the second half got under way with a well-worked score for Millie Hyett. Quins fought back with a try for Ella Cromack, whose perfect kicking from the tee continued as she converted her own score, but while a close battle ensued, Bristol secured an away bonus-point win.

The second round of the PWR will take place next weekend, with Harlequins travelling to Ealing to play Trailfinders in a London derby, while Bristol host Exeter. The Bears will be buoyed up by their performance at the Stoop, especially after a poor season last campaign, where they finished eighth.

Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 18:35:14 GMT

Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at ­Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for ­denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liver­pool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s history.

“Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.

• Accounting for 3pts/win all-time, Manchester United’s eight points this season are their fewest after 11 games of a league campaign since 1972-73 (7). That is also the previous season in which the Red Devils managed only one win through their first 11 league matches.

• Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) suffered the joint-heaviest defeat by a Manchester United manager in his first game (0-4), along with a defeat by the same scoreline for Lal Hilditch in October 1926 (0-4 v Bolton Wanderers in the top flight).

• Manchester United end the day in 19th position in the Premier League, with this the first time since November 1986 that they have been within the bottom two places of the league table having played at least 10 matches (21st in that case).

• Mauricio Pochettino was the first manager in Premier League history to see his team concede twice and receive a red card in the first half of his first match in charge of a club. Opta

That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that quickly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool, under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.

De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

Pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

Liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

The first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.

Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. ­Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from the £116m recruit. ­Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. ­Barcola turned provider in ­devastating style, however, to ­create the goal that Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.

Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend, the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

• Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Liverpool's four wins by 4+ goals against Manchester United are the most any Premier League team has achieved against another across all competitions.

• Andoni Iraola is unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against Manchester United (W3 D4). The only manager to record a longer unbeaten run against the Red Devils in the competition is Jürgen Klopp (8 between 2018 and 2022).

• This was the quickest Liverpool had gone 2-0 up in a Premier League match against Manchester United, going two ahead after just 12 minutes and 40 seconds.

• Rio Ngumoha (18y 85d) became the youngest player to score and assist in a Premier League game for Liverpool since Michael Owen on Boxing Day 1997 (18y 12d v Leeds United).

• Dominik Szoboszlai (pictured) scored his fifth direct free kick for Liverpool in the Premier League; only Jamie Redknapp (8), Steven Gerrard (7) and Trent Alexander-Arnold (6) have netted more for the club in the competition.

• Florian Wirtz created 10 chances in open play for Liverpool, the most by a player in a Premier League match since Manchester City’s David Silva against West Brom in March 2015 (11). Opta

Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 18:06:58 GMT

The summit’s failure was due to a refusal to admit we cannot confront the climate crisis without shifting to renewables

The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned.

“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.”

The Australian president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, did not quite apologise for the failure. “Unfortunately we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision,” he told journalists outside the hall. “And that’s disappointing, very disappointing.”

For two weeks, ministers and high-level officials from 190 countries laboured over a few pages of convoluted text, only to produce, at the end, almost nothing. What was proposed as the main outcome, the prematurely named “Antalya pact”, inviting countries to electrify their economies and address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond 1.5C above preindustrial levels, was abandoned after a lengthening roll call of countries rejected it, during the final dramatic meeting on Sunday afternoon.

The collapse was almost unprecedented in the long history of Cops, because it was so clearcut. Other conferences have produced mediocre outcomes, but usually tried to salvage some face-saving semblance of unity at the end. But after a marathon final negotiating session that carried on more than 40 hours beyond its scheduled end, a small group of countries led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept an outcome that mentioned the need to “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Normally, as Cops proceed by consensus and even a few holdouts can change the outcome, that refusal would have been enough to force through a weakened final compromise that excised such commitments in favour of the presidencies’ preferred wording, referring only to an “irreversible transition towards lower greenhouse gas emissions”.

Instead, a large group of other countries led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries, decided they would not accept such a weak deal. When it came their turn to take the microphone, each in turn declared their objections – close to 40 countries registered objections or refusals.

Irene Vélez Torres, a former Colombian environment minister who earlier this year chaired a conference of 57 countries on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said this was the right outcome. “This Cop has failed, not because there are no pathways to advance climate action, but because there has been an attempt to erase from the final decision a reality that science has demonstrated and a growing number of countries already recognise: there is no way to confront the climate crisis without ending our dependence on fossil fuels,” she said.

Yet the developed countries that led the charge are riven with contradictions over the issue, as Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, pointed out. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow.”

In place of the cover decision, there was agreement on some side issues, including a “just transition mechanism” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to the low-carbon economy, which was decried as toothless by campaigners. Commitments on finance to help the poor and vulnerable cope with the impacts of the climate crisis were sidelined.

Tasneem Essop, the executive director of Climate Action Network, cried foul. “This was the worst Cop ever,” she said. “We are witnessing human suffering on an unimaginable scale, and we had hoped this Cop would take steps to protect people from the worsening climate crisis. Instead, rich nations gutted the very measures that could have made a difference. Negotiating room after negotiating room, developed countries systematically blocked measures that would require them to provide finance to protect people’s lives and address the climate crisis.”

The result also threatens the “multilateralism” on which Cops depend, which is crucial for many of the smallest nations and disadvantaged groups. For them, Cops are the only forum in which they can confront the authors of the fossil fuel crisis – the rich nations and petro states which have benefited from coal, oil and gas up to now.

“Despite the discouragement we feel today, we will keep betting on multilateralism,” said Juan Carlos Jintiach Arcos, the executive secretary of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities. “We start from a clear premise: multilateralism is not built by political leaders alone. We remain hopeful that the world’s governments will find the courage to join us in this fight.”

The question now is how the world can put this right. For that, what is happening outside the windowless air-conditioned conference halls of Cop may be far more important than any Cop decision, or lack of one.

Renewable power has overtaken coal in China, reaching 60% of generation capacity, investment in clean energy around the world is twice that into fossil fuels, and electric vehicles have taken off, making up a third of new car sales in Europe and a majority in many other countries around the world, from China to Vietnam, Singapore and Iceland.

As Bowen said, in his final address: “The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable. It’s happening, it’s happening at speed, and it’s irreversible.”

Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:49:12 GMT

Laura Brand says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand

Russell Brand’s wife, Laura, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Russell Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

Laura Brand began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”

She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” she said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”

In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Laura Brand read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.

The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.

That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the last year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.

On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

Peter Fluck obituary

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:47:04 GMT

Artist and caricaturist who co-created the hugely popular ITV satire Sptting Image with Roger Law

Peter Fluck, who has died aged 85, was, with his fellow artist Roger Law, half of the Fluck & Law partnership that revived satire on TV with Spitting Image, the ITV puppet sketch show lampooning celebrities, politicians and the royal family.

Two decades after the BBC’s That Was the Week That Was spoofed the British establishment and, in particular, the last days of Harold Macmillan’s Conservative government at the time of the John Profumo affair, Spitting Image, from 1984 to 1996, mined another period of Tory rule rich in distinctive characters, exaggerating elements of their personalities.

Margaret Thatcher was portrayed as domineering, aggressive and, as time went on, increasingly tyrannical, verging on madness; Norman Tebbit as a tough thug in a leather jacket; Geoffrey Howe as dull; Nigel Lawson as incompetent and a panicker; Cecil Parkinson as a playboy; and Douglas Hurd with a Mr Whippy hairstyle.

When John Major took over as prime minister from Thatcher, he was not only represented as colourless and dull, eating peas, but physically painted grey all over.

The leaders of opposition parties, Neil Kinnock and David Steel, were treated just as cruelly, while Ronald Reagan was seen as genial, elderly and dangerous, and big names of the time – from Mick Jagger and Ian Botham to Rupert Murdoch and Laurence Olivier – made the celebrity lampooning all-embracing.

Most controversial in the early days was the inclusion of the royal family, including a gin-soaked Queen Mother, and Queen Elizabeth II always wearing a tiara, even under her headscarf.

In creating each puppet, Fluck produced a drawing from photographs, making it a recognisable caricature, before the pair developed a clay head and sculpted the facial features.

“I’m quicker when it comes to putting a likeness down on paper, but Roger Law is faster at breaking down a likeness in clay than I am,” said Fluck. “We kept turning the clay mould around on the board, switching it between us until we suddenly decided it was finished.”

From this, the puppets’ heads were cast in foam latex, with bodies mostly of foam. In front of the camera, facial features were operated by a system of wires, rods and cables devised by Fluck.

The pair met at the end of the 1950s as students at the Cambridge School of Art (now Anglia Ruskin University), where a part-time tutor was Paul Hogarth, an “artist-reporter” whose paintings and illustrations depicted events from the Spanish civil war, apartheid South Africa and other countries on his travels. He inspired in Fluck and Law an interest in political caricature.

After creating grotesque plasticine models of public figures, which were then photographed, for the Economist, the Sunday Times Magazine and others, they were approached by the graphic designer and branding expert Martin Lambie-Nairn in 1981 about bringing their characters to life on TV. Fluck and Law decided that would be best with puppets.

John Lloyd, after producing the BBC’s live-action satirical sketch show Not the Nine O’Clock News, helped to pitch what was originally titled Spit N Image to broadcasters. LWT, Thames Television, the BBC and Channel 4 all turned it down before the ITV company Central Independent Television took it on.

With Lloyd as producer, Spitting Image was launched and, after a shaky start, it captured the public’s imagination and won an International Emmy award two years running (1985 and 1986).

But it was an expensive programme to make and, by 1996, audiences had fallen from 15 to 6 million, so it was axed.

Returning to being a full-time artist and sculptor, Fluck showed no interest in being part of a Spitting Image revival for the joint ITV-BBC subscription channel BritBox in 2020, when Law returned to lead the creative team.

Born in Cambridge, to Ada (nee Hughes) and Herbert Fluck, a gardener at Magdalene College, Peter grew up birdwatching and drawing stuffed birds at the university’s Museum of Zoology. Leaving Cambridgeshire high school for boys aged 16 with “four rather miserable O-levels”, he started studying at Cambridge School of Art and reflected that Hogarth helped to guide him and Law “into the politicised 1960s”, when they marched with CND and helped with its promotional material, designing pamphlets and making woodcuts.

The pair moved to London and became freelance illustrators, with Fluck supplementing his income by teaching at Hornsey (now part of Middlesex University) and Colchester schools of art.

They then worked together on 2D and 3D plasticine models. These were photographed for publications such as Private Eye, the New Statesman, glossy magazines and newspaper colour supplements, and even seen in Germany in Stern and Der Spiegel, and the US in Time and the New York Times.

In 1976, the year in which they formalised their partnership as Fluck & Law, working from a defunct temperance mission hall in Cambridge, they produced a Radio Times front cover of an “all-American family”, including dog, engrossed watching television to promote programmes marking the American bicentennial.

Following the end of Spitting Image, Fluck moved to Cornwall and, living in a cliff-top house in a fishing village, worked and exhibited as an artist whose creations included mobiles, ceramics, interactive installations and sculptural pieces.

In 1963, Fluck married Anne-Cécile de Bruyne. She and their son and daughter survive him.

Peter Nigel Fluck, artist, born 7 April 1941; died 21 November 2026

Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:32:14 GMT

Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review

A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped.

The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister.

Its conclusions, shaped with the input of disability rights advocates, are understood to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which called for a series of changes, particularly to the system of assessment, to take better account of conditions that vary over time.

This would involve significant changes to Pip, which is intended to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability. An interim report by Timms’ committee described the benefit as widely valued but “no longer fit for purpose”.

However, it would retain the system for all ages, while last week’s report by Alan Milburn on worklessness among young people called for it to be scrapped for adults under 25 and replaced by an “additional cost allowance”, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.

Government officials have pushed back on the idea of a clash, saying Milburn’s review was commissioned after the Timms process had begun, and that about 90% of the Pip caseload involves people over 25.

But with Timms’ recommendations understood to be quite broad, Burnham and his ministers will need to make a series of decisions about what comes next, on a deeply sensitive subject. Keir Starmer was forced to abandon planned changes in 2025 after a rebellion by Labour MPs.

There was widespread shock among disability campaigners and charities at the Milburn report’s recommendations to scrap Pip and universal credit health benefit payments for under-25s as part of efforts to boost jobs and training for young people not in education, employment or training.

The review steering group is co-chaired by Timms and the disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, and most of its 12 members have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions.

There are reportedly worries among some members of the Timms review board over the scale of Milburn’s proposals on Pip, which would cut £3.6bn from spending on young people. “Some members are really concerned,” one source told the Guardian.

The report will include short-term overhauls, within the current spending round, and longer-term ones. Many of the specifics for the latter would need to be decided by ministers before they legislate next year.

Burnham faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. He has said this is his plan but he has pushed back against the idea of what he called “crude cuts”, saying these often just created costs elsewhere.

The Timms review, framed by ministers as a groundbreaking “co-produced” policy initiative, was seen as an attempt to restore trust among disabled people after the collapse of the Pip plans under Starmer, which were based on £5bn in cuts.

The interim report in July and further emerging findings in September confirmed a consensus view that Pip was unfit for purpose and that a major overhaul was needed to make the benefit fair, humane and efficient.

It raised the prospect that some claimants could in future receive “in kind” awards such as services, aid or training alongside basic cash awards.

But it underlined that cash payments were “the foundation” of a future reformed disability benefit, that it would not be means-tested and that any “reformed benefit will be designed with disabled people and those with long-term health conditions, and tested to make sure it works before it is rolled out”. There was no mention of scrapping Pip for under-25s or any other age groups.

Until recently, most disability charities had been optimistic that the Timms review – the remit of which did not include the costs of Pip or potential cuts in spending – would lead to much-needed changes and improve the lives of the 4 million adults who claim it.

But the timing and scope of the Milburn review, which has been conspicuously welcomed by ministers, has dented that confidence.

A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “The Timms review interim report made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose. When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”

The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:30:32 GMT

Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values

Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities.

Beyond that, the unique nature of the moment suggests a journey without political maps. The new government will have a substantial majority. But it will be made up of novices, and the broad nature of the coalition assembled to defeat Mr Vučić comprises figures from the right as well as the liberal left. A governing programme published for the campaign tends to deal mainly in general principles, and although the students have said they intend to exercise a form of oversight over parliamentary decision-making, it remains unclear how that will play out in practice.

The direction of travel in relation to stalled European Union accession talks, which began in 2012, is more easily discernible. At an EU enlargement forum last week, the Student List MP Aleksandar Baucal received a standing ovation after pledging that rule-of-law reforms to which Mr Vučić paid only cynical lip-service would be fast-tracked. But for now there appears little prospect of the new government signing up to key EU foreign policy commitments, such as the recognition of Kosovo’s independence and support for sanctions on Russia.

Brussels should be patient on the geopolitics and generous in terms of investment and support, as Serbia’s new leaders focus their attention on domestic reform. A recent poll found that 42% of Student List supporters saw a closer relationship with the EU as the best way to protect Serbia’s interests, compared with 9% who opted for Russia and China. But after effectively tolerating Mr Vučić’s authoritarian excesses in a failed effort to woo him away from Vladimir Putin’s influence, European leaders must seize the opportunity to deepen links with a movement that genuinely shares its democratic values. The benefits of enhanced partnership with a country that sends two-thirds of its exports into the EU can become the gateway to alignment in other areas.

In 2000, a similar wave of student-led protests eventually led to the toppling of Slobodan Milošević and the election of a more orthodox coalition government committed to reform. A rising star under Milošević, Mr Vučić then spent the last 14 years reversing the progress made. His ousting and the tenacity and courage of the student movement have become symbols of gen Z ambitions across Europe for a new political settlement. The EU must do all it can to help ensure that, this time, Serbia’s democratic revolution is irreversible.
