The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 17:25:32 GMT

The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

But 12 months after the introduction of a report card to replace the old grades, Ofsted’s critics remain frustrated. The National Association of Head Teachers tried to challenge the revised framework in the high court. Two-thirds of teachers who responded to a survey said that the new inspections were as bad or worse than the old ones. In October the education secretary, Lucy Powell, said that further reforms were on the way. (After devolution in 1999, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland rejected England’s model of school competition, academies and league tables.)

If, as expected, the framework is adjusted to take more account of a school’s context, and to ease workload pressures, that will be a good result. Analysis shows that schools in England with more deprived intakes are much less likely than schools with low deprivation to meet expected standards. This raises questions about whether inspections fairly account for the challenges facing schools in poorer areas. As well as being wrong in principle, a framework skewed against demanding socioeconomic conditions has practical effects, lowering morale in schools that are judged to be underachieving, and potentially making it harder for them to recruit staff.

The Department for Education and Ofsted must take responsibility for such missteps, and for an inspection regime that many now find more onerous. Advocates of more radical reforms, whose goal is a less adversarial alternative to Ofsted, should be listened to as part of this process. Peer review between schools can be a constructive route to improvement. Local authorities already monitor standards in the schools they oversee, as do academy trusts – although their highly uneven results offer some of the best evidence of the need for an independent inspectorate with a focus on governance as well as other aspects. Resource pressures must also be considered; the current level of funding does not enable the kind of exchange between inspectors and schools that some would like.

It is shocking and tragic that Ofsted needed a coroner’s warning to seemingly recognise its duty to treat school staff with courtesy and respect. The new framework, evidence suggests, remains flawed. Ms Powell must ensure that inspections help schools improve, rather than merely find fault.

Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 16:14:46 GMT

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels

The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”

Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.

Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.

But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “I am deeply disappointed that Cop31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 16:12:54 GMT

Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of the, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe” and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.

The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.

In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.

This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.

A new constituency-level poll on Brexit sentiment found that hundreds of previously leave-backing areas, including Burnham’s Makerfield seat, now support rejoining.

Of the 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, it found that voters in 512 would rejoin the EU, with 47 too close to call. Just 73 areas – slightly over 11% of the total – still want to stay out.

For the Conservatives, the battle has not ended. Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday. Her deputy, Alex Burghart, has already promised that a future Tory government would unpick it.

But make no mistake, Europe is no longer the Conservatives’ defining political thread, and division, as it was for several decades. May might, understandably, be unable to move on from the issue that made her PM and then destroyed her career. But her party, like the country, has no choice.

McBurnie’s added-time double snatches win for Hull to shock 10-man Brighton

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 16:10:48 GMT

Amid the talk of Brighton being surprise title contenders this season, these are perhaps the afternoons which show the margin that still exists, and how the Premier League can provide the most punishing of wake-up calls at any moment.

Make no mistake about it, Fabian Hürzeler’s side will play far worse than this over the next few months and win. They are still second in the table. How they left Hull without even a point almost defies belief given the dominance they enjoyed for large parts of the contest. But for all the statement victories and the headline-grabbing moments, these games are the ones which can trip you up the most.

A blisteringly cold November afternoon in Hull, against a promoted side where the expectation for a team challenging for the title is to win, and perhaps win with minimum fuss, too. On another afternoon, Brighton may have done just that, were it not for the heroics of Hull’s goalkeeper, Konstantinos Tzolakis.

But the best teams, the ones that end the seasons lifting the silverware, almost always seem to find a way. Tzolakis was the Seagulls’ scourge with a string of sensational saves that kept Hull in a contest where, for large periods, they were struggling to keep their heads above water.

However, the goal Brighton deserved never arrived – and as this game wore on you wondered if a team like Hull, whose commitment can never be questioned and who are tough to beat on their own turf, could dig in for long enough to provide a sucker punch on the counter. That moment arrived, not perhaps with Oli McBurnie’s goal that broke the deadlock in stoppage time, but two minutes before.

When João Costinha was shown a second yellow card in the 89th minute for a foul on Sorba Thomas, the MKM Stadium responded. They sensed that Tzolakis’s heroics could perhaps produce more than just a point, with Brighton forced to sit in and try to hold out for the closing moments. Hull surged forward, with McBurnie bundling home from close to range to spark delirium among the home support.

Two minutes later, with Brighton now left pressing just to try to find an equaliser, Hull caught them cold and McBurnie would tap into an empty net to seal the most unlikely of victories for the Tigers, who remain unbeaten at home since promotion. This was their first win since August, however, and a welcome tonic to put breathing space between themselves and the bottom three.

“We played against an excellent team who play intensive football,” Hull’s manager, Sergej Jakirovic, said. “I wish this feeling would never stop because we’ve had to wait for this.” But this was an afternoon that was as much about Brighton as it was Hull.

A win here would have closed the gap to Arsenal at the top to three points. In the end, this was a huge missed opportunity, with Hürzeler understandably crestfallen post-match.

“In the Premier League you can never expect to win,” he said. “For us, it’s very important with our identity and every game you have to lift your standards. If you drop, the Premier League is too good and it will punish you.”

Two minutes later, Georginio Rutter was the next to be denied by the Greece international with another smart save before the pick of the bunch: Tzolakis made a reaction save with his foot to turn Gómez’s effort wide after Brighton cut Hull open at will again. At that stage it felt like when, not if, the visitors went ahead. Nobody told Tzolakis that.

Half-time did little to change the flow of momentum. Pascal Gross was next to be denied by Tzolakis before Gómez then shot wide from six yards out. At the other end, Hull were showing signs of coming to life, with two Mohamed Belloumi breaks a warning sign of what was to follow for the visitors.

Tzolakis was finally beaten by Charalampos Kostoulas when his chipped effort beat his fellow countryman, but Regan Slater was on hand to clear off the line. Then, as time ebbed away, Costinha’s second yellow decisively swung the momentum and within two minutes, Hull scored the goal Brighton had craved.

First, McBurnie bundled home before Belloumi’s break led to him squaring for the Scotland international to tap into an empty net. Was it what Brighton deserved? Probably not. But try persuading anyone of a Hull persuasion to care about that.

I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 16:00:31 GMT

What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful

I’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

Mortifyingly, notice he did not. Even when I told him, “You’re a classic!” and laughed “Haha I know right” with nary a comma.

There was worse to come. Because that-which-shall-eventually-rule could tell I’d used its proposed sentences, it was encouraged, and proposed more, which I was tutting and scoffing at until it recommended a reply that ended with the nickname I call my husband. Not darling, honey, or whatever – something unique.

A chill descended in my soul as the penny dropped that these weren’t generic phrases everyone gets – they were specific. My phone was impersonating me, showing me who I really was, and – long story short – I was awful. Cheesy, exclamation-mark-addicted, and full of bantz with a definite z.

Humbled in a way it is probably impossible to ever fully recover from, I realised that in conducting this experiment, I had utilised the very artificial intelligence I was battling to remove just hours before. I’d hate-used it, yes, but I’d used it all the same. Further proof, not that it was needed, that resistance is futile. Luckily I surrendered immediately and have always been fully on board with AI, so when the day comes, I’ll be absolutely fine. Haha I know right.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

The stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth sustained a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.

Rivals author Jilly Cooper accused of ‘extensive and deliberate plagiarism’

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 15:07:42 GMT

Analysis reportedly finds striking similarities in dialogue and narrative structure between late author’s novel, Prudence, and two of her contemporaries

Jilly Cooper has been accused of plagiarising the works of two other novelists.

The bestselling author’s fifth romance series novel, Prudence, published in 1978, allegedly includes several plagiarised passages from The Serial by Cyra McFadden and The Franchise Affair by Josephine Tey.

According to a report in the Observer, Cooper, who died last October, committed “what appears to be extensive and deliberate plagiarism” by lifting at least 35 passages from The Serial alone.

McFadden’s daughter, Caroline McFadden, told the publication: “To steal her work so extensively and to profit off it is unconscionable.”

She said she was considering legal action, saying: “It absolutely boils my blood to think of someone stealing my mother’s work because I know how hard she worked at her craft.

“I will be looking at legal options as this can’t be allowed to stand. I sincerely hope that all of Dame Cooper’s work will be scrutinised to see if this was a pattern of hers and other talented authors’ work stolen.”

Cooper, who has sold more than 11m copies of her books in the UK alone, was given a damehood in the 2024 new year honours list for her services to literature and charity.

Disney+ is currently airing the second series of Rivals, the award-winning television adaptation of her most famous work. The show combines TV industry intrigue and racy sex scenes against the backdrop of the Cotswolds countryside in the fictional guise of Rutshire.

In its investigation, the Observer detailed 15 allegedly plagiarised passages from The Serial, which was first published from late 1975 as a weekly serialisation in a US newspaper before it was released as a book in May 1977.

In The Serial, McFadden, who died in 2024, created the off-and-on-again couple Kate and Harvey Holroyd, two progressives in California’s Marin County. The Observer noted several similarities with the dialogue in Cooper’s character, Berenice, an American feminist.

In The Serial, Kate says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open, loving relationship, based on growth and trust and sharing, and Harvey wanted his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we just weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

In Prudence, Berenice says of her ex-husband: “I wanted an open living relationship based on trust and growth, and all he wanted was his jockey shorts ironed. I mean we weren’t coming from the same place at all.”

The publication also cited another example from The Serial in which Harvey was offered lifestyle advice. The passage said: “Cut out the nine-to-five shit, Harv. You gotta get in touch with the universe. That’s the first step.”

In Prudence, Berenice offered similar advice. “You ought to cut out that nine to five shit … And get in touch with the universe.”

The Observer said it began looking at Prudence after a reader pointed out similarities with a scene in Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair.

The publication alleged that Cooper “lifts directly” from chapter 22 of the novel “both in narrative architecture and in line-by-line choice of words”. Tey died in 1952 and left no heirs.

Cooper is said to have praised The Serial for its parody of the modern feminist in a 1982 Mail on Sunday column. She said she was “tremendously comforted” when she “came across a passage in the novel The Serial by Cyra McFadden, a marvellously funny send-up of American trendies in the late seventies”.

An inquest held last year concluded that Cooper suffered a fatal head injury in a fall at her Gloucestershire home. She was found by family on 4 October 2025 and died in hospital the following day.

The Guardian has contacted Cooper’s agent, Felicity Blunt at Curtis Brown, and her publisher, Penguin, for comment. The Observer said both had declined to provide a comment.

Unfortunately, cold weather rarely lives up to the fairytale in my head. The reality is often thermostat battles, dry skin, chapped lips, thick practical jackets covering cool outfits, and answering the door to the postman dressed in a shamefully crusty blanket hoodie.

How did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 15:00:30 GMT

Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the US in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as here

Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the country in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as North Carolina.

Democrats flipped a US Senate seat for the first time since 2008, as well as five House seats, one of which Cook Political Report had rated “solid” Republican, and four others considered “likely” Republican. Democrats also held power in the state’s first district, which Republicans had targeted in a redistricting effort.

One of the seats Democrats flipped belonged to Richard Hudson, a representative who led House Republicans’ re-election efforts as the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. It was the first time an NRCC chair had ever lost a general election.

As of Monday, the Associated Press hadn’t called four of the House races, but two were leaning in favor of Democrats.

North Carolina’s statehouse flipped for Democrats for the first time in more than a decade and Republicans are holding onto the state senate by a one-seat margin – which is currently headed to a recount.

This was all in a state that had only voted for one Democratic presidential candidate since 1980, and hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 20 years. So how did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?

“They took voters for granted,” said Anderson Clayton, the 28-year-old chair of the North Carolina Democratic party.

“They thought they could gerrymander themselves into having a seat and not actually have to go out and fight for it, and I think voters looked at them and said: ‘That’s not how we roll. That’s not how it works in North Carolina.’”

Clayton, who has been working to flip North Carolina blue since she was elected in 2023, points to multiple factors this election cycle: Trump’s unpopularity fueling North Carolinians’ frustrations with the current status quo, and a fleet of younger candidates running for office.

But she emphasized Republicans’ failure to address issues affecting voters, especially in North Carolina’s rural districts, as one of the top reasons.

As an example, she pointed to a recent quote from Donny Lambeth, a seven-term Republican state representative, who lost by eight percentage points.

Lambeth told the New York Times that he mistakenly listened to members of his caucus who told him he was in a “safe district” and did not need to spend “any money”. In 2024, Lambeth had won by approximately 14 percentage points.

“I was like: ‘Well, did you go out and talk to any of your voters?’” Clayton said in response to Lambeth’s admission. “‘Like, did you actually speak to somebody on the ground in your district?’”

Felice Pete, an RNC committee member from North Carolina and longtime Republican activist, acknowledged Republicans’ shortcomings.

“You have places where we didn’t think we’re going to lose, like Virginia Foxx, and looking back, people took it for granted. These were safe, red counties. And it’s just getting out the vote effort,” Pete said.

The Associated Press has not called Foxx’s race in North Carolina’s fifth congressional district because of an ongoing recount, but her Democratic opponent, Chuck Hubbard, is ahead by a thin but likely insurmountable margin.

“The 2024 win for Republicans was not done with traditional Republicans,” Pete said. “They were first-time voters, they were independents, there were a lot of young minority men, a lot of young college-aged men.”

“I just think, with redistricting, we just did not have the effort focused with getting out the votes,” Pete said.

Republicans had invested time, money and energy into maintaining their majority through redistricting, under pressure from the US president. They redrew lines to try to flip the first congressional district, but it didn’t work; the incumbent Democrat, Don Davis, held onto his seat.

Clayton accused Republicans of getting “elitist” in the midterms and relying too heavily on consultants – a criticism Democrats often face.

“Instead, you had real grassroots energy from Democrats that won seats that honestly, they shouldn’t have, in some ways, on Tuesday night,” Clayton said.

In parts of the state that are comfortably red, such as Davidson county, located in central North Carolina, the electorate moved 16 percentage points in favor of Democrats compared with 2024, according to NBC’s decision desk.

Christopher Jessup, the chair of the Davidson county Republican party and a longtime Republican advocate, said he wasn’t sure why that happened but attributed it to “probably some voter turnout”.

Jessup highlighted that his county still overwhelmingly voted for the Republican candidates in the midterms, and praised the work his colleagues and teams did. Despite that, the sixth congressional district, where Davidson county is located, flipped for Democrats.

When asked what the top issue for voters in the county was, Jessup said “a very negative view of Roy Cooper”.

Cooper, the former governor of North Carolina, defeated Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee and chosen directly by Trump, by nearly 20 percentage points.

Republicans had anticipated Cooper’s win. By October, the top Super Pac for Senate Republicans cancelled remaining ads that it had booked in the state.

Like many Republicans, Pete is still dissecting why messaging that won over North Carolinians in 2024 didn’t resonate in 2026. But she has some theories, starting with the fact that Trump 2024 voters felt “betrayed”.

“The word that I hear over and over is betrayal,” Pete said. “Many of those people felt like voting did not matter because they felt like 2024 was their last hope to have this correction, and then they go, and here we are.”

Pete pointed to Trump’s campaign promise not to start more wars, which he failed to deliver on when he started a conflict with Iran in February. That conflict, which Congress never formally approved, has pushed gas and diesel prices up, causing a chain reaction that has affected other everyday costs, such as groceries.

She added that messaging that won voters over in 2024 “started to shift” or wasn’t being communicated well from “some higher-ups, or even our administration”. That includes mass deportations; during his campaign, Trump promised to target every undocumented immigrant, but administration officials now claim they target undocumented immigrants with violent criminal histories.

Citing a personal example, Pete said the young men that she gathered to go out door-knocking in 2024 did not want to work for the 2026 midterms; she called the experience “a microcosm of what happened”.

“We have to have an honest assessment of that and just the detriment of not fulfilling, or seemingly fulfilling, the promises you make,” Pete said.

The footballer-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 15:00:29 GMT

Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms

Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich.

The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace. In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “Tolstoy enigma”.

Strangest of all was what he learned after an internet search: the source of the interest was Gustavo Scarpa, a 32-year-old Brazilian footballer.

“I’ve been named the best player in the Brazilian league [in 2022] and won two Copa Libertadores titles [South America’s equivalent of the Champions League, in 2020 and 2021], and I’ve never felt as famous as I do now – and not because of football, but because of my book recommendations,” Scarpa said in an interview at the training ground of his team, Atlético Mineiro.

The left-footed attacking midfielder had a six-month spell at Nottingham Forest in 2023 before returning to Brazil to join Atlético Mineiro, one of the country’s most popular clubs.

But Scarpa is now enjoying a second life as a “BookTuber”. His recommendations regularly go viral in his country – and had already sent The Death of Ivan Ilyich to the top of Amazon Brazil’s overall sales ranking before inspiring the excitement at Scatolaro’s bookshop in neighbouring Argentina, which, unlike Brazil, is not even a Portuguese-speaking country.

His literary fame has grown so much that in late October he was invited to be one of the presenters at Brazil’s leading literary awards and, for one night, swapped his kit and boots for a suit, tie and dress shoes to present the newly created Reading Promotion category, for influencers who encourage the habit. Perhaps next year he will be among the nominees.

“This is all fascinating,” said Alicia Klein, a sports columnist for the website UOL. “It’s almost a social experiment: will people listen if a classic of Russian literature is recommended by a footballer? They clearly did – and they liked it!”

What makes it even more striking, in her opinion, is that Brazilian footballers often come from poor backgrounds, with limited access to education, and that even those who had better opportunities “mostly choose to remain disengaged” from social or cultural debates.

She wondered whether, in a country where more than half the population has not read a single book in the previous three months, Scarpa’s influence could be an “antidote” to that of global star Neymar, who is now struggling as a player at Brazil’s Santos but is still highly active on social media, promoting everything from frozen food to car insurance.

“Footballers are role models for a lot of children. While Neymar was advertising betting companies [before they were banned in Brazil], Scarpa was recommending books,” said Klein.

Scarpa said his passion for books came late in life. Raised in the interior of São Paulo state, he had barely read anything beyond the books assigned at school and the Bible – twice – as he became an evangelical Christian, as most players in Brazil are.

After emerging at Rio de Janeiro’s Fluminense, he moved to São Paulo’s Palmeiras, where in 2019 a fitness coaching intern said that for every goal or assist Scarpa registered, he would give him a book. There would be plenty of them to come over what became the best years of his career.

“I would read even while walking around the training ground; before matches, the other players would be listening to music, and I’d be off in a corner with my headphones on, reading,” said Scarpa, who admits some teammates would occasionally tease him for it.

He began reviewing books with short, humorous captions on his Instagram account. On Niccolò Machiavelli’s The Prince: “liked this one. Didn’t find it as controversial as people said”. Franz Kafka’s The Trial was “incomprehensible, but cool”. Stephen Hawking’s Brief Answers to the Big Questions was “pretty cool”, too – “even though we disagree on a few things LOL”.

His reviews had already attracted curiosity in the Brazilian press but really took off when, while recovering from an injury, he began recording them on video for social media and his YouTube channel.

It coincided with a good run for Atlético Mineiro, which may have helped more fans embrace his BookTubing. A group of them created Galeitura – a play on the Portuguese words “galo”, meaning rooster, the club’s mascot, and “leitura”, meaning reading – and then a book club that also organises donations and activities in schools. With more than 130,000 followers on social media it has now inspired supporters of other clubs to do the same.

“A lot of people came to us saying they had never read a book or that they didn’t like reading, but had started because of Scarpa,” said one of Galeitura’s organisers, 22-year-old literature student Carolina Marques Martins. “And some also said they thought The Death of Ivan Ilyich would be much harder to read than it actually was.”

Vladimir Tolstoy, the author’s great-grandson and director-general of the Leo Tolstoy State Museum in Moscow, recently recorded a video thanking Scarpa, saying his “popularity has allowed Tolstoy’s work to become a bestseller in your beautiful country”.

Other recent Scarpa recommendations include Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God and William Golding’s Lord of the Flies; when we spoke at the training ground he was reading Art Spiegelman’s The Complete Maus.

His favourite genre is “self-destruction”, he said. “Like Dostoevsky – something a bit difficult; not melancholic, but about internal conflicts.” His favourite book? Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables.

He said he had persuaded five teammates to start reading, while the coach, Eduardo Domínguez, an Argentinian, said Scarpa’s book recommendations were helping him learn Portuguese.

“I’ve been in football for more than 20 years, and I know how passionate fans can get, to the point of killing someone simply for supporting a different club,” said Scarpa. “So to see rival fans coming together around reading, inspired by a movement that was itself inspired by me, is incredibly rewarding.”

Manchester City’s WSL title bid hit by Spurs after Vinberg and Naz’s late double

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 14:59:23 GMT

This most unpredictable and evenly contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive defeat, by virtue of a terrific performance from a Tottenham side who moved within three points of the European places.

The shock result came just 24 hours after City’s title rivals Chelsea had dropped points at Liverpool. It was the first time City had failed to win a home league match during Andrée Jeglertz’s 16 months in charge, let alone lose.

Nevertheless, the victory was fully deserved for Tottenham, who made Khadija “Bunny” Shaw wait to equal her teammate Vivianne Miedema’s all-time WSL goalscoring record of 97 goals.

Jeglertz described the defeat as a “wake-up call” for his team, adding: “Tottenham were a little bit more urgent than us. Each duel counts, each moment counts, each ball counts. That was something that I missed with our players, especially in the second half where we needed to score and we needed to beat them in one-versus-one situations. I missed a little bit of that urgency, which I think is the most important in a team, and if we drop a little bit in that, this league is so tight and tough and the teams are so good, you will drop points and lose games.”

Before the game, the anticipated storyline felt almost too obvious. Shaw, needing three goals to surpass Miedema, was facing a club against whom she had scored four hat-tricks, including on Tottenham’s most recent visit to this stadium in March, when she recorded the WSL’s fastest treble. Persistently their tormentor, Shaw has scored more goals against Spurs than any other player has managed against a single opponent in the competition.

When Shaw opened the scoring inside 10 minutes, everything seemed to be following the script. Jade Rose, pressing very high up the pitch for a centre-back, won the ball and played a precise low pass across to Shaw, who tucked into the bottom corner from inside the box to record her 96th WSL goal and her 16th against Tottenham.

That, however, proved to be the only effort at goal – on or off target – that City would register during the opening 45 minutes, as Tottenham impressed. Kirsty Hanson drew a good save from Ayaka Yamashita and Hanson also felt she had a very strong claim for a penalty when Carlotta Wamser appeared to foul her inside the area, but it was not long before the visitors were deservedly level as Cathinka Tandberg expertly turned home Hanson’s cross with a clinical near-post finish.

Tottenham continued to threaten after the break, although Rose scooped over the bar to spurn a huge City chance on the rebound after a Lauren Hemp free-kick had been parried by Lize Kop. Some very effective counterattacking football then deservedly won the game for Tottenham as they scored twice to stun the defending champions.

First, in the 74th minute, an exquisite Drew Spence through ball found the run of Matilda Vinberg – who was a late addition to the starting side after the withdrawal of Olivia Holdt during the warm-up because of stomach pains – and Vinberg showed her quality to turn Rose and fire past Yamashita. Vinberg turned provider five minutes later, to set up Jessica Naz for another good finish.

after newsletter promotion

Martin Ho, the Tottenham head coach, hailed his team’s “outstanding” display, saying: “Every time we play a team who has been in the top three consistently, the conversation is: ‘Can you get one over the line?’ And, for the players, they need to feel what that feels like and enjoy that. Today we nullified a lot of their threats. That will give us a lot of confidence.”

Manchester City had won 12 of their 13 previous WSL games against Tottenham, and all of their past 17 WSL home games, but this defeat added a further dent to their title challenge after their loss at Stamford Bridge last weekend. Chelsea, held to a goalless draw by Liverpool on Saturday, remain two points clear.

Arsenal remain winless at home in the WSL this season after being held to another frustrating draw at the Emirates, this time by West Ham. Arsenal had 22 shots at goal but were unable to break the deadlock, as their under-pressure head coach, Renée Slegers, oversaw a sixth home league draw out of six, leaving Arsenal eight points behind the top three.

Manchester United left it late to come from behind and beat Birmingham 2-1 but Simi Awujo’s last-gasp header from a corner gave them a valuable win and extended Eva Olid’s side’s club-record unbeaten run to 14 matches in all competitions. Birmingham had led inside four minutes through Lee Geum-min’s expert volley but Elisabeth Terland’s close-range finish with 10 minutes to go and Awujo’s 94th-minute winner snatched it, moving Olid’s fourth-placed team just six points off the top.

Elsewhere, the bottom side Charlton collected their first point of the season as they drew 1-1 with Aston Villa, while Brighton moved into the top half with a 1-0 victory at Everton, courtesy of Maz Pacheco’s early own goal. Tom Garry

Jeglertz continued: “We will bounce back, I’m not worried about that. I know the qualities in this group. But it’s the good habits, the small details that matter. Those are the things that win titles – this was actually the first time that I missed that in a game and I’m pretty sure it’s not going to happen again.” With just seven points now separating the top five, his team can ill-afford for it to happen again.

Sorting through my mother-in-law’s belongings was heartbreaking. One generation’s treasure is the next’s trash

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 14:00:29 GMT

Medals, ornaments, yellow-rimmed plates – so much life packed into binbags. What unwanted trinkets am I going to pass on?

My mother-in-law recently moved from her apartment of several decades into sheltered housing and my husband and his brother were summoned to help. We arrived to find her arranging the last of 200-plus glasses on the table; the cupboards were still overflowing with oyster forks, tablecloths and, bafflingly, patchwork fabric artichokes.

It went better than this threatened: after a whirlwind long weekend, we escaped with some crockery, a photograph of my husband as a cherubic spherical tot and “Queen Alexandra’s Christmas Gift Book 1908” (sepia snaps of scowling royals holding terriers).

We might have travelled home light, but the experience was heavy: so much life shoved into binbags. Packing up the yellow-rimmed plates we’ve eaten so many meals from, to donate to charity, was a reminder that the family’s grande bouffe (they’re French) days are over: there’s no space in my mother-in-law’s new digs. My gentle, clever father-in-law has been entirely unravelled by Alzheimer’s and his tricolore mayor’s sash, carefully folded in tissue, undid us all; she dug in her heels about keeping 20 years of A3 plain cardboard calendars, the scribbles reminders of their busy, happy, sociable lives. We unearthed a long-forgotten trunk of heirlooms in the garage, inherited from her own parents, who possibly inherited it from theirs: a forgotten uncle’s medals, ornaments, broken pottery.

One generation’s treasure is the next’s trash. I’ve read two thoughtful, pained articles recently about trying to sort through a mother’s stuff – never just stuff, but affective landmines, freighted with meaning and memory. It’s a central preoccupation in Barbara Kingsolver’s new novel, Partita, too: the heroine is mired in the emotional swamp of clearing her hoarder mother’s house, expressing a fervent, relatable desire to set fire to it all.

That’s the reality of “the great junk transfer”: the inheritance we don’t really want, thanks. In a recent removal company survey, nearly half of 2,200 people across three countries said they would “rather inherit nothing” than deal with a relative’s belongings. One weary man on Instagram explained that he spent 80 days and filled three skips clearing his parents’ house. His message for boomers? “You’re going to die … Guess who’s going to have to deal with all your shit if you haven’t cleaned it up?” Millennial Inheritance on YouTube humorously catalogues the mindboggling crap adult kids are left contemplating – figurines, so many bloody figurines (no wonder my local auction house is full of them), 668 shot glasses, Christmas kitsch.

It was probably ever thus, but inheriting a bit of bedlinen and cutlery is a very different proposition from tackling the mountains of mass-produced knick-knacks and gadgets that filled homes following the postwar cheap consumer-goods boom. Plus generational junk transfer has become vastly more problematic in this broken housing economy: who has space for 12 boxes of VHS cassettes and three fondue sets? It’s depressing to see how things our parents loved, or at least wanted, become a burden.

We reached home determined to embrace austere minimalism, but a few hours later I bought a hedgehog-shaped incense holder. Over my shoulder as I type lurk skips’ worth of stuff: plasticine dinosaurs and pewter goats, creepy religious ephemera and Victorian mugs.

Because I really like stuff; humans do, generally. We always have and that’s going nowhere: Gen Z love their trinkets and I’ve just been reading about “shoptimism” – shopping carefully, for pleasure, from independents – as self-care.

But those Pokémon cards and noughties “graphic tees” will be someone else’s problem soon enough too. Is there anything to be done? Swedish death cleaning – disposing of your own shit – suggests a briskly unsentimental solution, but it’s one few of us feel emotionally up for (with honourable exceptions: my stepfather’s relentless geordie death clean will leave him standing naked in an entirely empty house soon). Maybe we should revive the ancient tradition of grave goods? Funeral directors could pack us up with all our worldly possessions, then burn the lot (“waste-to-energy recovery” in recycling centre parlance).

More realistically, we should probably accept that relieving our parents of the burden of decades of accumulated stuff is just one of those caring jobs everyone ends up taking on, eventually. One day all this (crocheted owl, capybara keyring, assortment of useless but attractive tins) will be yours, my sons. Sorry.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 13:24:10 GMT

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness.

Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology.

The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw.

Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.

Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.

One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.

Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.

Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.

Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.

The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.

NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

A police spokesperson said the force was addressing “areas of learning” and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: “Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.”

The IOPC said the family had a right to ask for a review of the internal investigation and that it had not yet received a request.

How to make nasi goreng – recipe

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 13:00:27 GMT

The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it

Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time.

Prep 25 min Chill 2 hr+ Cook 5 min Serves 2

200g jasmine rice, or other long-grain rice, or 525g cooked and cooled rice 2 tbsp neutral oil 1 garlic clove, peeled and finely chopped 2 eggs, beaten (optional) 2 tbsp kecap manis (see step 5) 1 tbsp light soy sauce 4 spring onions, trimmed and chopped on the diagonal 1 bird’s eye chilli, sliced, to serve

For the paste 50g Asian red shallots (about 4) 1 garlic clove 1 red bird’s eye chilli , or similar 1 tbsp neutral oil 2 tsp terasi (Indonesian shrimp paste; see step 4)

Optional toppings Crispy shallots (bought or homemade) Fried eggs Sliced cucumber or tomatoes Lightly blanched vegetables Cooked meat or seafood or cubed tofu or tempeh Salted peanuts, roughly chopped

Should you happen to have cooked and cooled long-grain rice ready to use, start at step 3; the amount suggested above is fairly elastic, and the recipe easily scaled up or divided. If you’re cooking rice (preferably jasmine, but any long-grain variety will do) specially, put it in a pan with 400ml boiling water, then bring to a simmer, stirring once.

Cover the pan tightly and turn the heat right down. Cook for 15 minutes, then take off the heat and place on a damp tea towel or cloth for five minutes. Fluff the rice with a fork, then spread it on a baking tray and put in the fridge to cool and dry out, ideally overnight, or for up to two hours in the freezer.

If you can’t find small, fiery Asian shallots, use 75g of the larger round ones instead, to compensate for their milder flavour. Peel and roughly chop the shallots and garlic. Trim the chilli (remove and discard the pith and seeds if you’re nervous of heat, or use a milder variety instead), then roughly chop and put in a mortar or mini chopper.

Add the oil and terasi (Malaysian belacan, Thai kapi or Vietnamese mắm tôm make good substitutes for this Indonesian fermented shrimp paste); if you can’t find any of them, use a teaspoon and a half of fish sauce and two anchovy fillets (or two teaspoons of red miso mixed with a teaspoon of crumbled dried seaweed). Pound or whizz until smooth.

Kecap manis is a thick, sweet soy sauce that’s easily found in specialist Asian food shops and online. To make your own, put four tablespoons of light soy sauce in a small pan with the same amount of soft brown sugar, simmer until reduced to a slightly syrupy consistency, then leave to cool and use in the recipe below (note: this will make more than you need).

Prepare the toppings according to taste; nasi goreng exists in countless permutations across Indonesia and Malaysia, so it’s a great home for leftovers and various odds and ends from the vegetable drawer. Like many fried dishes, this one comes together fast, so have everything ready and within easy reach of the hob before you even think about starting the cooking.

Put the oil in a wok on a high heat, then fry the chopped garlic until just lightly golden. Pour in the eggs, if using, leave to cook until half set, then break up. Carry on scrambling until the eggs are just beginning to brown, then stir in the spice paste and cook for another minute or so.

Once the shallots in the paste have lost their raw smell, sprinkle in the rice by hand, breaking up any clumps as you go, then stir-fry, tossing vigorously, until it’s thoroughly heated through. Stir in the kecap manis, soy sauce and chopped spring onion, ensuring the grains are brown and evenly coated with sauce.

Fry, stirring, for another minute or so, until the rice is just beginning to caramelise and crisp, then taste and season as necessary with more kecap manis and chilli. Divide between plates and top with the sliced chilli and crispy shallots, if using, plus your chosen accompaniments. Serve immediately.

As the real world falls apart, Grand Theft Auto looks more and more appealing

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 12:00:29 GMT

All these tech outages are a reminder we’re at the mercy of powers beyond our comprehension. At least in GTA we have control

This week marked the release of the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI. Millions around the world checked out of their usual responsibilities in order to immerse themselves in a game where you run errands for your girlfriend in between murdering people.

I feel completely alone in not caring about GTA VI, as I famously only play video games where you get to be RoboCop – issuing public nuisance citations to graffiti taggers in between murdering people. I’m a man who knows what he likes.

GTA VI has been over a decade in the making. The anticipation built to a fever pitch, with gaming enthusiasts practically going feral at the prospect of finally getting to schlep groceries and engage in casual bird-watching after brutally running over a pedestrian with a stolen Porsche.

Our collective addiction to virtual mayhem is guaranteed to crash productivity all across the globe. I shudder to think what would happen if the game glitched out for everyone all at once, rendering your PS5 a slickly manufactured plastic paperweight. Would there be Paris-style riots turning every major city into a dystopian nightmare riddled with flaming trash bins and smashed shop windows?

In a sense, that would be a boon to fans of the game, as the world of flesh would start to resemble GTA come to blood-curdling life.

Meanwhile, gaming is trending in the opposite direction. Most modern video game systems don’t even accept physical media anymore. The days of buying an actual disc in a little plastic box are nearly gone. Each game purchase is now just exchanging invisible digital money for the right to access the pixels and data that make virtual worlds come to life on your TV screen. It’s ephemeral, intangible, and it could all disappear in an instant.

But hey, that’s life in 2026, a time when hackers can turn off your refrigerator from halfway around the world. GTA VI digitally vaporizing at random would be catastrophic, but it wouldn’t be the first computer-related global inconvenience of the year, let alone the month or the week.

For the last seven days, the news has been dominated by outages in our tech infrastructure: grounded planes, broken email systems, bank accounts fritzing in and out of existence like a flickering lightbulb. The troubles have been blamed on software bugs, faulty patches, and outdated equipment.

The truly bored among us prefer to claim worldwide conspiracy theories, malicious hackers, or government manipulation that would have James Bond tossing his martini in the air and screaming: “This is all too much for me to handle.”

Meanwhile, AI companies like Anthropic are growing exponentially as they seek to further entangle everyday life on Earth with their complex, interdependent, free-thinking computer systems.

Even if these outages aren’t the direct result of AI, it’s all part of our brave new world. For the simple price of your money occasionally being completely inaccessible, you can have AI write a novel for you or remind you to pay your car insurance bill with the money you can’t use.

This plan seems to be a huge success for everyone but actual human beings with normal, non-billionaire lives. Besides tech companies, I suppose the other biggest winners in all this are bar owners, especially the ones at airports. When absolutely nothing works, the only sane response is to have a pint and laugh about it.

Increasingly, reality resembles a video game like GTA VI. Maybe without all the gruesome, wanton mayhem and surface-to-air missiles, but certainly with all of the other bits. As games start folding in more mundane tasks like shopping, going to the gym, or fixing a leaky roof, real life is taking on the rigid, mission-based thrill ride of the arcade.

Sorting through a health insurance claim is almost as annoying as a boss fight in a classic Sonic the Hedgehog game – repeated button-smashing, gnashed teeth, and frayed nerves. The mere notion of a shadowy cabal flipping switches to shut off various critical services makes me think of a caffeine-addled bachelor cackling as they wreak havoc in a particularly malicious game of Sim City.

I often feel like a cuckolded non-playable game character, or NPC, watching more exciting events happen around me that I’m unable to control. If I want to be able to get on an airplane that actually leaves on time, I’m going to have to level up my XP or purchase a pay-to-win upgrade.

It’s not uncommon for me to imagine myself as an NPC avatar while strapped into the back of a Waymo driverless taxi, tooling from one checkpoint to another, silently praying the computer shuttling me to my destination doesn’t decide to change its mind and fly off a bridge into a river.

We’re all at the mercy of virtual powers beyond our comprehension. One can’t help but sink into the despairing realization that life is now a series of slights perpetuated by an algorithm with a callous disregard for the whims of corporeal beings.

So, what do we do when nothing works and everything is impossible? Go outside and do some actual bird watching? Repair a real roof instead of one in a video game?

Surely not. If anything, these technological disruptions further underline our need for our gadgets and gizmos to exist. Absence, as they say, makes the heart grow fonder. When Microsoft Outlook crashes, it just reminds people how much they need Microsoft Outlook.

Our dependency on these tools has become second nature, so ingrained in the hum of the world that every so often, they have to go away for us to even notice them. When you can’t access your Chase bank account for a few hours, why wouldn’t you fall to your knees to give thanks to the benevolent tech lord for seeing fit to bring it back to life?

Better, then, to stop worrying about things you can’t control and focus on what you can … in GTA VI. The last vestige of absolute power is inside video games, a realm where you can do everything and anything you want, down to even the most antisocial behavior the mind can conjure.

The main characters of video games have all the agency real people lack. If they run out of money, they can steal a car and get away with it. If all flights are grounded at the airport, they can hijack a helicopter.

The only sane response to the feeling of ineffectual reality is to further retreat into the digital frontier, where anything is possible. After all, there’s only around a month left before Christmas, and your fake digital girlfriend is expecting a gift.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

‘Great coach, terrible streamer’ – Erasmus gets thumbs-down for his weird watchalong

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 12:00:29 GMT

In a hotel conference room, South Africa’s banned coach divides opinion with his Trumpian utterings while watching his team get beaten by Ireland

Watchwithrassie. com had been the surprise internet sensation of the week. Logging on a few hours before South Africa kicked off against Ireland on Saturday, one thing was immediately clear. When it came to rugby’s latest scandal – “RassieGate 3.0” as Bryan Habana called it – this was not a place for balanced debate.

Rassie Erasmus’s “match-fixing” rant, in the aftermath of the Springboks’ defeat by France in Paris, had caused a depressingly familiar furore and earned him a six-match World Rugby ban. Steve Borthwick and Fabien Galthié, among countless others, had made their views known.

Across social media, Boks fans had been in overdrive for days, busily defending their oppressed supreme leader and double World Cup-winning coach. With kick-off in Dublin looming, in this new and strange corner of the internet, an Erasmus-powered echo chamber had been created.

“Rassie,” wrote Griffort on the message board, “do you feel there is a vendetta against you from refs and rugby unions around the world, because you are such a successful coach?”

“Free Rassie,” wrote another. “Rassie for president,” added someone else. George from Gqeberha wrote: “I support Rassie 100% for being outspoken and honest … Rassie is Rassie. Please don’t change.”

Rassie is Rassie. Indubitably true: “They are all out to get me.” His Trumpian post-truth strategy had worked again. “Behind you 100,000%,” wrote Nonnie. “They are messing with the wrong coach, team and fan.”

Excitement was mounting for the big online reveal, and even ITV were hyping it up. “Rassie Erasmus is having his very own online watchalong,” said the anchorman Mark Pougatch. “That won’t be dull.”

Won’t it? Erasmus, sporting a Boks cap and black tracksuit top, appeared about 10 minutes before kick-off. “I’ll probably have my sound mostly off,” he said. “At half-time, if I’m calm enough, we’re going to have a little chat. And obviously afterwards. It’s always easier to chat when you’re winning.” As we would discover.

There was no play-by-play analysis. No rolling tactical masterclass. There was, in fact, under four minutes of talk during the entire 2hr 12min stream. Just a static camera, pointing at a fiftysomething coach, sitting in a hotel conference room in the Dublin suburb of Stillorgan.

It takes a special ego to respond to a disciplinary ban by building a website, featuring a bizarre AI-generated country song about “hard yards”, for the purpose of inviting supporters to “watch along”.

But for that online content to in effect include … no content? That’s another level of self-regard. Erasmus did occasionally rotate his baseball cap, pour a drink, or slam his fist on the table. He’s always been an innovator. This was the latest perplexing creation in the Rassie-verse.

And there was no shortage of interest. Around 10 minutes after kick-off there were 88,717 viewers. But some were growing restless. “Thought we were going to watch with Rassie commentating,” wrote one on YouTube. “This is disappointing.”

“Rassie my bru,” wrote another, “We got no sound.” Had Erasmus found a way to alienate his public, this week of all weeks? @ncjhood’s pithy comment summed up the mood: “Great coach, terrible streamer.”

Tacitly acknowledging it was all becoming a bitter disappointment for many, Erasmus’s backroom team took action. A caption appeared, top left, reading: “SOUND WILL REMAIN OFF UNTIL RASSIE WANTS TO SPEAK.”

after newsletter promotion

There were some interesting elements, aside from these unintentionally comedic ones. His burning passion for the game, and for the Boks, was clear. Facing a sensational Ireland performance, Erasmus looked disgusted when his fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu misjudged a kick. He looked incandescent when Andy Farrell’s industrious side turned the ball over later in the half.

And this being Rassie, there was intrigue. He frequently covered his mouth to talk pointedly and at length to someone, somewhere. As a tense second half continued, he increasingly ducked down behind his laptop screen to conduct conversations beyond the camera’s view.

Who was he talking to? And why? On social media people were beginning to wonder. “Car insurance renewal,” speculated Monk, on X. “He’s catching up on admin.” (World Rugby’s ban states Erasmus is not permitted “any match-day involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players”.)

Erasmus said he would talk afterwards. It wasn’t to be. The fans could wait, apparently, because South Africa lost. After angrily hammering his fists down three times as defeat was confirmed – sending his brandy and Coke splashing across the table – he packed his laptop away and the stream ended. As he said, it’s easier to chat when you’re winning.

Earlier, on ITV, Pougatch and Habana discussed it all with David Flatman. “He boiled over,” Habana said, sympathetically, of last Monday’s media conference that led to Erasmus’s ban, adding: “I think we all really understood where he was coming from.” That was debatable, to put it mildly, and the final word was left to Flatman.

“He knows what he’s doing,” said the former England prop. “It’s the third time. He knows he’s lighting fires under people. He knows these people [match officials] are going to get slaughtered online … it’s led to death threats against people’s families. It’s impacted people’s lives and careers.

“I find it almost cultish that every South African I speak to defends him blindly. It doesn’t matter if the point he was making was correct … stop impacting people’s lives with your behaviour.”

In one of the day’s stranger moments, Erasmus had earlier stood, alone, for the South African anthem. How long will it be before he gets his own one?
