‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 12:00:29 GMT

Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con?

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. (Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.)

There are panel discussions about getting your confidence back at work, a prosecco bar and a hula‑hooping session. A woman selling pairs of magnets that clip to your knickers swears they helped with her hot flushes. Though she is somewhat vague about how exactly “the magnetism gets into your bloodstream”, she’s commendably frank about the downside: she has to take off the pant magnets to do a food shop, for fear of sticking to the metal supermarket trolley.

As the tagline for Stripes Beauty, the actor Naomi Watts’s new wellness brand, puts it: “Welcome to a world where menopause isn’t a dirty word.” But has it become an overused one instead?

The global perimenopause market is projected to be worth up to $25bn by 2030, according to the consultants PwC, as pharmaceutical companies catch up with the previously underserved health needs of women whose periods are drawing to an end. But it’s the consumer side of the market that is growing most rapaciously, as brands churn out menopause-friendly versions of everything from shower gel and herbal tea, to cooling pillows and toothpaste (less daft than it sounds, given perimenopause is linked to shrinking gums and tooth loss). The consumer magazine Which? has meanwhile warned that in some cases women are paying a “pink tax” premium for standard products, from moisturiser to vitamins, that manufacturers have discovered can be sold at a higher price if rebranded as specifically for menopause.

“Companies have realised that middle-aged women have money. And they’ve also realised that we are maybe going through a tricky time – kids leaving, navigating long-term relationships, looking after parents … I think they see a little window of vulnerability, both with menopause symptoms and other symptoms of ageing,” says Joyce Harper, professor of reproductive science at UCL and author of Your Joyful Years: Empowering Good Health and Happiness Beyond 50. A paper she recently co-authored for the journal Climacteric reviewed more than 200 menopause supplements and found wide variations in ingredients and price, suggesting an unusual lack of consensus about what – if anything – works. (Nearly half didn’t even contain vitamin D, which, along with calcium, is the only supplement with sufficient proof of efficacy to be recommended by medical experts in menopause, and then only for bone health.) The paper concluded supplements were being sold to menopausal women “despite the limited empirical evidence currently available” that they actually worked, prompting Harper to warn of a “menopause gold rush” in which women risked being exploited.

Yet even with her professional expertise, she acknowledges it’s not always easy to resist the social media hype. “I’ve got a dodgy knee, and every now and then my algorithm sends me, ‘Oh, this cream is going to sort you out’, and every now and then I almost click on it,” she admits. “I get that close to thinking, ‘It’s only £20, might as well try it.’ And I’ve been researching this for years … I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in.”

That women are now queueing up for products advertising their perimenopausal status, rather than suffering in embarrassed silence, is arguably progress of a kind. It suggests a stigma lifting, and a market finally taking older women’s needs or desires – not to mention their spending power – more seriously. However, with that welcome change has come concerns about “menowashing”, or brands using women’s health needs to sell them things they don’t need at a potentially vulnerable time. Who, exactly, is this market serving?

For many of the women I meet at Pause Live, it’s more about a fun day out than a search for miracle cures. Helen, 61, is off out dancing later but has dropped in here first because, “I’m really into wellness and health,” she says. She runs an Instagram account about ageing stylishly called Silversparkles1965, and says she could have done with something like this years ago when she was going through menopause. “I’m on HRT now but I’ll take anything that works,” she says. Her friend Marina, 55, nods vigorously, adding: “It’s wonderful that now it’s being acknowledged.”

But not everyone is simply here for a good time. Ali Stripling, a workplace coach and motivational speaker, was plunged into early medical menopause after treatment for anal cancer. “I’m interested in pelvic health, sexual wellness, breaking the stigma that has been around midlife. There’s a lot of menowashing here,” she says. Her friend Georgia Swift, who works for the NHS, says she has had an “amazing facial” but is disappointed there isn’t more on mental health.

Anxiety, depression and loss of confidence are all common in perimenopause, and it’s not just hormones that can make this time a vulnerable one. Midlife is also the season of children leaving home, parents dying, the creeping suspicion that your boss would like to trade you in for someone younger, and, for some women, a feeling of being dismissed by wider society. It’s precisely that anger that some brands are latching on to.

The cosmetic giant L’Oréal recently launched a campaign featuring the 58-year-old actor Gillian Anderson lashing out at the way women over 50 are made to feel invisible: “Even if you think I’m easy to dismiss as an angry menopausal feminist, the fact is I have never felt better. I’ve never felt more alive in my skin, clear-headed, purposeful, free of self-judgment.” Anyone who doesn’t accept her right to take up space in the world can, she says scathingly to camera, just “fuck off”. Perhaps the wellness industry’s most seductive promise to this age group isn’t eternal youth, but the feeling of being cared for and taken seriously – even if it is by a wrinkle cream.

According to a survey of Mumsnet users this spring, 68% do not think the NHS takes women’s health in general seriously, and 64% report having been told their symptoms were either normal or “in their head”. More than half say the NHS is institutionally misogynist. “It doesn’t matter how many reports or inquiries we have [if you don’t] grapple with the culture – which is women being constantly dismissed, their pain and their symptoms being dismissed,” says Justine Roberts, the chief executive of Mumsnet. “Half of them said they don’t even bother seeking care because they won’t be taken seriously. We don’t have nearly enough research on hormones in menopause and what HRT means for later life outcomes.” The lack of perimenopause training for doctors is, she says, driving women to look elsewhere for help with symptoms. “Social media is filling the gap.” But platforms full of influencers being paid to post gushing praise for products is the last place to look for disinterested information.

In his new book, Make Me Well, the doctor turned broadcaster Xand van Tulleken argues that “Big Menopause” first took off as an industry back in 1990, when studies linking HRT to breast cancer prompted frightened women to seek other ways of coping with the hormonal transition around the end of their periods. (Even now, although research suggests the cancer risk is smaller than originally thought and outweighed for some women by other benefits, only about one in seven British women takes HRT). Sales of herbal remedies such as evening primrose oil, black cohosh – thought to help with hot flushes, though it has subsequently been linked to liver damage – and red clover surged, fuelled often by word of mouth between friends. Three decades on, social media has supercharged that process, though now supplements are often promoted as a boost alongside HRT rather than an alternative.

I usually scroll straight past the junk ads on Instagram for supposedly menobelly-reducing diets with which women over 40 are bombarded. But I click on a few while researching this piece, and the algorithm instantly responds. It’s like opening a portal to another universe, full of female celebrities in their 50s raving about creatine powder (Davina McCall, presenter of a viral Channel 4 documentary on menopause, who says she uses it to combat midlife muscle loss) or gut health supplements (Mariella Frostrup, broadcaster and menopause awareness campaigner) or drinkable collagen (the actor Kate Winslet). After several days of this, a small seductive voice starts to whisper in my cynical ear: well, maybe there’s something in it?

When I ask friends, acquaintances and Bluesky followers, I’m amazed at how many smart women somewhat sheepishly confess to having experimented with things like anti-bloating skin patches (“I can’t believe I’m admitting to this in public”), energy-boosting maca powder (“expensive dust”), home hormone testing kits (“mad expensive and not that useful”) or a £30 serum to rebuild thinning eyelashes.

“I know better. We all know better. But you just think, ‘It can’t hurt to try’,” groans Sam Baker, host of The Shift podcast and Substack for midlife women. Having just cancelled all the supplements she was taking, Baker says so far she has noticed precisely “no difference”. So why do we keep on falling for it?

For the unlucky 25% of perimenopausal women experiencing severe or debilitating symptoms, desperation may be part of the answer. But most of the marketing I see seems to be targeting the other three‑quarters, encouraging them not to settle for anything less than the energy levels or skin elasticity they had when they were younger. It’s hard to work out whether it’s perimenopause they’re claiming to solve, or age itself.

after newsletter promotion

Menopause-friendly branding has in some ways taken over where “anti-ageing” left off, Baker points out, as beauty brands in particular respond to a backlash from customers against the idea that there is something innately wrong with getting older. “The companies have listened. They have found a different word for it. But we are still trapped in this place where if you are a woman getting older, there are two ways to do it and they’re both wrong. You either go grey and go quietly into that good night, or use everything possible to stop it, and both of those things are open to criticism.” For all Gillian Anderson’s fighting feminist talk in the L’Oréal campaign, she’s still the face of its Age Perfect range of creams to combat sagging skin and wrinkles.

The ads I find most seductive aren’t the ones about rolling back the years; they’re the ones carrying the soothing, flattering message that as a busy woman I must have a lot on my plate, so why don’t I just put myself first for once. It’s the siren call not of anti‑ageing but of self-care, targeted at women who feel they have spent decades putting their children’s or their partners’ or their ageing parents’ needs first, and are now beginning to wonder if anyone is ever going to do the same for them.

The air conditioning inside Heather Jackson’s pop-up store on Kensington High Street is turned up refreshingly high, and the music dialled down low enough for middle-aged ears to hear a conversation. Aromatherapy scents waft over us as she walks me through the carefully curated shelves: moisture-wicking pyjamas for easing night sweats, low-temperature straighteners designed to be kinder to thinning hair, body lotions for skin that is suddenly drier than it used to be, and neatly serried rows of the inevitable menopause supplements. It’s a luxurious concept store, designed to show retailers what prioritising their perimenopausal customers might look like in practice. Compared with the nearest busy branch of Boots, where I eventually find two shelves of menopausal health products in the basement, sandwiched between the Nicorette gum and the thrush cream, it makes the end of your periods feel practically aspirational.

“I wanted to create something like when I was a child and went into Hamleys and it was all for me,” says Jackson, an immaculately groomed but down-to-earth Yorkshirewoman whose background is in corporate talent development and getting women into senior roles. (Research suggests one in 10 women aged between 40 and 55 have quit a job because of menopause symptoms, she points out, just as they should have been hitting their professional peak.) Sh e founded the brand partnership GenM after struggling to find practical perimenopause-friendly products – like foundation that didn’t melt in a hot flush – to get her through her own menopause seven years ago. Its MTick symbol, inspired by the V for vegan-friendly logo, now appears on the packaging of more than 170 member brands in high street stores from Tesco to Boots. It’s not proof of efficacy – GenM doesn’t do its own independent testing – but brands are at least required to show evidence of their workings when making claims about menopause.

The idea, she insists, is to help women seek out better-tailored versions of the products they would normally use, rather than settle for the ones they have always bought. “I want more women to wake up and go: we fought hard, and just when we’re about to peak we’re letting ourselves say, ‘It’s not about me any more.’ Well, it is about you. If we can’t have our best life now, when can we have it?”

Surely in the end it’s about driving sales? “Money makes the world go round. I’m not ever going to dispute the commercialisation of menopause. But money driven purposefully can make society change.”

Though Harper dismisses MTick as merely “amazing marketing”, Jackson insists her process is rigorous enough that some big brands have failed to pass. “I didn’t want menowashing and exploitation, I wanted choice and trust,” she says. “Women of our generation, we’ve been exploited all our lives.”

For those who can afford it and have a realistic idea of what it’s likely to achieve, a special menopausal hair mask seems no more unreasonable a purchase than a bunch of flowers or a nice coffee, or anything else women buy to cheer themselves up after a rough day. If something works for you – and plenty of women swear by alternative menopause remedies, including those for which there’s zero clinical evidence – does it really matter if it’s just a nicely packaged placebo? (One 2015 study on placebo effects in treating hot flushes found a third of the group given the dummy pill saw a significant improvement in their symptoms after eight weeks, which for some lasted weeks after they stopped taking it.)

Placebo effects can, Harper concedes, be powerful. “There are some studies that show if you just take part in a study, you do better – because someone cares.” But her advice to women is always to stop, think and Google for the clinical evidence first before buying. “I want to empower women with the correct information, and when I see women with misinformation going down some rabbit hole, it makes me very sad.”

Women should also be aware, she argues, that relying on the wellness industry rather than conventional medicine can be risky. Ingredients in some supplements can interact with prescription drugs, while self‑diagnosing symptoms from depression to joint pain as simply the effects of perimenopause may mean missing another underlying illness that needs treatment. “Her joints might be hurting because she’s got osteoarthritis. Her lack of energy could be her thyroid.”

What many women really are missing out on, Harper says, is the one menopause remedy that’s not only backed by decades of robust clinical evidence but often free or cheap: lifestyle medicine like exercising, eating well and moderating alcohol intake, which might not cure serious symptoms but should at least be the first line of defence. “If you do all the good things – no short cuts, no quick fixes – there’s so much scientific evidence that you will feel better. But the biggest thing when you get to this age is the realisation that you will lower your risk of all the chronic health conditions: cancer, diabetes, heart disease, dementia,” she says, emphasising that this advice applies to women on HRT as well as those who can’t or don’t want to take it.

“My motto this year is to make lifestyle medicine sexy. I don’t see it as a chore to cook a lovely meal when you get home from work. Tonight I’m going to go do BodyAttack and yoga, and I can’t wait – I just love the buzz. But everyone’s got their thing, whether it’s going for a walk in nature, a wild swim, putting some music on and dancing round your kitchen for 10 minutes – and all these things are pretty much free.

“Paying £100 a month for some supplement? Spend that money on going to have a blooming massage.”

How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 12:00:27 GMT

Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

The work of Freud still dominates the public and medical imagination here, even though there are important ways in which he was wrong. Freud proposed that quite dramatic physical symptoms can arise as a result of repression, where the memory of an upsetting experience is pushed into the unconscious, leaving a sort of free-floating emotional energy. He saw the mind as being like a pneumatic device: emotions represented energy and that energy had to go somewhere, often leading to the development of a physical symptom.

These days, psychologists are more sceptical about this, but the influence of Freudian psychology lives on in the way we talk about psychosomatic illness – a condition where there’s no damage or disease, but clear impairment nonetheless. The terms “conversion” and “somatisation” are derived directly from Freud and still pop up frequently in the literature.

Their use is a stark reminder of the fact that, when it comes to explanations, our language can lead us astray. Importantly, the words conversion and somatisation strongly imply an active, even deliberate, process; that the patient with a psychosomatic illness is doing something that brings their symptoms about. They are converting their distress into paralysis, or somatising their sadness into pain. Is that how things really are?

There is still much to be explained about how, in the absence of damage or disease, a body can produce a symptom as dramatic as paralysis or a seizure-like episode. But we are beginning to understand what seems to be important in getting these experiences going.

First, remember that our bodies often respond to acute distress in dramatic ways. Strong emotion can entail so called tonic immobility, in which motor areas in the brain are inhibited, and voluntary movement prevented. More familiarly, it can induce trembling, speechlessness and confusion, all of which resemble neurological symptoms. Our perception of these experiences is important. Recognising strong emotion for what it is makes it more manageable. If I tremble while understanding that I am afraid, I might give myself time for the fear to pass and my nervous system to settle down.

But when these feelings are taken as a potential sign of disease, we tend to become anxious, with consequences for how we experience and attend to our bodies. Fear increases pain, so any feeling that there is bodily damage (a frightening idea) can be enough to turn up the perceptual volume on physical discomfort or unusual sensations. Paying attention to and trying to control a shaking limb will tend to increase the trembling; attending to a difficulty with movement is likely to increase how severe we think the problem is. What might have started small becomes amplified.

People vary in terms of how easy they find it to identify emotions. The term “alexithymia” (translatable as something like “no words for emotions”) refers to a difficulty with labelling and distinguishing feelings. It can range from a near full-on emotion “blindness” to a coarser grain of emotional experience, with distinctions only between, say, feeling “good” and feeling “bad”. It is not uncommon for people with psychosomatic illnesses to report that they struggle to identify emotional states.

What this could point to is that psychosomatic illnesses arise not because of what a patient is doing with their emotions, but because of what they have not been able to do with them. When we label our emotions, when we allow them to find their expression, we are allowing ourselves to know more fully what we are feeling and what we need. In a clear departure from the Freud-inspired model, it’s not that patients with these problems are “converting” their emotions into something else. It’s that they aren’t always registering them as emotions in the first place. Instead, they’re interpreted as something having gone wrong with the body, beginning a vicious cycle of anxious attention.

This is still an uncertain area of clinical practice. Emotion is not the whole picture, but it is important for understanding why some people find themselves with otherwise unexplained symptoms. For example, one way of thinking about non-epileptic seizures (a deeply distressing and disabling experience with all the hallmarks of a seizure, but without any of the expected electrical anomalies in the brain) is that they might start off with physiological elements of a panic attack – the muscular tension and the involuntary movement – but without the accompanying subjective feeling of dread; “panic without panic”.

Diego found it helpful to consider that his symptoms could be rooted in bodily expressions of anxiety and physical overload. He was a determined and upbeat guy who had taken on a second and third job to support his children financially. He had studiously avoided engaging with the possibility that this might be getting to be too much. His symptoms showed him his limits.

Psychosomatic illness is sometimes dismissed as being “all in the mind”, but this gets things back to front. When our emotions get wrapped up with physical symptoms, they are very real – “all in the body”, in fact. Bringing our emotions into our minds by thinking about them, and heeding the needs they represent, can be an important step in finding relief.

Huw Green is a clinical psychologist working in neuropsychology

Further reading The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk (Penguin, £14.99)

Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow review – these audacious pranks are tell-your-friends funny

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 12:00:26 GMT

Butler is a serious talent. These punchy, pacy shows see him taking on the establishment, industry by industry. He’s like a hipster Robin Hood

It feels fitting that on the same weekend Nathan Fielder’s much-discussed You Can See Everything finally arrives in UK cinemas, Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow launches on the small screen. This wildly entertaining show confirms Butler as the British heir to Fielder’s crown as the clown prince of documentary-making. Butler doesn’t even need a gift-wrapped subject like Theranos grifter Elizabeth Holmes.

If you enjoy satire that punches upwards at the rich and powerful, you’re in for a riotous treat. If you prefer a ghost-faced buffoon from Birmingham donning fancy dress to run rings around idiots, you’re also in luck. He might have a name like a valet-ordering app, but Oobah Butler is a serious talent.

A gonzo Vice journalist and self-styled “professional chancer”, Butler made his name with viral stunts. Most infamously, he created a fake restaurant in a shed and, by gaming his ratings, turned it into London’s top-rated eaterie on Tripadvisor, despite never serving a dish. He has since spread his DIY documentarian wings with Channel 4 one-offs such as The Great Amazon Heist, in which he sold discarded bottles of delivery drivers’ urine as a bitter lemon drink on Amazon itself.

Now he makes his full series debut with this audacious, hilarious set of films. Armed with little more than his laptop and cojones the size of cannonballs, Butler embarks on a mission to tweak the establishment’s nose, pull down the elite’s pants and slip ice cubes down the back of The Man. Boy, it’s a bracing exercise.

Each of five punchy, pacy half-hours sees Butler infiltrate a different industry to disrupt it from the inside. They’re framed as “experiments” rather than stunts, and fair enough. There’s a genuine spirit of inquiry and subversive intent behind them. They are also tell-your-friends funny.

“Wellness” gets things under way with a bad science bang. If you’re going to pick any sector to lampoon, the home of vibes-based medicine and miscellaneous woo-woo would come high on any list. “It’s a gold rush of bullshit and I want in,” says Butler. He’s soon selling a skin serum containing children’s tears (“ethically extracted”, of course) and a supplement made of lab-grown human meat. When Butler consults a $1,500-an-hour attorney, she asks about the severity of his crimes. “Fraud bad,” he admits. “Cannibalism bad. Prison bad.”

He pays influencers to plug his pretend products and gets a glowing endorsement from Cameron Diaz (actually an Hispanic bloke who shares the film star’s name). Extending the You Can See Everything parallels, Patrick O’Neill – former chief creative officer of Theranos – pops up to advise on marketing strategy. How reassuring.

This is followed by “Wine”, in which Butler repackages smoke-tainted swill – rendered undrinkable by wildfires in Napa Valley vineyards and fit only to make barbecue sauce or hand sanitiser – as premium plonk costing $500 (£380) a bottle. It includes a glorious scene in which Butler cheats his sommelier exam by inserting a vibrating butt plug to get hints from a hidden expert. Well, it works at chess tournaments. Allegedly.

“Dating” sees Butler create a matchmaking app for the AI era. Users communicate with a “fully conscious chatbot”, which will find their soulmate. They are in fact talking to real people, inadvertently learning how to flirt. Actual human contact is better than relying on tech. Who knew? “Music” finds Butler taking another swing at AI by manufacturing a fake rapper named Nepo and getting machine-written tune Who’s Your Daddy? to trend on TikTok. He makes it look alarmingly easy, exposing the algorithm-gaming that’s rife in the pop business.

The season ends on a high – and more legal trouble – with “Royalty”. After marrying a real-life Cambodian princess, Prince Oobah samples the gilded life of a royal. He hobnobs at hoity-toity dinners, blags high-end freebies and is protected by government-funded armed guards. He’s soon getting grilled by police and at genuine risk of jail time for treason.

Is it big and clever? Yes, actually. Hefty HBO budgets means he clocks up serious air miles in pursuit of mischief. Behind his deadpan humour, Butler is ferociously smart. He not only fizzes with bold ideas but has the bottle to carry them through to their logical conclusion and beyond. He can sell anything to anyone, as long as they’ve got more money than sense. He’s easy to root for because his irreverent pranks are largely victimless. He targets institutions, rather than individuals, like a hipster Robin Hood.

In the process, he provides a sobering insight into exactly how morally bankrupt the modern world is. Regulation is laughable. Loopholes are exploited. Respected critics are way too gullible. Venture capitalists are worryingly keen to invest in Butler’s outlandish schemes. Yet it’s also strangely feelgood, somehow restoring your faith in humanity.

With his Warhol-esque hair and emoji-like features, Butler rather resembles a South Park character come to life. Let’s hope his distinctive look doesn’t limit his shelf-life as an undercover agent of chaos. Then again, Sacha Baron Cohen is still getting away with it. Perhaps people really are that stupid. Pass the kiddie tears and worthless wine.

Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow is on HBO Max

Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 11:59:28 GMT

Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

Criminals are using cloned plates to evade detection and avoid paying penalties for dangerous or illegal driving.

A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for: most of which are believed to be a result of cloning. The number of complaints was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the number recorded in 2018.

To help victims, a new reporting tool has been launched in England and Wales. The tool is designed to make it easier to alert the authorities by allowing victims to report a cloned plate directly to the police online who will also inform the DVLA. There is a new section on the government’s website that explains how to appeal against incorrect fines or charges.

The government has also issued consumer guidance on how to avoid falling foul of driving with an illegal number plate after it emerged that a third of motorists stopped in number plate operations this year had no idea they had one.

Early findings from the police suggest that, as well as deliberate criminal use, the public are unwittingly being sold incorrect plates. Stolen secondhand cars can be fitted with cloned plates and the government advises that you check the car’s registration number is consistent with information held by the DVLA.

The roads minister, Justin Madders, said: “Illegal plates are being used by criminals, but it is also the case that innocent motorists can have illegal plates on their vehicles without their knowledge.

“We are going to make it easier for victims of cloned plates to report them as well as [launching] webpages to help drivers when they buy number plates and used cars from reputable sellers. These are small everyday fixes from the government which could help you avoid unwelcome attention from police.”

It took Yarwood months to sort out the mess left by the criminals who racked up the fines in six days.

“I never paid any of them … but the difficulty contesting them is gobsmacking,” she said. “You have to prove your innocence and the fact that I was not in the country was not enough.”

She said after she had reported the cloned plates her husband was stopped while driving the car. “But not in an unpleasant way,” she added. “It was fine.”

If it happens again, Yarwood has been advised to change her registration which she says is a “whole thing I didn’t want to have to do. So I’m waiting. I hope they don’t.”

Max Verstappen says George Russell is ‘so far below my level’ after Vegas win

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 11:49:11 GMT

Red Bull driver delighted rival crashed out of grand prix

Leclerc and Hamilton relationship is ‘unmanageable’

Max Verstappen escalated his feud with George Russell after a stunning victory at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, stating the British driver was barely worth consideration because he was “so far below my level”.

The Dutchman competed with Russell for much of the race in Nevada but it was the Red Bull driver who came out on top and Russell ultimately fell to ninth after he suffered a lock-up late in the race.

The pair have long had a testing relationship and after they clashed in practice in Las Vegas, Russell accused Verstappen of believing he was “bigger and better than everyone else” and that he had to be confronted. Verstappen was blunt in his pleasure at then beating Russell.

“He speaks a lot next to the track and honestly it doesn’t really bother me because he is so far below my level that it doesn’t make any sense for me to try to challenge that,” he said. “Today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [as Russell locked up].

“I was like: ‘Fantastic, my day is only getting better.’ When I crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Russell has not been able to match the performance of his Mercedes title-winning teammate, Kimi Antonelli, this season and Verstappen went on to twist the knife further. He told the Dutch broadcaster Viaplay that Russell was “nowhere near me. He’s been an absolute joke this season.”

Russell completed his media commitments before Verstappen made the remarks and has yet to respond.

The Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, admitted after a dramatic race that the relationship between his drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, who hit one another in Las Vegas, was unmanageable and that the pair no longer had a level of understanding. Race stewards found Leclerc at fault and gave him a 10-second penalty, putting him in 10th, three places behind Hamilton.

Vasseur gave a damning assessment of what appears to now be a broken relationship between the pair and was squarely holding Leclerc to account in Vegas. He said: “The pressure is definitely building and it’s much worse now than it was 18 months ago. Lately, the situation between them has become unmanageable. In the end, there’s a human misunderstanding between them.

“We asked Charles to think about the team while he was behind Lewis, but he didn’t listen. That’s a professional mistake. He forgot that 2,000 people work day and night for him, and that’s completely unacceptable. I repeat, [it] is totally unacceptable.”

After the Mexico City GP, where Hamilton and Leclerc vied with one another, Vasseur had sat them down to put the team’s position and both drivers agreed they had cleared the air and all was well. There was no such amiable cooperation evident in Vegas.

Vasseur notably had not said they would use codified rules of engagement as Hamilton had requested but it left the British driver clearly frustrated. After incidents in racing with Leclerc at Monza, Mexico City and now Las Vegas, his exasperation was clear that his efforts were not making a difference.

“I’ve done all I can, I’ve said everything and more,” he said. “It’s been difficult. All I can do is show up and give everything I can, and hopefully in the background they can sort it all out.”

Leclerc admitted his error and agreed the situation needed addressing. “We just need to fix whatever is not working,” he said. “It’s a tricky situation to be in and obviously speaking about these things it’s difficult in a way, it’s not acceptable, this is all I can say in a way. It’s always tricky whenever we find ourselves on track.”

The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 11:24:22 GMT

‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

On Wednesday, the regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January, pushing the annual bill to £2,166 for a typical household.

Rising petrol prices and diesel hitting a record high lifted the UK’s headline inflation rate to 3.6% in October, its highest level in a year. The Bank of England says inflation could hit 5% next year.

It is now half a decade since inflation first went above the 2% target set by the government. Consumer prices have galloped by almost a third over that same time. A return to the target is not expected until 2028 at the earliest.

So far, households have proven surprisingly resilient. Consumer confidence surveys bear this out. Retail sales in October were stronger than expected, even though some of this was driven by a rush to stockpile emergency supplies.

But there is a storm coming. Especially if the El Niño forecast is right and we have a very cold January.

As autumn gives way to winter, low-income households will be hardest hit as the mercury drops. Record numbers of families cannot afford the essentials. The places feeling the pinch most will also be the ones where Burnham has promised to turn things around.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows that after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, inflation rose most in towns and cities that entered the cost of living crisis in a precarious position. Small towns in the north of England, Midlands and Wales were most exposed. Households in Burnley, Blackburn and Blackpool faced an inflation rate nearly three percentage points higher than those in London, Reading and Cambridge.

Part of this is because the recent inflationary burst has been driven by the price of energy and food, hitting low-income families most because they spend proportionally more on essentials than the wealthiest. And that means some places are harder hit than others because despite the promises of successive governments, Britain’s regional income gaps have barely shifted in three decades.

According to research from the Resolution Foundation, the places that were performing worst in the late 1990s are still at the bottom of the living standards league table a generation later. Disposable incomes in Kensington and Chelsea, at £60,584, remain four-and-a-half times higher than in Leicester, at £13,398.

But in response to the cost of living squeeze, Burnham’s government has, perhaps surprisingly, taken a remarkably blunt approach.

At the autumn budget, the “breathing space” measures announced by John Healey prioritised an across-the-board freeze in fuel duty and £100 energy rebate for every household in council tax bands A to D. The removal of standing charges from gas bills that was also announced will not come into effect until the end of 2027.

The poorest households will benefit from the £150 warm homes discount, on top of a universal VAT cut to electricity bills. But charities warn that overall the government’s limited ambition and relatively poor targeting will fail to meet the moment.

Despite the gloom, there are caveats. After more than three decades of entrenched regional inequality, it would be unreasonable to expect Burnham to turn things around overnight. The legacy of austerity and Britain’s tight fiscal position make his task harder. After years of politicians pursuing a quick fix – often with disastrous consequences – his long-term approach is to be commended.

There are also signs that the outlook could improve. The global oil price has fallen back since the blow to Donald Trump’s authority in the US midterm elections. Brent crude has dropped to about $90 a barrel, down from a peak of close to $120 as recently as the end of October. Growth in Britain’s economy has proven more resilient than feared, helped by the rollout of AI, and unemployment has fallen back in recent months.

Figures show food price inflation was lower than expected in October, at 0.9%, the lowest increase since September 2021. How long this lasts, however, is a moot point, amid expectations of a surge in grocery prices next year linked to higher energy costs and El Niño hitting harvests worldwide.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, suggested last week that the pull back in global energy prices could lead headline inflation to fall short of Threadneedle Street’s forecasts for next year.

However, the longer the Iran war rumbles on, the greater the chance of the Bank raising interest rates to keep inflation in check. Financial markets predict three quarter-point increases next year, adding to the financial squeeze for most households. The first could come as early as next month.

In Britain’s poorest postcodes, a tough winter looms. For Burnham’s No 1 political priority, that is a problem.

Now, having time and space in the house where we don’t have to worry is a luxury. It has made sex a lot more fun, as I don’t feel split or divided in my role as a wife and mother. Sex feels a lot more like play. We both enjoy role play and I enjoy Richard taking photographs of me.

Sex with Richard was always positive and pleasurable, but it didn’t feel the same way as it does now. About 90% of the time I was in my conscious brain and overthinking, but now I can much more easily switch into a different space where I’m really not thinking consciously at all. And there’s real pleasure in that escape. On top of the physical pleasure, that in itself is a joy.

Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 11:00:26 GMT

I believe human judgment remains essential

Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?

In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.

I earned my PhD in 1993 and built a life around research, teaching, and mentoring. I’d love to prove that Ramanujan’s tau function never vanishes, or that half of the partition numbers are even. My 25-year-old self would have been crushed by what we are witnessing today. Nothing I write can reassure someone just starting a career. I can explain why I stayed.

My father, a number theorist, died in January. As a boy, I learned from him about Ramanujan, whose notebooks have occupied mathematicians for generations. Ramanujan believed a Hindu goddess gave him mathematical formulas in his dreams. When I considered working on AI, I feared my father would see it as abandoning mathematics. Instead, he told me AI reminded him of Ramanujan: discoveries from an unexpected source might leave us much to understand. I do not take that comparison literally. Ramanujan was a human with an extraordinary imagination and life. My father’s response brought me to tears. It gave me permission to keep being a mathematician in a way I had not anticipated.

Today, I am on leave from the University of Virginia and work as Founding Mathematician at Axiom Math. We use AI to formalize, verify and extend mathematical proofs in Lean, a language in which a small checking program verifies each step. This work can expose gaps and make proofs inspectable and reusable. Human judgment remains essential: we must check that the formal statement says what we intended.

We released the first complete Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, one of mathematics’ largest proofs. Announced in 1983, the classification required decades of work by many mathematicians; a major gap was filled in 2004. Our AI helped produce 43.1 million lines of Lean code. In the process, we found a problem in a published route to a key theorem and supplied an alternative argument. Lean’s kernel checks the resulting formal proof. The mathematics belongs to the generations who developed it. Our formalizations of the classification and other bodies of math are already helping us build and check further mathematics.

After 24 days of work, I watched the final milestones land on my laptop. I cried. I thought about the people who had made the classification possible, and about the father I could no longer tell. But I am 58. I’ve advised 35 PhD students, 17 postdocs, and hundreds of undergraduates. I’ve had opportunities young mathematicians cannot assume. I cannot ask a graduate student to regard uncertainty as an adventure because I have found rewarding work within it.

At a Berkeley colloquium two days after OpenAI announced its Navier–Stokes solution, a scheduled lecture became a town hall lasting almost two and a half hours. Students asked about credit, transparency, hiring, and how mathematicians whose work came first were treated. Some asked me what I would do to help them. Campus security was locking the building as we left.

The declaration A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, signed by Terry Tao and other Fields Medalists, warns about rushed announcements, inadequate attribution and the loss of mathematical understanding. I share those concerns. At a National Academies meeting, I put my position this way: hope is not a plan, and nostalgia is not mentoring.

Universities, journals, employers and funding agencies must decide what they support and reward. Students and younger colleagues should have a voice while those decisions are still open, as should mathematicians who choose to work without AI. In the discussions where I have a voice, I will argue for that participation.

Students need room to struggle with mathematics and learn to question the tools they use. In my advising, I will ask what a young mathematician understood, originated, or made possible. Access to a powerful system is no substitute for those contributions. For work I help publish, readers should know what has been proved, what remains assumed, and who contributed the ideas.

I want my students, and their students, to develop ideas that are genuinely their own. I want them to have colleagues who listen and the material support to pursue a mathematical life. My work at Axiom is one part of how I am trying to contribute. It does not replace my obligations as a teacher and mentor. I may be wrong about how this will unfold. I am still learning what it means to be a mathematician.

Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.

These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 10:00:24 GMT

Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

The Welsh writer Richard King’s oral history of his home country, Brittle With Relics, contains a fascinating quotation from Nicky Wire of those sons of the South Wales coalfield the Manic Street Preachers. Wire’s father was a miner before he joined the army and then came home to work as a carpenter and builder in a local economy that was thriving. Back then, to be working class did not axiomatically mean you were short of money; workers’ collective clout, moreover, delivered exactly what the 21st-century labour market so lacks.

“The pay levels in the 60s and the 70s were brilliant for working-class people,” says Wire. “Everyone in our valley was wearing suits and going to Tunisia on package holidays … My dad just worked his bollocks off; he was one of the great workers. When he passed away, we had ‘Father, son, brother, worker’ on his memorial stone, because that’s what he did.”

Far too many lives, in wildly diverse parts of the economy, are now a long way from that kind of everyday pride and contentment, something proved by no end of research. Only a few weeks ago, for instance, the Resolution Foundation published analysis of new information from the British Social Attitudes survey. The headline findings were that job satisfaction in the UK has dropped to the lowest level ever recorded and that “the proportion [of workers] willing to work harder than required to help their employer succeed has fallen to its lowest ever level over the past decade” (it stands at a pretty miserable 55%). The proportion saying they had an interesting job fell from 74% to 63%. The share reporting opportunities for advancement went from 35% to 26%.

In its soul Labour still thinks its basic mission is to right such wrongs. But from the Tony Blair years onwards, the party’s thinking has also been regularly warped by inclinations that it ought to find objectionable: to shove people into work irrespective of what that entails, and to emphasise the need to redesign human beings to somehow fit with the mercurial, often cruel ways of modern capitalism rather than making perfectly justified demands for the latter to change.

Which brings us to the report about young people and employment – and more specifically Neets, or those not in education, employment or training – put together by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn and published this week. On a long train journey I read all 1,005 of its numbered paragraphs and was struck by a few things: the thoroughness of its research and the urgency of its tone – but one glaring absence: of any meaningful examination of what might be shorthanded as “bad work” despite its centrality to just about everything Milburn has worked on.

Milburn partly blames the current crisis on how the state delivers benefits, education and health. (There is a whole other piece that could be written about how a proposed £3.6bn of cuts to so-called “welfare” risk so impoverishing vulnerable young people that they will be pushed even further away from the labour market.) He rightly points out a “long-term decline in entry-level employment, youth apprenticeships and employer investment in training”. But though he also rather grandly proposes “a new bargain between government and employers to create and sustain more opportunities for young people”, you soon realise what he means – as evidenced by whispers currently circulating about the abandonment of some of Angela Rayner’s new programme of improved workers’ rights, Milburn gets close to proposing not to expect more from employers but less.

“Employers have faced higher costs, a maze of schemes, fragmented support and growing uncertainty about the rules of the game,” he says, and have been “treated as if they were the problem rather than a central part of the solution”. He has picked up concerns about Rayner’s workplace changes, he adds, centred on “the impact the new legislation may have on youth hiring, especially in hospitality and retail”. But that kind of talk risks defending the indefensible: a recent report from the TUC not only highlighted the low pay and job insecurity seemingly endemic to those sectors of the economy but also pointed out how they contribute to “economic inactivity generally and specifically the rise in mental distress and economic inactivity among young people”. Letting them off the hook, in other words, may not ease the Neets crisis but worsen it.

There is another very illuminating TUC report, published in 2020, about working for Amazon (the company, for some reason, is thanked in the Milburn report’s acknowledgements). Its central beef was “a business model that functions on driving down workers’ rights”, and what Amazon demands of its employees: in the UK, it said, “pickers are expected to pick and pack around 300 items per hour, [and] employees tend to only either do day or night shifts and working weeks average around 55 hours… especially over the peak Christmas period”.

Both Milburn’s interim report and his final text are full of telling phrases: on this score, although he does acknowledge that the quality of work available to young people has generally “worsened”, he merely observes that “warehouse jobs require speed, precision and compliance with tightly managed performance systems”, while the 1980s’ chaotic decimation of traditional work that opened the way for businesses such as Amazon is blankly – and hilariously – summed up as “industrial restructuring”. That suggests order and purpose, but the result has been anarcho-capitalism and lives rendered all but impossible. In 2022, the company’s annual employee turnover in the US was reckoned to be 150%. The rational response to that kind of working culture is what sits at the heart of the Neets story: people recoil and retreat.

In the short term what Milburn recommends – among other things, a new youth opportunities service and increased spending on subsidising young people into work – may well lessen the crisis he says he wants to solve. But it will also leave such fundamental problems almost completely untouched. The point is plain: not least for the young, until work is comprehensively reinjected with respect, humanity and decent levels of pay, the Neets crisis – and our national malaise – will go on.

How do you even begin to do that? As the venerable Wes Streeting once said, the only thing worse than no hope is false hope, but the prime minister has suggested that he might know, talking confidently about reindustrialisation and – oh yes – somehow rolling back 40 years of neoliberalism. His fabled 10-year plan is apparently due before the end of the year – for now, along with all those Neets, we carry on waiting for the great leap forwards.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

England aim to avoid Gold Coast traps as Will Jacks heads home with injury

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 10:00:24 GMT

Harry Brook’s T20 side to play at ground famous in Ashes folklore after setback against below-strength Australia

As England’s cricketers arrived on the Gold Coast on Sunday at the start of schoolies week, it was hard not to wonder whether, a year on from their notorious break in Noosa during the Ashes, this was some kind of trap.

Schoolies, for the uninitiated, is when hordes of high school graduates kick back at the end of the academic year: one final week of revelry before going their separate ways. To give a flavour, one of the first things your correspondent saw on arrival was a young man on a Lime bike, shirtless, holding an inflatable phallus. Good lord.

English cricketers have a bit of history of mischief in these parts themselves, of course, with Tuesday’s second T20 international against Australia the first time the senior men’s side will have played at Carrara Oval since January 1991 – aka “the “Tiger Moth” incident that is very much part of Ashes folklore.

It came during a tour match against Queensland when David Gower and John Morris sneaked out to the neighbouring airstrip, hopped in a biplane, and persuaded the pilot to buzz the outfield while Robin Smith and Allan Lamb were batting out in the middle. The press got wind and fines were issued – even if the pair have doubtless since turned this into a profit on the after-dinner speaking circuit.

Last year’s brief escape to Noosa on the Sunshine Coast, 140 miles north of here, slightly pales in comparison, even if that “mid-tour break” involving a few beers on the beach garnered significant local media attention. Harry Brook called it a “belting time” when pitching up for the third Test in Adelaide afterwards – a quote that took on a new complexion at the end of the 4-1 defeat, when news of his ill-fated night out in Wellington on the preceding New Zealand tour emerged.

Brook has since bucked up his ideas and England’s white-ball sides have made tangible progress too. Saturday night’s three-wicket defeat by Australia at the MCG was a setback, however, especially since only Mitch Marsh, Tim David and Adam Zampa of the victors can claim to be bona fide first-choice players in this format. Word has it the hosts have christened themselves the “BBL All Stars” during this low-key series.

England are not at full strength either but still boast plenty more experience and caps. A further dilution has occurred, however, with confirmation that Will Jacks sustained a broken right hand on Saturday and is flying back to the UK. It was a sickening blow, with blood pouring on to the outfield and Jacks visibly nauseous as he walked off after being struck by a crunching return drive from Ben Dwarshuis while bowling.

England are working on a replacement squad player but, as a middle-order batter who bowls spin, James Coles is the logical choice in terms of Tuesday’s XI. The 22-year-old will be hoping his international debut goes better than the outing as a sub fielder on Saturday, when a needless shy at the stumps during the final pressure moments of the chase handed Australia an extra run.

after newsletter promotion

Coles is a better cricketer than that brain fade and will be keen to show that his summer struggles with London Spirit in the Hundred – having been signed for a staggering £390,000 in the auction – were similarly not representative. By his own admission, Coles battled with the attention that huge price tag brought, even if a string of binary scores were mildly offset by some tidy work with the ball.

No Jacks presents another problem for England, with the all-rounder previously lined up to captain the fifth T20 in Canberra on 3 December when Brook will have left for the Tests in South Africa. Tom Banton, in form on tour and a close ally of Brook ever since their England Under-19s days, has been named as the new vice-captain.

For now, though, with distractions aplenty in this part of the world, England’s focus is squarely on levelling the series and ensuring that, come Wednesday morning, the only headaches belong to the local schoolies.

‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 10:00:24 GMT

The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in

Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …”

The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker.

The pair are two weeks into filming series five of The Trip, the show devised by director Michael Winterbottom as a kind of blurry version of the actors’ real lives. Each season sends them on a kind of Epicurean road trip, under the guise of a journalistic commission; this time, the conceit is that Brydon is making a podcast for the Guardian, and Coogan has agreed to tag along.

Over the past 16 years, The Trip has taken them from the north of England to a meandering tour of Italy, via Spain and Greece. Now they have reached Scandinavia, heading through Sweden and Norway and up to the Arctic Circle, taking in luxury hotels, fishing huts, brown cheese and reindeer.

It has been six years since they last convened. Since then, much has happened in their lives. Brydon is an established national treasure, hosting gameshows and voicing Julia Donaldson adaptations, even writing a children’s book of his own. Coogan has combined a broad populism – revisiting his comic creation Alan Partridge and a turn in The White Lotus, with more nuanced projects – playing Jimmy Savile, for instance, and writing and producing Stephen Frears’s film The Lost King.

After breakfast, filming moves to the hotel spa, where Coogan and Brydon sit in bathrobes to record a podcast episode, their conversation drifting once again from saunas to birch twigs to an analysis of their own physiques. Meanwhile, the crew fold themselves into tight corners, hover behind camera lines, try not to laugh. All these years in, the show remains joyously funny. Still, in this quiet landscape it is hard not to notice the sense of contemplation that runs through this series; a rumination on age and friendship, pleasure, purpose, isolation and joy.

It is the following summer when we meet again: a wildly hot day in a central London hotel. By this stage, the series is finished, and Coogan has watched three episodes. “I was surprised at how much I laughed,” he says. “My memory was that it was just a bit haphazard and a bit silly, but different enough for it to be charming. What I wasn’t expecting was to find it so warm and welcoming. Throughout all the cynicism and arguments and spikiness, it has a real humanity.”

For a time they sit and discuss the moments that did not make the final cut: James Bond references, digs at other comedians, a plunge into a bracingly cold river. Some established elements of the show remain: there are the famed impressions, jabs about the directions of their respective careers, the appeal of light entertainment, the allure of politics, their differing relationships. But there are shifts in this series, too: subtle turns in subject matter, the old prickliness of their exchanges often giving way to a kind of tenderness.

They are keen, as ever, to differentiate between their onscreen relationship and a real-life friendship that has run for 30 years. These days, Brydon says the pair “get together and talk about middle-aged things”. Coogan nods. “We talk about things that are achingly middle-class preoccupations,” he says. “Things that are very, very unsympathetic.” He reels off a couple of examples: second homes, complaining about staff. “You see, when I was young and from a lower middle-class background, people used to laugh and joke and say: ‘Oh, you just can’t get the staff …’” he says. “And now I’m 60, and I’m in a different socioeconomic position, I do know what that means.”

Brydon looks up. “By the time this comes out, you’ll be 61,” he says. “It’s probably better to say 61. Let’s just say you’re mid-60s.”

Coogan frowns. “No,” he says. “Don’t say that.”

The matter of age runs through The Trip to the northern lights. Today, they talk about the subject with a kind of zeal. “What you notice is that thing of being a bit more carpe diem, a bit more living in the moment,” says Coogan. “Just trying to stand outside yourself, and celebrating if things are good.”

He noticed this growing feeling in his late 50s, though it only seemed to gather pace as he reached 60, and became a grandfather. “It’s a visceral, animal thing,” he says. “I’ve got a granddaughter, and I just want to see her, I just want to be with her, in a way that transcends all of the stuff. I want that almost like a child wants something.” He smiles. “Getting old is quite like being a child,” he says. “Children live in the moment, and they absorb, and they’re quite visceral. And I think when you get older, you start to do that too. I just want to do funny voices. And make her laugh and that’s enough.”

“What do you do for her, Neil Kinnock?” asks Brydon. “The wheels on the bus go round and round,” he sings in a recognisably Kinnockian intonation.

Coogan nods. “Yes,” he says. “Just because I know that when she gets older and she starts asking, what does it mean: ‘Hiring taxis to scuttle around handing out redundancy notices to its own workers’?”

For Brydon, 61, age has brought a sense of broadening fascination. “I’ve become interested in other things,” he says, “and I love the feeling – and this is going to look awful written down – that I’m evolving.” He speaks of a reverence for nature: birdsong, trees, the feel of his bare feet on the grass. But also for jazz and old cars. “I’m in a very fortunate position,” he says, “to have lots of opportunities to experience new things.”

“That’s the thing,” Coogan says. “Because at a certain level, where we are, we are infantilised. And that can be good and bad. The term ‘behaving like a child’ is double-edged: you can be conceited and selfish, but you can also be curious and open.”

“Which of those would you say you are?” Brydon wonders.

“Sometimes I’m spoilt and I feel like things should just be done for me,” Coogan says. “But I also feel like I’m still able to have a sense of play. Children, when they’re really young, they’re not worried if they’re cool or not, they just do things.” Sometimes, he adds, he looks at politicians young enough to be his own child, and they seem so grown up. “There’s no sense of any playfulness or childlike qualities left in them,” he says, and sighs heavily.

We meet on the day that Nigel Farage is rumoured to be triggering a byelection in his Clacton seat. “Has he resigned?” Brydon asks. “Let’s find out.” He slips into the voice of a TV news anchor. “Steve Coogan is in central London. Steve, what’s the latest on this?”

Coogan checks his phone. “Latest one hour ago. Oh, seven minutes ago. Oh, oh, oh. He’s resigned. He has resigned.” He reads Farage’s statement aloud. “Now, that’s a gamble. A bit like old Burnham’s gamble.”

“Which position will you be taking up in Andy Burnham’s cabinet?” Brydon asks him. In 2025, Coogan was appointed co-chair of the Middleton Mayoral development corporation – a move by Burnham, then still mayor of Greater Manchester, to regenerate the actor’s home town. When Burnham duly campaigned for election in the Makerfield byelection, Coogan joined him on the doorstep. “So what would it be, Defence?” Brydon continues, as Coogan explains his role in Middleton. “Secretary of state for defence, Steve Coogan?”

Coogan bats the idea away. “I am very supportive of him,” he says. “He’s trying to do something really distinctive to get away from Westminster-centric politics. I blame the rise of Reform squarely on what I would call north London intellectual liberals who are part of the cabal of centrist moderation, where they think whether you’re left or right is just an intellectual position, like a game of chess.”

He leans forward in the overstuffed armchair, gathering speed and intensity. “It’s been a game that’s been going on for the last 40 years,” he says. “And people in the provinces, in post-industrial areas, it means nothing to them and nothing has changed. The only relation to working-class people they have is when the plumber comes round. But they have no real empathy for them. And as long as we have people who seem like they’re just a sensible chap, doing a sensible job, Reform will continue to gather momentum because working-class people are fed up, they’re lashing out, they want an alternative, and there are no alternatives around. And that is squarely the fault of the Hampstead Pansies.” He pauses, breathes. “That’s it,” he says.

Brydon describes himself as “probably one of those centrists”. He is not without passion or belief, but when he speaks about his experience of life it is with more contentment than hunger. “I don’t subscribe to more, better, best,” he says. “I feel my role in life is to entertain people.” He talks of how often people approach him to thank him for his work – in Gavin & Stacey, say, or hosting Would I Lie to You? “And I’m very happy with that. I’m happy doing it. And I feel that that is what I put into the world. I try and do good. But I’m not an activist. I’m just not that person.”

It is interesting, then, to think of the young Brydon. The son of a car salesman and a teacher, he grew up in Baglan, near Port Talbot, coming of age at the height of Thatcherism, and just as the nearby steelworks was forced to lay off half its workers. There was certainly something in him that did not want to stick around; like Coogan, he applied, unsuccessfully, to Rada. Surely that shows a dream of something more or better?

“Yes,” he concedes, “in those days, of course. But success came to me later. Steve was successful in his 20s. I was 34, 35, and I had been around the block. I’d had limited success in Wales as a radio and TV personality. And by the time I met Steve, I was making a nice living – ski holidays, two cars, all that stuff – because I was a voice artist. But then it came. So I think I’ve always appreciated it more. I already had three children so I’d matured to a certain degree.”

“The thing Rob has done, what’s not often addressed, is he could have gone down the route of just being a lightweight, fringe act – someone who gets by with getting the stuff that more successful people reject,” Coogan says. “Mopping stuff up, making a living, just getting by by being affable. But, no.” There was a period, he points out, where Brydon was writing and starring in the devastatingly dark comedies Human Remains and Marion & Geoff, and simultaneously making appearances on the Home Shopping network. “The thing I’ve always said to Rob is, he’s a brilliant character actor, but he’s sort of …” he tries to find the most diplomatic way to put it, “… he’s not neglected that, but he’s …”

“Well, I did a bit,” says Brydon. “But when you talk about being content and everything, what no one ever mentions is my five children. When people talk about people’s careers, it’s as if they’re existing in a vacuum. And for me, the choices that I make are because I don’t want to go away. For the last 30 years I’ve had children growing up and the need and the want to be around. So that has been a big part of my career.”

By contrast, Coogan has one daughter, who is now 30. It has been a long time since he was bound by the restrictions of childcare and school holidays. “I do feel like I’m a bit like I’m 24 and have no responsibilities,” he says. “I’ve got a partner, but she has a career, she has another life.”

The divergent paths of their careers is sometimes puzzling to Coogan. He is confused by Brydon’s willingness to be a personality, his ease at being recognised. “You’re so accessible and approachable, they feel like they know you,” he says. Once, the pair walked together up a mountain, and as other walkers approached, Coogan found himself looking away for fear of being recognised. “But he would be face-forward, open and friendly. I would want to avoid that like the plague.” It is easier, sometimes, for him to play a role; Partridge, for example, or even the augmented version of himself we see in The Trip. “Basically, because I don’t feel entirely comfortable in my own skin,” he says.

“That’s the difference,” Brydon interjects. “I do.”

Accordingly, Brydon is quite happy with the span of his career – one week hosting ITV gameshow The Floor, the next playing Peter O’Toole in a Radio 4 drama, followed by “a big animated film” and a new sitcom, Bills Included, for Coogan co-founded production company, Baby Cow. He is never quite sure where the road will take him.

“But the joke I always say is that ‘Steve is driven. I like to be driven. In an S-Class Mercedes or equivalent.’” Coogan laughs. “It was you who said to specify that,” Brydon tells him.

“Well I don’t like people carriers,” Coogan says affably. “The Mercedes – which I wouldn’t drive, but I’d quite like to be a passenger in – is because you can make the rear seat recline. And that’s very important because I like to nap. Now that might sound like I’m a prima donna, but I do like to nap, because I’m 60.”

They joke for a moment about how they are ageing “properly”; a careful balance of somnolence and wonder. I think back to one night in Norway, when Brydon had headed off to bed, and a member of staff rushed in and urged us all to hurry outside. In the cold night air we gathered in the courtyard and looked up. There, high above the silent rooftops, the northern lights undulated across the sky: pale green and pink and golden. I remember how we stood there, quite rapt. And how I looked across at Coogan, and saw his face, lit up like a child. There in the moment, enjoying everything.

The Trip to the Northern Lights starts Thurs 10 December on Sky Atlantic & Now.
