There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 07:00:22 GMT

As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action

Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never.

They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street.

Today, I support survivors through Surviving Universal UK, the country’s only Black-led specialist organisation dedicated to spiritual and cultic abuse. After years of campaigning, 2026 is shaping up to be a historic year for survivors in Britain. The silence is finally beginning to break.

On Monday, MPs debated support for people leaving what are officially called “high-control religious groups”. Led by Labour MP Sam Carling, the debate brought a neglected issue into mainstream British politics. Carling explicitly described the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG) as a cult. Other groups were also named in the debate. MPs raised concerns about constituents harmed by high-control groups and inadequate protections.

For survivors watching, the significance was immense. Many had waited years for this moment of public acknowledgment and political attention. The UCKG is no obscure underground movement. It is a registered charity with branches across Britain, investigated by the BBC’s Panorama and by national newspapers.

But what made the debate even more significant was the discussion of change. MPs pressed for stronger protections and a serious examination of whether existing legislation is fit for purpose. The government was urged to act. Survivors were finally being heard openly in parliament itself.

I welcome that political attention. I also know that recognition alone cannot protect anyone.

There have been other encouraging developments. In February, the Crown Prosecution Service included spiritual abuse in its updated guidance on honour-based abuse, including harmful practices associated with supposed demonic possession. Plans for an all-party parliamentary group examining spiritual, ritual and cultic abuse are taking shape. Meanwhile, Surviving Universal UK has demanded a national call for evidence.

Britain has hardly been short of warnings. From the Jesus Army to SPAC Nation, alleged and documented cases of abuse involving high-control groups have made headlines for years. Yet each scandal is treated as isolated.

Such abuse is not exclusively religious. High-control groups can emerge in political movements, therapeutic settings or around charismatic individuals. What matters is not what members believe, but how power is exercised over them. We already recognise coercive control within domestic abuse. We understand how manipulation erodes independence. Yet when similar behaviour occurs within a group, our legal and safeguarding responses become far less assured.

I know how frightening that control can be. When questioning authority supposedly endangers your relationships or salvation, leaving is rarely as simple as walking through a door. In February, the Home Office said it did not intend to extend the coercive control offence under the Serious Crime Act 2015 beyond personally connected relationships. Asked specifically about cults, extremist groups and gangs, it argued that expansion could create uncertainty for police and prosecutors.

That response troubled me deeply. Since when did the complexity of protecting survivors become a justification for leaving them without adequate safety? Existing laws can address rape, assault and fraud. But sustained psychological coercion does not always fit neatly into those offences. Survivors should not have to wait for another crime to occur before the harm they are experiencing is recognised.

Elsewhere, governments are beginning to approach this differently. France has a dedicated public body, Miviludes, monitoring harmful sectarian practices. In July, a parliamentary inquiry in Victoria, Australia, made 39 recommendations concerning cults and organised fringe groups, including consideration of legislation addressing group-based coercion.

The inquiry focused on harmful conduct, not legitimate belief. That distinction matters. Religious freedom is fundamental, but it cannot mean freedom from scrutiny when abuse is alleged. Accountability is not persecution. Britain should be capable of upholding both principles.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The consequences extend beyond courtrooms. Someone leaving an abusive relationship can, at least in principle, access established safeguarding procedures and specialist services. A person escaping a cult may discover that the professional responsible for helping them has little understanding of what they have endured.

For Black and global-majority survivors, those barriers can be compounded by racism, religious stigma and a shortage of culturally competent support. I have spent years advocating for people whose experiences are too often misunderstood by the very institutions to which they turn for help.

And we must challenge the idea that people join cults because they lack intelligence. People seek belonging. They want answers, reassurance and somewhere to feel valued. Exploitative groups can manipulate those entirely human needs until the community that once offered comfort becomes almost impossible to leave.

Britain needs a national call for evidence, specialist training for frontline professionals and serious consideration of legal protections against group-based coercion. Survivors must be central to shaping that response. Survivors still struggle to have their experiences recognised as abuse.

As 2026 draws to a close, the shift is unmistakable. New guidance, growing parliamentary scrutiny and Monday’s debate have made this a historic year for recognition. Parliamentarians acknowledged the problem and called for change. Those words carry weight, particularly for survivors who have spent years fighting to be heard. But parliament must now turn its attention into action. I hope, for the sake of current and future victims and survivors, that those who spoke so powerfully make good on their commitments.

Britain is finally confronting its cult problem. Better late than never. But survivors have waited long enough for recognition. What we need now is protection, and a meaningful route to justice and recovery.

Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline. org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org.

Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 06:00:19 GMT

After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide, although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals.

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. They immediately spun this to the media, suggesting that all software, everywhere, is extraordinarily vulnerable to AI-driven hacking – and offering their tools to banks and spying agencies.

Some have argued that this hype is not entirely justified, suggesting that many vulnerabilities these models discover are not particularly useful to hackers. But the threat of AI-driven hacking has changed the game.

One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer, a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip.

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items, as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

More troubling hacks, and more conspiracy theories, are probably on the horizon. The senior cybersecurity professional said heightened public awareness of cyber disruption had led to hypersensitivity about any incident.

“It’s like the tide has gone out on cybersecurity in terms of public perception, and there’s the same amount of wrecks out there as there have been for years. Any time you change a complex system, stuff happens.”

However, the professional is concerned that AI, with its capacity to identify flaws, help plan attacks and execute them, will be harnessed by “already very competent” adversaries. Referring to the general state of IT security around the world, the source added: “Thank goodness we haven’t had an AI-sourced vulnerability that is easy to exploit. Because that would be carnage.”

For many, though, recent events have been bad enough.

When Josephine’s* prescription request for lithium for her bipolar disorder was lost “in the ether” during the global Microsoft outage, she admits she was “freaking out”.

“My medication is life-changing and keeps me stable,” said the 26-year-old, a student living in the east of England. After an agonising wait, she was finally able to collect her prescription, but the experience has left her deeply troubled.

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

* Name has been changed

Additional reporting by Jane Clinton

The Trump-Putin alliance threatens every European country – yet gushing populists still cheer them

The Guardian Sun, 22 Nov 2026 05:00:17 GMT

Europe’s future will be fought over at the ballot box and on Ukraine’s frontline. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits

On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940.

For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 35 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size.

Not that they have needed much of a reminder. Over the past decade, there has been interference in its politics, propaganda targeting Estonia’s Russian-speaking minority, and a host of cyber and hybrid attacks, the most recent of which was an attempted arson attack targeting an Estonian defence company last Saturday.

“The goal is to create fear in our society,” Margus Tsahkna, Estonia’s foreign minister, told me by phone from Tallinn. The only thing protecting Estonia’s independence, he said, was membership of the EU and – most importantly – Nato. “Without Nato membership we couldn’t have this conversation. Estonia would have been 100% occupied.”

Long before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Vladimir Putin was arguing that the decision of former Soviet or Warsaw Pact states in central and eastern Europe to seek sanctuary in Nato was an act of aggression. It’s an argument that tramples on those countries’ independence, denying them the basic right to decide their own security arrangements. Countries previously invaded, occupied or controlled by Moscow want to be protected against any repeat.

Until recently, Putin’s case gained little support among mainstream western politicians. But since Donald Trump’s return to office in January 2025, Putin has found a valuable ally in high office. “It’s my friend!” Trump excitedly said, as he greeted Putin on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen this week.

Trump and Putin share the same view of Europe: a once-great Christian civilisation that has destroyed itself through migration, particularly from Muslim-majority countries. They also share the dangerous belief that great powers – and they both think they are – should be able to control their own back yards. For Trump, that means the western hemisphere is his; for Putin, that means the west should not interfere in central and eastern Europe. The trilateral summit in Shenzhen alongside Xi Jinping, combined with the genuine bonhomie between the two men, was partially aimed at cementing this idea.

Throughout the stop-start peace talks led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and his former real-estate pal Steve Witkoff, Putin has pushed the idea of broadening the discussion to include Europe as a whole, not just Ukraine. He wants Nato to withdraw its troops and bases to its 1997 borders, meaning 16 nations in the alliance would have no outside support. Estonia and the other Baltic nations would, for instance, be left without air defences. Putin has also demanded that Britain and France rule out using their nuclear weapons to protect any other European nation. Any deal for Ukraine, Putin argues, must be part of a wider agreement on Europe.

Trump seems to like the idea. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office last week, he talked about the prospect of a grand deal. “It’s going to be very big. It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled,” he said. Anyone who believes in a free Europe won’t be “thrilled”, but Trump doesn’t want a strong Europe, which he has long seen as an adversary. It also tallies with Trump’s other main position on Europe: that it’s a continent of freeloaders that the US has been protecting against its own national interest.

For more than a year, Europe has largely been excluded from the Ukraine talks. In Abu Dhabi, where a group of European national security advisers had come to meet on the sidelines, Kushner was upbeat about the continent finally having a formal role in future talks. But Europe has finally found itself at the table – only to discover that Europe itself is on the menu.

The Trump-Putin alliance threatens the future of Europe, not least because there are some European politicians who welcome it. In the next three years, far-right or hard-right parties could win power – or at the least join the governing coalition – in western Europe’s four biggest nations: the UK, France, Germany and Italy. The leaders of all four parties are either openly sympathetic to Putin or, at very least, critical of Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Marine Le Pen, who remains favourite to win the French presidency next spring, has vowed to “end financial aid” to Ukraine within six months of taking office and has refused an offer from Zelenskyy to visit him in Kyiv. In the past, she has been far happier meeting Putin – a photo of the two shaking hands featured prominently on her election leaflets in 2022, until the war in Ukraine made the image electoral poison.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), doesn’t attempt to hide her contempt for Ukraine. If the AfD were in power – and they currently lead Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats by eight percentage points – Germany would end all military and economic aid. In an interview with the Economist last month, she questioned Ukraine’s democracy, arguing it was “impossible” for them to win and, in an echo of Putin, said “Russia’s security interest” must be taken into account.

after newsletter promotion

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has surprisingly been one of Ukraine’s staunchest allies, but now faces a new far-right challenger, Roberto Vannacci, whose policy on Ukraine echoes the AfD’s. Vannacci has questioned whether Alexei Navalny was killed by the Russian state, claims that Russia is a democracy and, when asked who he prefers between Putin and Zelenskyy, chose the Russian leader.

And then there is Britain. Nigel Farage is smart enough to realise that Putin is deeply unpopular in the UK, but in the past he has repeatedly expressed his admiration for the Russian leader. Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Farage claimed the west had “provoked the war” by “poking the bear”, and he blamed Zelenskyy for Trump’s Oval Office ambush, accusing him of being “rude”. Last month, Farage claimed Ukraine was “one of the most corrupt countries on earth” and a Reform government would take a “keen look” at British aid to the country.

The growing popularity of the anti-Ukraine far right, most notably in France, has not gone unnoticed by Kyiv’s biggest supporters. Merz has not only promised to block the next seven-year EU budget unless there is a substantial aid package for Ukraine, but he has also proposed making any future lending subject to qualified majority voting rather than unanimity. This would mean that if a President Le Pen wanted to block an EU-wide aid package, she would need to get several other countries to join her.

But support for Ukraine may be slipping, not helped by a continent-wide cost of living crisis. “It is easy to manipulate people with easy solutions,” said Tsahkna, the Estonian foreign minister. He fears the elections in France and Germany could fundamentally reshape the continent.

Zelenskyy has long argued that Ukraine’s frontline is Europe’s frontline. The future of the continent is being fought in the Donbas, at the negotiating table and at the ballot box. The Trump-Putin alliance threatens every European nation, but the greatest danger is that those nations elect leaders who support it.

Steve Bloomfield is a Guardian international affairs commentator

This article was amended on 22 November 2026. An earlier version said that it was 25 years since Estonia became independent. Estonia became independent in 1991, 35 years ago.

China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

The Guardian Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:47:57 GMT

Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

Five Great Reads: Brand, the first ‘weird Bond’ and female loneliness

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 21:15:25 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Welcome to the weekend.

As this year slowly winds up, you may be counting down the days – or dreading the holidays (for readers in the United States, Thanksgiving is right around the corner). Either way, we have a great selection of reads for you to gobble up.

Enjoy.

From the court case to the sentencing, the Russell Brand trial dominated headlines, features, podcasts and social media. With 108 journalists listening to proceedings at Southwark crown court, the Guardian’s Amelia Gentleman wondered what else she could add to those collective thoughts. So on the fifth day, she turned left instead of right when she came out of the tube and made her way to a different rape case – just 15 minutes in the other direction.

Notable quote: This is the story of two rape cases: one that the whole world is paying attention to, and one that has attracted no attention at all.

Amelia is the only journalist at court 9 of Inner London crown court, where Michael, a 32-year-old data analyst, is accused of raping a 17-year-old girl. Away from the media circus, similarities run through both cases – tired old court rooms, a lot of praying, power imbalances, rape myths, a defence that rests on consent and the process of justice.

How long will it take to read: 15 and a half minutes.

Further reading: Why did Russell Brand convert to Christianity?

The “epidemic” of loneliness is talked about a lot – the World Health Organization has declared it a priority for public health – but often, notes Elle Hunt, the coverage and conversation focuses on men. Why? She looks at research that suggests women are suffering just as much.

Equally lonely: While global Google searches for “male loneliness” spiked suddenly in mid-2023 and have since seen frequent surges, interest in “female loneliness” has remained a trickle. But studies consistently show similar prevalence between genders. “There’s not really any difference … They’re equally both lonely,” says Michelle Lim, a principal research fellow at the University of Sydney who is also the chief executive of Australia’s Ending Loneliness Together campaign and an adviser to the WHO.

Notable quote: “A man alone is self-sufficient, taking this bold, brave step, versus a woman living alone is a failure, left on the shelf … a weird, unlovable spinster.” – Laura, 41, Auckland

How long will it take to read: Just over four minutes

Further reading: What are you yearning for? We took to the streets to find out.

Robert Pattinson, former teen heart-throb and Twilight star, has been cast as the new James Bond (thanks to Jeff Bezos). Since his early days playing a vampire, Pattinson has become known for his mature and assured performances across a wide range of films. But having been in the spotlight for so long, the star has a checkered Hollywood history ripe for revisiting. In honour of the first “Weird Bond”, Elle Hunt walks us through Pattinson’s “bizarre and baffling lore”.

Would James Bond tell a lie? While on the press circuit, Pattinson is famous for straying from the truth. Why? He says he often makes up stories during interviews out of panic, but has also admitted to telling white lies out of boredom. In 2011, he told the Today Show he witnessed a clown die after their “little car exploded”.

Pastagate: The Covid lockdowns were a weird time for us all. Pattison “let his freak flag fly” like the rest of us, giving an interview to GQ over Zoom that went instantly viral. He claimed to have designed a new form of portable pasta that “you can hold in your hand”. He spent the rest of the interview attempting to show the interviewer how to make his signature dish. How did it go? Read for yourself.

How long will it take to read: Just over four minutes.

Further reading: The best and worst Bond films in one big chart.

Built for short attention spans, viral moments and vertical video, slap fighting is exactly what it says on the tin. The dangers are clear – but is Power Slap the sport we deserve?

The origin story: More than 10 years ago, Raymond Hernandez was bored. After remembering a Japanese gameshow where five men each took a turn slapping each other, Hernandez had an idea and got to work. The first professional slap took place in Texas, and on the second slap, the fighter was knocked out. The footage of the falling fighter went mega-viral and birthed a new sport.

The rules: You must keep your feet on the ground to reduce a slap’s power. No hitting with the heel of the palm and no contact anywhere but the cheek. And above all, no flinching.

The characters: One contestant, Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii, was scouted by producers at a strongman festival. The Siberian farmer was competing in both a slap-fighting and a dumpling-eating contest. Kamotskii won both. His first paycheck for his newfound profession was $25,000 and three goats.

The dangers: are obvious, and experts say the concussion risk is “shocking”.

Further reading: Death is a “distinct possibility”, according to a concussion expert.

Fresh off an appearance on Celebrity Traitors, the enigmatic James Blunt answered 10 chaotic questions with deputy culture editor for Guardian Australia, Sian Cain. From living in Ibiza to working through You’re Beautiful-inspired hatred, the former soldier and singer is leaning into the humour of life.

The James Blunt museum: is a small tribute to the artist based in a Herefordshire phone booth. Reports of its origins are murky, but Blunt says, “I have been known to go there just to give it a quick clean from time to time. It’s not too far, just a quick six-hour drive. I go there for the morning, clean it, head back home. It’s worth a visit if you find yourself in the northern hemisphere. I really recommend it.”

Notable quote: “I do a really good gorilla impression” – Blunt on his secret talent

Sensible quote: “Perspective is everything” – Blunt on dealing with negative reviews

How long will it take to read? The track currently stuck in your head is 3 minutes and 32 seconds. You can read this article in just over two.

Further reading: More chaotic questions.

Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:04:46 GMT

African ministers say they ‘didn’t come here to beg’, with civil society groups calling it the ‘worst Cop ever’

Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.

The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.

On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.

Several Cop insiders said Saudi Arabia was one of the countries playing an obstructive role. The petrostate has gained a reputation over the decades for using the Cop process to slow action. Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in the final agreement as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at the advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there”. He said: “It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests.”

Eight countries called for reference to “a clear transition away from fossil fuels” to be restored into the text of any agreement. Panama, Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, the Solomon Islands and Sweden outlined vital issues they said must be addressed, including ensuring polluting countries paid into funds for developing countries to adapt to the climate crisis.

Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, said: “It is not acceptable to have a Cop or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly.”

Panama had sent an open letter to the president of the negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, with a list of demands the country said were not negotiable.

“Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work,” said Bowen. On Friday afternoon, he said: “There is still a spirit of making it work. People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, let’s give up and go home.”

In a dramatic press conference on Friday morning, African ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone said African people were being asked to pay for a crisis they did not cause. They accused rich countries of simultaneously attempting a third exploitation of the continent – after slavery and colonialism – by using carbon taxes to prevent Africans from making use of their wealth of critical minerals to industrialise.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who was ministerial chair of the African group of negotiators, said: “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them. We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries, that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

A vital request of African nations was for discussion of climate finance. All week civil society observers have accused richer countries, led by the EU, of obstructing progress in talks on money.

The chief climate negotiator for Europe said on Friday that it was already the world leading climate finance donor. A senior EU official said: “We, together with the EU member states, are providing €32.3bn [£27bn] from public sources and mobilising €9.3bn in private finance in 2025 to support developing countries. We’re doing by far the most.”

The last Cop meeting to finish on time was in Italy in 2003. Some talks have dragged into the Sunday after the scheduled Friday finish.

Pochettino’s fiery start, Las Vegas Grand Prix and ATP Finals finale – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:27:24 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The international break is over as domestic football boogies back. Primed to feel the force is Dominic Booth at the helm of our essential gateway to the weekend’s action. Saturday offers a magnificent seven Premier League matches, bookended by Manchester City v Fulham and Newcastle v Arsenal. There is also a full programme of Championship, League One, and League Two fixtures, plus Celtic and Rangers taking to the Glasgow greensward in Scotland. In the WSL, Liverpool host Chelsea before rich kids London City prepare to receive Crystal Palace. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday. live@theguardian. com.

To the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago. The Melbourne Cricket Ground has not always been a happy hunting ground for touring England sides but Harry Brook’s last two visits as captain have been triumphant. A two-day win at the 90,000-capacity venue in last year’s Boxing Day Test was not only the high point of a traumatic Ashes campaign; it was their first red-ball victory on Australian soil since 2011. MCG also hosted England’s T20 World Cup triumph in 2022, where Brook was part of the side that defeated Pakistan to lift the trophy behind enemy lines. Rob Smyth has over-by-over coverage with Ali Martin reporting from Melbourne.

The lunchtime kick-off is a vital one for the hosts. City have wobbled of late, three straight Premier League defeats leave the beleaguered club in third with 21 points from the first 10 games of Enzo Maresca’s tenure. In stark contrast, the Cottagers are unbeaten in their last four games, after four defeats and two draws in their first six. Wins over Hull and Coventry came before draws with Aston Villa and Newcastle. Barry Glendenning helms the blog as Will Unwin reports from the Etihad Stadium.

England are have been transformed since stumbling through the Six Nations and then falling to South Africa at Ellis Park, winning four consecutive Tests, amassing 36 tries and addressing their disciplinary lapses. Aided by thumping victories over Fiji and Japan, they have rebuilt impressively to secure a shot at reaching the Nations Championship final, but New Zealand provide the true measure of their progress. Only South Africa are higher in the rankings and a year out from the 2027 World Cup final, it is the opportunity for Steve Borthwick’s men to make a statement. Lee Calvert blogs the action and the trio of Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher making up our Twickenham reporting team.

Katy Murrells is at the controls of our tennis liveblog as the semi-finals pan out in Turin. The first session starts at 2.30pm, with the evening match due to start at about 8.30pm.

Emillia Hawkins keeps the updates flowing on the five afternoon kick-offs: Aston Villa v Sunderland, Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Chelsea v Leeds, Coventry v Crystal Palace, and Tottenham v Ipswich – the pick of the bunch. Roberto De Zerbi seemed to be making an impact at Spurs before a defeat by Leeds tripped up his side. Their record is grim against the Tractor Boys: four defeats in their last five Premier league games.

Lee Calvert is back on deck as Ireland risk a Springbok backlash from a side bruised by defeat by France and furious at their coach, Rassie Erasmus, for getting banned after his incendiary “match-fixing” comments. There is more at stake in this November’s meeting between the sides than last year’s chaotic Test. The Irish were down to 12 men at one stage and the Springboks won 24-13 for their first win in Dublin since 2012. Both countries are still in the running to top their respective pools and play in the final on Finals weekend at Twickenham. Brendan Fanning reports.

City’s slump has allowed the defending champions, Arsenal, to seize early control and they will hope to continue their relentless start to the season. They head to Newcastle where a toxic reception awaits Bruno Guimarães as he returns to Tyneside in Arsenal colours for the first time since his summer move. The Gunners are five points clear of second-placed Brighton at the top after winning nine of their first 10 games. Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent hosts have managed just one win in their past five league matches, losing to Everton and Aston Villa along the way. Join Rob Smyth for MBM commentary, with Louis Taylor reporting.

Kimi Antonelli may have already won the drivers’ crown, but second place in the standings is still up for grabs and Max Verstappen can tighten his grip in Sin City. The Red Bull driver is 17 points clear of Mercedes’ George Russell, who moved back up to third place, one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton after his fourth place at Interlagos. Krishani Dhanji be live blogging the race in the small hours, with Giles Richards reporting from Las Vegas.

Dominic Booth and Emillia Hawkins clock on with all the latest news and reader views for a Sunday featuring the Premier League fixture of the weekend. Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of Manchester United at Anfield just days after wrapping up his reign as USA men’s coach. Victory would give him instant momentum as he fights to lift the club up the table. Earlier, hard-charging Brighton will fancy their chances against Hull, who have not won a Premier League match since August. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Emillia Hawkins and John Brewin keep track of Sunday’s WSL fixtures from midday as Birmingham face Manchester United and Charlton host Aston Villa. Then it is Everton v Brighton at 2pm followed by a London derby as Rita Guarino’s in-form West Ham visit Arsenal, with the Irons having notched four wins in their past five matches in all competitions. The Gunners are toiling, and they sit sixth in the standings going into the weekend, with just three wins from their opening 10 matches.

Second-placed Brighton have become the most unlikely title contenders with their free-scoring football and have every chance of continuing to defy the sceptics as they take on Hull. The Seagulls are the league’s top scorers with 26 goals, 11 more than Arsenal, and have the second-tightest defence, with just seven goals conceded. Join Dominic Booth for minute-by-minute coverage, with Aaron Bower reporting from MKM Stadium.

Rob Smyth buckles up for the big one at Anfield with all eyes on the latest United manager, Mauricio Pochettino. United’s tally of eight points and one win after 10 games is their lowest at this stage of a league season for 40 years. The former Southampton, Spurs and Chelsea manager says he needs time to turn the dysfunctional club’s fortunes around but he will be aware of the need to show progress quickly, with Liverpool in no mood to offer their most bitter rivals any favours. Looking for omens? The Argentinian’s first game for Chelsea was against Liverpool, which ended in a 1-1 draw at Stamford Bridge. Andy Hunter and Jamie Jackson make up our reporting team on Merseyside.

Daniel Harris offers live coverage of the final from Turin as the season-ending indoor hard-court tournament featuring the top eight singles players and top eight doubles teams draws to a thrilling close.

Graham Searles returns with his essential NFL liveblog covering the seven 6pm clashes. The division-leading Buffalo Bills (8-1), who boast the top scoring offence and second-best rush attack in the NFL, meet the Miami Dolphins (1-8) in the big AFC East clash. The other early Sunday games are Bears v Saints, Lions v Buccaneers, Panthers v Ravens, Cowboys v Titans, Chiefs v Cardinals, and Eagles v Steelers.
