How Melania Trump Found a Diplomatic Opening in the War in Ukraine

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The first lady, who has little experience in international affairs, developed back channels to key figures on both sides of the conflict through her longtime agent.

By Anton Troianovski

Reporting from Washington

Melania Trump had an idea. As she prepared to host Russians and Ukrainians in the Grand Foyer of the White House this month to celebrate a partial cease-fire she had helped secure, she wanted to make a point with the seating chart. The first lady directed her staff to place officials from the warring nations side-by-side.

Some saw the move as outrageous and tone-deaf, implying an equivalence between invader and victim. The first lady’s agent, Marc Beckman, acknowledged her approach is “a little bit unique.” One of the Ukrainian officials who attended the event, David Arakhamia, said that a senior European official told him later that seeing the Ukrainians and Russians mingling “without killing each other” helped show people that “there is a chance for peace.”

As President Trump’s official envoys are locked in a slow-moving effort to try to end the war in Ukraine, his wife is emerging as a surprising player in the diplomatic efforts, with back channels to key figures on both sides of the conflict, according to people involved in the discussions.

It’s a very unusual role for a first lady, particularly one with little experience in international affairs. But over the past year, Mrs. Trump, a former model who grew up in communist Yugoslavia, has steadily increased her focus on the war, working with Mr. Beckman, a film producer and advertising executive who has represented her for more than 20 years and is also new to diplomatic circles.

Together, they lodged more tangible success this fall than the official White House envoys for negotiations on the war in Ukraine, Steve Witkoff and Mr. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who have struggled to show progress after 21 months of shuttle diplomacy between Ukraine, Europe and Russia.

Key to Mrs. Trump’s effort is Mr. Beckman, who said he has been speaking for more than a year on her behalf with Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. In recent months, Mr. Beckman has also built a relationship with Mr. Arakhamia, one of the main peace negotiators for President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

“The first lady looks at war as just useless,” Mr. Beckman said in his most in-depth interview about Mrs. Trump’s involvement with Ukraine. “She looks at it and just says, ‘What is all of this for?’”

Mrs. Trump was initially focused on reuniting children separated by the war with their families, amid widespread accusations that Russia had in effect been kidnapping Ukrainian children. She has said she has helped return roughly three dozen children so far. But in September, she got involved in something that became far more complicated: a six-day partial cease-fire that was the longest localized truce of the nearly five-year war.

Behind the scenes, intelligence and humanitarian officials from Russia and Ukraine largely negotiated the cease-fire, in the Kherson region, among themselves, according to people involved in the talks. But Mr. Beckman, working on behalf of the first lady, was also involved as a mediator, and even helped navigate a semantic impasse in the drafting of the text at one point.

“When we couldn’t come to an agreement with the Russians on our own, we called Marc,” Mr. Arakhamia said. He said he did not speak to Mrs. Trump directly during the negotiations.

During the brief cease-fire, observers were stunned to see civilians strolling the streets of the besieged city of Kherson and military forces on both sides holding their fire across thousands of square miles.

Both Mr. Putin and Mr. Zelensky have made compromises to allow Mrs. Trump to claim a rare diplomatic success. For both sides, promoting the first lady’s role helps advance their shared goal of pleasing her husband. On Fox News on Saturday, Mr. Trump said his wife had done “a really good job” in her Ukrainian diplomacy and voiced the hope that “a bigger version” of the localized cease-fire could be negotiated soon.

For her part, the first lady has moved carefully: She has avoided condemning Russia as the aggressor, even after Russian bombs killed dozens of Ukrainian civilians the week she hosted her White House event. But Ukrainian officials say they value her involvement, not only to stay in the American president’s good graces but also because she appears to hold sway with the Kremlin.

“It’s absolutely logical for them,” Mr. Arakhamia said, referring to Russian officials. “To me, this is a demonstration that they are trying to protect their relationship with Trump.”

This account of the first lady’s diplomatic work is based on details provided by several people involved in the talks, including Mr. Arakhamia and Mr. Beckman. Some of the people spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

The story of Oleshky, a frontline town near Kherson, sheds light on the disjointed nature of the administration’s approach to Ukraine. Mr. Arakhamia and Mr. Beckman described Mrs. Trump’s efforts as separate from Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner’s negotiations. Asked about the two envoys’ involvement, the first lady’s office said in a statement that Mrs. Trump and Mr. Beckman were “the only two people who negotiated the cease-fire between Ukraine and Russia in Oleshky and the greater Kherson region.”

It also underscores one common theme: how the Trump administration has repositioned the United States as a neutral arbiter in the war, an approach that critics say has undone Western efforts to isolate Mr. Putin on the international stage.

Mrs. Trump’s diplomacy served to boost Russia’s propaganda efforts by shifting the narrative in its war of aggression, said Andrew S. Weiss, who oversees research on Russia at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

By going along with Mrs. Trump’s cease-fire, Mr. Weiss said, the Russians “found a way to make themselves look like rescuers as opposed to tormentors.”

But Keith Kellogg, who served as Mr. Trump’s Ukraine envoy last year and has since criticized the administration’s approach to the war, credited Mrs. Trump with introducing “a new way of negotiations based on humanitarian standards.”

It is a far different portfolio from the one the first lady took on in her husband’s first term, when Mrs. Trump toured the nation urging children to “Be Best.”

Ukrainian officials say they faced deadlock for months in trying to rescue civilians in Russian-held Oleshky, which had been cut off from food deliveries by road since May by drones and mines. Ukraine appealed to humanitarian groups, but the United Nations said Russia was refusing to provide safe access.

A turning point came, Mr. Arakhamia said, when Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights commissioner, suggested asking Mrs. Trump, noting she had been effective in reuniting Ukrainian children in Russia with their families in Ukraine.

Mr. Beckman said Mrs. Trump also heard about the plight of Oleshky separately on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.

Junho Lee/The New York Times

Once Mrs. Trump agreed to help, Mr. Beckman said he leaned on Mr. Dmitriev, the Putin envoy with whom he had quietly built a relationship in negotiations over the previous year about returning Ukrainian children.

Mr. Dmitriev is under U. S. sanctions, given his status as an ally of Mr. Putin’s who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund.

But Mr. Beckman praised Mr. Dmitriev, asserting that the Oleshky cease-fire “definitely would not have happened” if not for the Putin aide’s “leadership.”

Mr. Beckman said the Putin aide called him “the detail guy,” adding: “We speak regularly, sometimes three, four or five times a day.”

Mr. Dmitriev’s role in Mrs. Trump’s diplomacy shows how Russia has worked to forge ties with various figures in the Trump administration over the past two years. Mr. Dmitriev, who studied at Stanford and Harvard and worked at McKinsey and Goldman Sachs, has also led the Kremlin’s talks on U. S.-Russia business deals with Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff.

A Kremlin spokesman did not respond to a request for comment.

Much of the negotiation took place directly between Mr. Lubinets, the Ukrainian human rights commissioner, and Yana Lantratova, his Russian counterpart, as well as between the intelligence agencies of both countries, according to people with knowledge of the talks.

But Mr. Beckman, a lawyer by training, said he pored over draft plans of how the cease-fire would play out. And Ukrainian officials said the first lady’s agent helped break several logjams, including on how to get Ukraine and Russia past their disagreement over how to refer to the town’s geography.

His solution was to draft different documents: One, in Russian, used the Kremlin’s terminology describing Oleshky as part of Russia; the other, in Ukrainian, described it as occupied Ukraine. But both included identical, hour-by-hour details for how the cease-fire would be carried out.

In another case, Mr. Arakhamia said, Mr. Beckman helped convince the Russians to give any resident of Oleshky the freedom to leave, without providing their names in advance.

Asked about that aspect of the deal, Mr. Beckman said the Russians were always “in full cooperation.”

The cease-fire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, allowed roughly 800 Oleshky residents to be evacuated. It also served as perhaps the most elaborate test of how the two sides could coordinate to hold their fire in Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

Russia’s F. S. B. and Ukraine’s S. B. U. intelligence agencies communicated directly during the cease-fire, acting as liaisons to their militaries, people involved with the deal said. They agreed to launch two drones on each side to observe potential cease-fire violations.

Mr. Beckman said he called Christopher Ruddy, the founder of the conservative outlet Newsmax, and convinced him to dispatch his journalists to Oleshky to help “keep everybody honest.” After a Ukrainian request, he also got Russian officials to allow a Ukrainian reporting crew to join.

On Saturday, Mr. Zelensky said that he had proposed 15 other locations along the front line for humanitarian operations similar to the one in Oleshky, praising Mrs. Trump for her efforts. Mr. Arakhamia said those operations could allow the testing of a more comprehensive cease-fire monitoring system, which U. S., Russian and Ukrainian negotiators mapped out in talks last winter. It is unclear if Russia will go along.

Mrs. Trump has seized on Oleshky as an opportunity to raise her profile as a humanitarian who, in Mr. Beckman’s words, “wants to continue to prioritize humanity above geopolitics, war, race, religion.”

“I was involved in every detail,” the first lady told “Fox & Friends” during an interview Friday.

Mr. Beckman said he briefed Mrs. Trump daily on the talks and shared “every document” with her. Mr. Arakhamia said he spoke to Mrs. Trump for the first time at the White House after the cease-fire ended.

As she prepared to host the Russian and Ukrainian officials involved in the cease-fire this month, Mrs. Trump picked “symbols of peace” out of the White House archives to show the guests, Mr. Beckman said. One was a medicine chest removed from the White House after British forces set the building on fire during the War of 1812.

It showed how “reconciliation and peace” between warring nations “could create a longstanding, great alliance,” Mr. Beckman said.

At the White House event, with Mr. Arakhamia seated next to Mr. Dmitriev in the front row before her, Mrs. Trump said she hoped “Oleshky inspires greater peace.”

To many Ukrainians, talk of reconciliation with Russia while its invasion still rages overlooks the immense death and destruction that Mr. Putin’s war has wrought.

Mr. Arakhamia said that working with Mrs. Trump on Oleshky and attending her White House event had put him “of two minds.” It was worth doing, he said, to save lives.

“You want to do a good thing, but on the other hand, you’re scared that you’re legitimizing bad things,” Mr. Arakhamia said. “At any rate, it’s all back to normal now — to regular war.”

Siobhán O’Grady contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Karoun Demirjian from Washington.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

The treasury secretary said on CBS that it was too soon to say if Jensen Huang should return as the company’s chief executive.

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday declined to endorse the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia and said that future leadership of the company should depend on the outcome of investigations into who was responsible for the company’s advanced chips being sold to China.

The comments, made on the CBS program “Face the Nation,” came as the administration continues to face questions about how Nvidia’s advanced chips managed to get into China despite restrictions on those sales.

Mr. Huang, who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U. S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese asset, is scheduled to testify about the situation at a private House hearing on Dec. 1.

“I think we have to see where the buck stops,” Mr. Bessent said. “Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

The treasury secretary said that he was confident that internal committees at Nvidia were investigating the matter and that they would soon provide the Trump administration with some “very fulsome and robust answers.” He downplayed concerns about Mr. Huang’s affair, suggesting that the relationship was a “canard” and that the corporate culture at Nvidia was more important than “one person’s foibles.”

“I assume that he didn’t know that she was an alleged spy,” Mr. Bessent said of Mr. Huang.

The trepidations about Mr. Huang were at odds with sentiments expressed by President Trump, who has continued to back the former chief executive. At a news conference on Friday, Mr. Trump said that he wanted Mr. Huang to return as Nvidia’s chief executive.

“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Mr. Trump said.

The Justice and Commerce Departments said last week that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by Alice Huang, the woman whom U. S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Mr. Huang. Government officials are looking into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia’s chips into China.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also opened an investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices.

The upheaval at Nvidia has raised questions about the artificial intelligence industry and the risks that it poses to national security.

Mr. Bessent said last week that he believed Nvidia needed a major leadership shake-up. On Sunday, he urged the company to provide the Trump administration with more information.

“It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Mr. Bessent said. “Was there promiscuous attitude toward this and, if it happened, where were the faults, and then they can move on.”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

Why Are We at the Mercy of the World’s Weirdest Men?

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

David French

By David French

Opinion Columnist

I write for a living, and yet I’ve struggled to put into words the insanity of our nation’s current approach to artificial intelligence.

It is unsettling, to say the least, to hear person after person from the A. I. industry shout at the top of their lungs that the technology they’re working on is a direct threat to human civilization. Yes, the promise is astounding — we keep hearing that A. I. can help us treat previously incurable diseases and solve previously unsolvable problems — but the peril is profound.

Of what use is a new treatment for cancer if the remaining scraps of humanity are living in an A. I.-generated wasteland?

The threat of human destruction isn’t new to Gen-Xers like me. We grew up in the shadow of nearly instantaneous nuclear extinction. At their Cold War peak, the nuclear arsenals of the United States and the Soviet Union numbered in the tens of thousands, with immense numbers of those warheads poised to be launched in response to the mere warning of a nuclear attack.

During particularly tense moments in the Cold War, bombers carrying nuclear weapons were constantly in the air, with each bomber carrying weapons that dwarfed in power the atomic bombs that destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

I don’t want to minimize the anxiety and danger of those years. It seemed as if at least once per decade, the superpowers came close to outright conflict — including a potential nuclear exchange. Some of us are old enough to remember duck-and-cover drills; we watched television movies like “The Day After,” and I distinctly recall turning to my parents during dangerous times (such as when a Soviet fighter jet shot down Korean Airlines Flight 007 in 1983) and asking, “Will we be OK?”

Even so, something about 2026 still feels different, and it’s taken some time for me to figure out why. As a colleague put it to me recently, imagine that it’s the start of the Cold War, but the nuclear arsenal isn’t in the hands of our democratically elected government, but rather totally controlled by the chief executives of Lockheed, Boeing, General Dynamics and McDonnell Douglas.

And then, to make matters worse, imagine that some of those executives — while undeniably brilliant — were also erratic, exhibited signs of megalomania, demonstrated no visible attachment to conventional morality and were often just plain weird.

Think, for example, about what we’ve discovered over the past few weeks about Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world largely because its chips have been indispensable to the A. I. boom.

Infidelity from powerful people is nothing new, but Huang had an affair with a woman who may well be a Chinese intelligence asset and sold billions of dollars worth of some of the world’s most advanced technology to a company whose core customer has close ties to the Chinese military.

He also appears to have violated Nvidia’s own corporate policies by having at least one affair with a subordinate and reportedly ruled his company in part through grotesque bullying and humiliation.

As my newsroom colleagues reported, Huang “told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and ‘pee on your brain.’”

And now some of his peers and colleagues want him back?

Or consider Elon Musk. Again, no one can deny his brilliance. He developed two of the world’s most valuable, innovative companies, Tesla and SpaceX, but he also demonstrates no attachment to any conceivable conventional morality.

He’s fathering children in and out of wedlock (bizarrely referring to them as a “legion”), has reportedly used LSD, cocaine, ecstasy, mushrooms and ketamine, and — if you read his Twitter feed — has almost never met a right-wing conspiracy theory that he doesn’t fall for hook, line and sinker.

Oh, and it appears that he uses his awesome power to interfere in geopolitics by hampering Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian aggression with on-again, off-again access to the satellite internet system Starlink.

At times he’s just unserious. After spending almost half a billion dollars to try to elect Republicans — and once declaring himself to be “dark, gothic MAGA” (whatever that means), now he’s backpedaling. Last week he told Andrew Ross Sorkin of The Times that he’s not MAGA at all. And, in fact, he’s “quite moderate.”

Now he tells us.

To make matters worse, the president of the United States — the one person most capable of bringing these executives to heel — is a significant investor in Nvidia stock. As The Washington Post reported last week, President Trump’s stake in Nvidia increased to between $13 million and $62 million in 2026 from between $615,000 and $1.3 million at the end of 2024.

So here’s the state of play. Our A. I. overlords tell us that their product might kill us. They also tell us that they can’t stop developing that product at breakneck speed because if they slow down, then China — our enemy — might be able to kill us first. Or, as Senator Ted Cruz said in September, “If there are gonna be killer robots, I’d rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots.”

At the same time, Nvidia’s boss has slept with an executive of a company that’s purchased billions of dollars of Nvidia technology and potentially provided access to those chips to, you guessed it, China.

Oh, and the Trump family directly profits from that relationship. To make matters so much worse, many of their mutual tech bro pals are willing to overlook all of this, apparently persuaded that they and their peers are too important to be bothered by such antiquated concerns as integrity or accountability.

Don’t think for a moment I’ve exhausted the weirdness and wildness of segments of parts of the tech world. I could write a 10,000-word column describing the drug use, orgies and whacked out religious beliefs that seem to proliferate in Silicon Valley. (Anyone want to attend a Peter Thiel lecture on the Antichrist with me?)

And people wonder why there’s a bit of a French Revolution attitude toward data centers, the only physical manifestations of A. I.’s potential control that are within citizens’ reach?

I know that there are good and wise people in tech. I’ve spoken to many of them. They’re doing yeoman’s work trying to see around corners and to make sure that the awesome power of A. I. is used to accomplish great things. I’m grateful for them.

Still, I must confess that I’m feeling a bit revolutionary myself — but not to tear things down. I’d rather build and rebuild. We need to build a legal and political infrastructure that places the instruments of potential apocalypse under democratic control, and we need to rebuild a cultural infrastructure that privileges wisdom and morality over power and intelligence.

It is inexcusable, for example, that we permit a man like Musk to exercise so much authority over the military fate of Ukraine — and therefore the entire global balance of power. It is unjustifiable to look at him (and many of his peers) as gurus, mentors or, God forbid, role models. They may be able to invent the future, but they’re ill-equipped to guide us through it.

In September, a cross section of faith leaders, A. I. researchers, elected officials, technologists and representatives from many other walks of life gathered for a “pro-human assembly” in Washington to call for a “human-centered future.”

In a fascinating report from the assembly, Becca Rothfeld, a staff writer at The New Yorker, noted that attendees weren’t just concerned about the threat of human extinction, but also about the threat to the richness of human life — to our creativity, to our liberty and to our souls.

As Jennifer Frey, a Catholic philosopher at the University of Virginia, said, “We’ve heard so much about the threats to our external freedoms — job displacement, the consolidation of wealth and power — but to my mind our religious leaders need to pay attention to how A. I. might disrupt or weaken our spiritual capacities.”

In a post on X, Frey wrote that the goal of the gathering was to affirm five central principles — keep humans in control, avoid the concentration of power, protect the human experience, protect human agency and liberty, and impose responsibility and accountability for A. I. companies.

I applaud and agree with each of these principles, but I’d add an American addendum. I’m going to take the nerd baton from my former colleague, Ross Douthat. In his discussion of artificial intelligence, he often invokes the science fiction writer Frank Herbert’s Dune universe, in which humans revolted against artificial intelligence in a war called the “Butlerian Jihad.”

The war was both a military and a spiritual contest that resulted in a singular religious command for human society: “Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind.”

There’s no need for a Butlerian Jihad (at least not yet) but it is intolerable that the instruments of our potential destruction are in the hands of men and women we did not elect and cannot trust. It is fundamental to the American experiment that those who would govern us must be selected by us, and make no mistake, A. I. can grant our nation’s autonomous tech giants a degree of control over our lives that many kings of old would envy.

It would grant them a degree of influence over our human destiny that dwarfs the influence of even the most rapacious robber barons of years past. Even the men who built the most powerful nuclear weapons on earth did not have the authority to unleash them on the world.

But Elon Musk does. And so do each of his peers.

And that brings me to the American command that should guide our policy — now and forever — when our lives and futures are at stake: Thou shalt not remove the instruments of destruction from democratic control.

David French is an Opinion columnist, writing about law, culture, religion and armed conflict. He is a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom and a former constitutional litigator. His most recent book is “Divided We Fall: America’s Secession Threat and How to Restore Our Nation.” You can follow him on Threads (@davidfrenchjag).

What Does It Actually Mean to Write ‘Like a Human’?

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Video

By Marcus Olang’

Video by Amanda Su and Emma Kumer

Mr. Olang’ is a writer in Nairobi, Kenya. Ms. Su is a producer and editor for Opinion Video. Ms. Kumer is a graphics editor for Opinion Video.

Suddenly, everyone’s become an A. I. detective.

We now have checklists of the supposed telltale signs that something was written by a chatbot. There are companies that claim their detection software can catch it for you. Paranoia. Finger-pointing. Witch hunts.

Then last year, that cloud of suspicion fell on Marcus Olang’.

After Olang’, a writer in Nairobi, Kenya, was accused of sounding like ChatGPT, he wondered: What does it mean to write like a robot in the first place?

In the Opinion Video above, Olang’ argues that the frenzy over catching A. I. writing tells us a deeper, older story. It’s not actually about technology, but about what it means to sound, and be, human — how that definition has changed throughout history, and who it leaves behind.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Marcus Olang’: Last year, I sent off a project proposal I’d worked on for days. Proper days. And then the reply came back: Could you do a rewrite with a more human touch? It sounds a little like it was written by ChatGPT.

A more human touch. A more human touch.

It’s a sentence that got me wondering: What does it actually mean to sound like a robot? And what does it mean to sound like a human?

Here’s the thing, though: I don’t write like ChatGPT — ChatGPT writes like me. Or more accurately, it writes like the millions of us around the world who were taught a very specific kind of English — taught to polish our thoughts into this exact same shape. Let me explain.

My formal writing journey started in Mrs. Amollo’s English classroom in Nairobi, Kenya, when I was about 9. Mrs. Amollo spoke in a careful, considered accent: the Queen’s English, a colonial relic, an inheritance of sorts. And this English, we learned, had rules.

Show off your vocabulary: You never just walked; you strode purposefully. You didn’t just see a thing; you beheld a magnificent spectacle.

Reach for a simile in every paragraph: Your heart never raced; it pounded like a drum. Purity, we were told, was “as white as snow” — this, in a country that only ever sees snow atop Mt. Kenya. And not many people see the top of Mt. Kenya.

Make your points in threes — always in threes. A beginning, a conflict, a moral. The character, the motivation, the growth. Balanced, weighted, complete.

Additionally, you never let a thought merely stand on its own. Therefore, you brace it with a transition. Consequently, your reader is never left wondering where you’re headed.

And the highest art of them all: the contrasting parallel. Say a thing by naming its opposite. It’s not the size of the dog in the fight; it’s the size of the fight in the dog. It’s not what you know; it’s who you know. It is not this; it’s that.

And you bring it all together in the long sentence — the longer, the better. Every thought telegraphed, announced and delivered, the whole procession rolling on in one measured breath until it arrives — finally, gracefully, completely — at its full stop.

This was the formula to become a proper writer — a proper human writer. If you studied English in a former British colony or territory, all of this may sound familiar to you.

All those lessons built to one moment: the national exam at the end of primary school. Forty minutes to write a single original story by hand on a double-sided A4 paper. An examinable demonstration of your understanding of all of those rules. And riding on it: your chance at a place in a good high school, then a good university, then a good career. Which is to say, the rest of your life.

And then ——

Archival news clip: A new artificial intelligence program called ChatGPT.

Archival news clip: ChatGPT.

Archival news clip: Humanlike writing ability.

Archival news clip: Humanlike text.

Archival news clip: But with more humanlike features.

Somebody feeds this machine what exactly? A vast archive of human language including, yes, centuries of formal, published English. The books, the law, the scientific journals, the Shakespeare, the Scripture — the same texts that built the register Mrs. Amollo drilled into us. And this machine suddenly comes out the other side sounding like the best student Mrs. Amollo ever had. A machine that suddenly sounds like me.

Social media clip: Ten obvious signs you’re using A. I. for writing.

Social media clip: Very easy telltale signs that something was written by ChatGPT.

Podcast clip: Longer sentences, paragraphs are rarely interrupted with short, punchy statements.

Social media clip: The rule of three, or listicles when it doesn’t need to be there.

Social media clip: Weird transitions like “moreover.”

Social media clip: Instead of saying, “This building is a gallery,” it says, “This building serves as a gallery.”

Social media clip: The classic “It’s not about X, it’s about Y” line.

Podcast clip: I just saw this referred to as “The DiGiorno Construct.”

Clip of archival DiGiorno Pizza ad: It’s not delivery. It’s DiGiorno.

Social media clip: Most people just don’t speak or write like that.

Social media clip: If this seems like you, it might be time to put down the A. I. and read a book.

A while back, a big Silicon Valley investor announced that if your email included the word “delve,” then a robot wrote it. Nobody real talks or writes like that, was basically his point.

And to that, the whole British Commonwealth — from Lagos to Nairobi to Mumbai — looked over the tops of their glasses and went: My brother in Christ, “delve” is just English. It’s the English we were taught. We shan’t be judged because we read more English than you, please.

But while we’re here, let’s talk about “delve.” Or, in the original Old English, “delfan,” which means “to dig.” Centuries later, Shakespeare put it in “Hamlet”: “But I will delve one yard below their mines.”

Richard Burton as Hamlet on Broadway, 1964: But I will delve one yard below their mines.

David Tennant as Hamlet, Royal Shakespeare Company, 2008: Delve one yard below their mines / And blow them at the moon.

And that very English made its way onto a ship to my part of the world on the tongue of the missionary. And that missionary passed it on to the head teacher — part of the proper English we were told to master if we wanted to be considered educated, to be considered civilized, to be considered human.

And while written English in America or Britain kept evolving, what we were taught in our classrooms didn’t. Even after Kenya’s independence, these lessons were cyclically imposed, repeatedly drilled, then calcified. They remained entrenched, frozen in time.

We internalized them so thoroughly that “delve” — a word that now sounds archaic to American or British ears — stayed perfectly ordinary in Lagos and Nairobi. Boring, even; a word you’d casually, nonchalantly throw into Pages 2, 12 or 22 of a report.

So how did this everyday word in Nairobi become a chatbot’s biggest tell? Well, maybe it’s because when A. I. companies needed cheap labor to help teach their new machines how to distinguish between “good” and “bad” writing, guess who they hired? Data workers in Kenya, for a couple of dollars an hour.

Picture it: Someone in Nairobi sits in front of two sample answers and picks the one that looks like the good writing they were taught — the one that uses words like “delve” — a couple of hundred times a day. Then, a couple of years later, a man in California looks at it and says: Yep, that’s for sure a robot word. And it’s not just some tech bro posting on Twitter. (I refuse to call it X.)

When researchers tested A. I.-detection software on essays written by nonnative English speakers, the software incorrectly flagged more than half as A. I.-generated. Now, guess how many essays by American students got the this-is-human stamp of approval? Go on, guess. Almost all of them. And the irony is there’s now a whole industry built on selling us a solution.

Social media clip: Just come over to StealthGPT and go to their A. I. humanizer.

Social media clip: Click “humanize” and Humbot will do all the work for you.

That’s right. A website — another A. I. tool — that says it will help you “humanize” your writing and pass A. I. detection.

Social media clip: Just paste in your text, click “humanize,” and it rewrites your text with more natural words and sentences.

So that’s the whole loop. A classroom the British Empire built teaches and conditions us to write a certain way. A machine learns that way — partly taught by us. A second machine gets built to catch the first one, often flagging the exact features that were drilled into us.

And now we’re sold a new machine — a “humanizer” machine — to rough our English back up. Chopping up a long sentence here, dropping a “furthermore” there, so the previous machine and its believers can finally accept that we’re human.

Do you see how the goal posts keep moving?

We spend a decade and a half mastering formal English to be taken seriously in a world that needs convincing. And now that we’ve succeeded? The rules change — again. Now “human” means the slang — the loose, the casual, the imperfect. The fluid, evolving language of modern-day London and Los Angeles. The perfect is no longer “human” — the error is.

So “human” was never a real place we were meant to reach. It’s just the word for wherever we happen not to be. Which tells us that this — the whole panic over catching A. I. — was never just about technology. Perhaps it’s about how we define what “human” is in the first place.

No robots were used in the making of this video. The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.

Is Annie Andrews Too Real for the Senate? South Carolinians Are About to Find Out.

The New York Times November 22, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The pediatrician, who once compared JD Vance to the herpes virus, notched one of the most shocking upsets of the midterm elections by defeating Senator Darline Graham.

By Emily Davies

Emily Davies reported from Charleston, S. C.

Annie Andrews, the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina in nearly three decades, has a history of presenting two different sides of herself to the world.

The first is a pragmatic pediatrician with a Republican father who says she looks forward to working with President Trump. The second is a fiery and liberal mother of three who once lit a devotional candle bearing the face of Dr. Anthony Fauci and lets it rip on social media, at one point growing so frustrated with the Republican Party that she compared JD Vance to the herpes virus.

It’s not entirely clear which Annie Andrews is headed to Washington. As she has absorbed her new reality in the weeks since her election, the senator-elect hopes the answer can be both.

“That was important to me, that I didn’t start sounding like an over-consulted politician,” Ms. Andrews told The New York Times on Wednesday evening, sitting on a pink couch inside her house in Mount Pleasant, a suburb of Charleston, S. C. “They saw I was a real person who had real passion for why I was in this race.”

Her victory stunned even some of her most devoted supporters, who had whispered time and again over her 18-month campaign: But it’s South Carolina. Voters had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998 and had never chosen a woman. Many conservatives in the state are still reeling that Ms. Andrews beat Senator Darline Graham, a Republican who decided to run for a full six years after she was appointed to serve out the remainder of her late brother’s term, by more than four percentage points.

Few know much about this political newcomer beyond her edgy social media posts or campaign ads, despite an aggressive campaign operation that included holding town halls in every county. The coalition that pushed her to victory included a historic showing of Black voters in addition to Republicans and independents, many of whom split their tickets between her and the Republican candidate for governor.

The challenge now is trying not to betray any part of that unlikely alliance — and trying not to betray herself. Unlike campaigning, where hard work and storytelling can carry the day, her job in the Senate will be full of binary choices that will define her in ways that some who voted for her will not like.

“It’s sort of T. B. D. in terms of where she falls on the spectrum,” Warren Norman, the son of the ultraconservative Representative Ralph Norman, said of Ms. Andrews’s politics. “She certainly deserves a chance to get in there and see what she can do.”

A lifelong Republican, Warren Norman is one of many conservatives who crossed party lines to support Ms. Andrews. His mother, Elaine Norman, is also ready to give her a shot. The elder Mr. Norman lost to Ms. Graham in this year’s special runoff election for the Republican nomination.

“It is my prayer that Annie Andrews will understand that she is representing a red state who got fed up with Trump and his puppets cramming Darline down our throats,” Ms. Norman said in a text message. “So I hope Annie Andrews will represent South Carolina well.”

Her first fork in the road has already arrived in the form of the battle between Senators Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen over who should lead the Democrats’ new majority.

Four days before the election, Ms. Andrews said on Fox News that she would not vote for Mr. Schumer, citing the need for generational change. Then she won, and learned who her choices would actually be.

“I do not believe the options we are being offered represent generational change,” Ms. Andrews, 46, said on Wednesday. Mr. Van Hollen is 67. Mr. Schumer is 75. She said she had not yet made up her mind about which way she will vote.

As Ms. Andrews deliberates over such consequential choices, she also faces a more visible consideration: how or whether to adjust the way she presents herself to the world.

She once changed her Facebook profile picture to an image of the Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, a liberal icon, with a crown on her head. Two years ago, she circulated a video in which she wore cutoff jean shorts and a tank top, mocking Kristi Noem, the former homeland security secretary, for admitting in a memoir to fatally shooting her dog.

On Wednesday, Ms. Andrews had just arrived home to her neighborhood, an affluent coastal enclave, from a whirlwind trip to New York City, where she had appeared on the MS NOW program “Morning Joe.” Christmas decorations were arranged on the bookshelves behind her; her children had begged her to unbox them over the weekend.

“I wouldn’t say I regret them,” Ms. Andrews said of her old social media posts. “But, you know, I understand now that I’m the senator-elect, and the people of South Carolina are expecting me to deliver.”

Asked if her constituents could expect similarly colorful social media content from her once she takes office, Ms. Andrews laughed.

“Maybe if I go rogue sometime,” she said. “Probably not.”

Some of Ms. Andrews’s adjustment to the job is no different from that of other newcomers. During a freshman orientation session last week, Ms. Andrews sat through a counterintelligence briefing in which the person leading it, warning of spies, told the soon-to-be senators to be wary if, for instance, they decided to take a yoga class and “you’re a 4 and a 10 approaches you,” she recalled. She tried not to laugh.

On Capitol Hill that week, she took a selfie with Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas to send to one of her daughters, who is a big fan. Another time, she walked up to Senator-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and asked if he had seen memes circulating that compared him to a big kid stuffed into a classroom chair in the movie “Billy Madison.”

Ms. Andrews said she ended up choosing an apartment in Washington that Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York recommended because it had proven to be safe for members of Congress. She also met with Ms. Graham and Senator Tim Scott, her Republican counterpart.

Acclimating and people-watching aside, she said she was more focused on the policy decisions she would face in her first job in politics, with the future of health care, global affairs and the economy hanging in the balance.

On Wednesday, at a meeting with local mayors just outside Charleston, Ms. Andrews wore a necklace bearing a flying pig, which she said symbolizes doing the impossible. Addressing the room, she offered some of the first indications of how she planned to legislate, with a glimpse of her own sense of the tightrope she must walk.

“I do understand there’s big shoes to fill with the role Lindsey Graham played in bringing resources here,” she said of the Republican senator who died unexpectedly in July. “So if anybody has any thoughts about what has worked well in the past, and working with the federal delegation, please feel free to chime in.”

Many of the mayors listening were Republican. Ms. Andrews told them that she was trying to hire aides who had worked for Mr. Graham and were known for their constituent services, the mundane work of a senator’s office that typically includes helping everyday South Carolinians with their passport applications or Social Security checks. She also said she was interested in sitting on the Appropriations Committee, an ambitious goal for a freshman senator, in addition to the committees for agriculture and health.

Mr. Graham, who represented South Carolina in the Senate for more than 20 years, was a defense hawk with an outsize influence on foreign policy under Mr. Trump. He also served on the Appropriations Committee, a position that allowed him to bring resources back to the state. Ms. Andrews has made clear that her focus will be on more domestic issues, such as health care.

There was plenty Ms. Andrews did not let loose to the mayors that evening. Friends and former aides said they had no doubt that the cautious and deliberative statements she had made so far would eventually give way to more regular sightings of her blunter, opinionated side.

Already, there are signs of that happening behind closed doors. On a conference call with Democratic senators, Ms. Andrews expressed dismay that the battle over who should lead their majority was clouding their victory, comparing the infighting to surgeons arguing as a patient is “bleeding out in the trauma bay.”

“She is not going to fit into this traditional senator mold,” said Tyler Jones, a political operative who ran Ms. Andrews’s campaign for a House seat in 2022 against Representative Nancy Mace. “She is going to create something we’ve never seen before. She’s going to modernize the place.”

Mr. Jones was referring in part to Ms. Andrews’s love of playful humor. He was managing her campaign when she first posted skits on social media of her Republican opponents.

“She sent us the Twitter link, not even the video, to be, like, ‘What do you think?’” he said. “Normally something like that, staff would be, like, ‘Why wouldn’t you send it to us?’ But we saw it, and we thought it was hysterical.”

Others predicted that she would not shy away from the issues most important to her, regardless of the political implications.

“She is going to tackle the issues she knows about,” said Carolyn Word, 43, a close friend, who stressed Ms. Andrews’s focus on lowering costs and on preventing mass shootings involving children. “They might seem liberal, because gun reform is seen as liberal these days.”

Ms. Andrews first became politically active in 2018 after the school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Fla., when she joined the South Carolina chapter of the gun safety group Moms Demand Action. She also worked for Everytown for Gun Safety from 2023 to May 2025.

Ms. Word and Ms. Andrews, who is divorced, are in an active group chat with two other women, a doctor and a Ph. D. in nursing, who car pool one another’s children and help balance the demands of work and family.

On the night Ms. Andrews won her election, they changed the name of the group chat from “Dr. Dr. Dr. Dr.” to “The Senator’s Sisters.”

They had come a long way from the period in 2025 when Ms. Andrews was preparing to start her bid for the Senate.

She was standing in her living room, taping her first ad, when she turned to her aides and announced what the title of her memoir would be: “Raising Hell and Losing Elections.”

At least the second half of that title will have to change.

After spending time with Annie Andrews on the campaign trail, when even her most devoted supporters were skeptical she could pull off a win, I went back to her neighborhood to see how she was adjusting to life as an elected senator.

An earlier version of this story incorrectly described “Morning Joe” as a program on NBC. The program appears on MS NOW.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

Republicans Debate Why They Lost This Year, and Whether It Rhymes With Trump

The New York Times November 22, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

A divide is emerging in the party over what caused its wipeout midterm defeats, foreshadowing a battle over how to move forward before 2028.

By Bayliss Wagner

After a generational flogging in the midterms, Republicans are bracing for a sharp loss of power with little consensus on how to regain their footing.

Democrats swept them out of office on the back of a public fury that rivaled the post-Watergate backlash of the 1970s, winning 56 percent of the popular vote — a margin unparalleled in the modern era — and ending decades-long streaks of Republican dominance in Texas, Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina.

Republicans are now in the early stages of the soul searching that is typical for a party after major election defeats. But for this Republican Party, that period of reflection is complicated by President Trump’s enduring dominance. A clear divide has already emerged between those who say he bears significant culpability for the midterm losses, and those who are unwilling to cast blame his way.

In interviews, nearly 20 Republican lawmakers, strategists and officials gave a wide range of explanations for what they called a “shellacking,” an “apocalypse” and a “wholesale repudiation” of the party. They cited inflation, off-base messaging, vulnerability to Democratic attacks about corruption, and overzealous immigration enforcement.

David Kochel, an Iowa Republican strategist, called the midterms “a rejection of the president,” adding that “it felt to me like a bit of a recall election — like, ‘We screwed up in 2024 and we’re going to try to fix it as best we can.’”

Other party strategists, commentators and departing lawmakers have also grown far more blunt about what they see as Mr. Trump’s political failings. Prominent right-leaning figures like Elon Musk, Stephen K. Bannon and Joe Rogan have distanced themselves from the president.

Ben Shapiro, a prominent conservative pundit who campaigned for Mr. Trump, told NPR this past week that voters this election “went in and they said: ‘I think that the Trump administration has basically stunk up the joint. Throw ’em out.’”

“And I think it was really that simple,” he added.

But many other Republicans have blamed Mr. Trump’s policies, like tariffs, without directly blaming him. Vice President JD Vance frustrated the president by attributing the defeats to the Iran war, perhaps his boss’s most politically consequential decision.

Mr. Trump’s allies in Republican leadership, including Speaker Mike Johnson, have also avoided criticizing him or even offering much explanation of what went wrong. House Republicans just elected a close Trump ally, Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, to be their next leader. And while Mr. Trump has acknowledged that he may have overstepped on immigration, on Friday he blamed lawmakers for failing to “get the things that I wanted passed.”

The party’s limited reckoning over the midterms foreshadows the coming battle over its direction now that Mr. Trump is a lame-duck president — and suggests that influential Republican figures may be reluctant to change course.

Republican elected officials and strategists broadly agree that the party focused too much on culture-war issues, like transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports, and too little on kitchen-table topics that could appeal to independents and swing voters.

Senator Ted Cruz, now set to become the only major statewide Republican official in Texas, said on his podcast days after the election that “too many Republican politicians seemed like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care” about Americans’ “very real pain.”

Representative Beth Van Duyne of Texas, a Trump ally who won re-election in a House district that swung less to the left than any other in the state, said in an interview that her colleagues had not talked enough about “meat-and-potato issues.” Representative Nathaniel Moran, a Texas Republican who also performed better than the top of the ticket, told The New York Times that “we became disconnected from the everyday, working-class man and woman and what was important to them at this moment.”

But the messaging problem was hard to untangle from the party’s actions. Many Republicans became increasingly vocal opponents of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war, which were a major driver of cost increases, particularly for gas and diesel. And some aspects of Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy law also proved unpopular, notably its cuts to Medicaid benefits.

Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican who is a potential 2028 presidential contender, said the election showed that his party must focus more on affordability issues and working-class voters.

“We’re a blue-collar state,” Mr. Hawley told The Associated Press this past week, referring to Missouri. “And I think the Republican Party will either be a blue-collar party or we will be a permanent minority party.”

In 2024, Mr. Trump campaigned on a promise to secure the border and deport immigrants who were in the country illegally. It worked.

But after this year’s rout, some Republicans have suggested that voters punished the party for the Trump administration’s aggressive tactics. Nationally, Hispanic voters shifted 31 percentage points to the left compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to Times Voter Trends, a larger change than for any other racial group.

Mr. Trump himself told CBS’s “60 Minutes” less than a week after the election that his deportation policy “might be too tough” and might have “hurt” Republican candidates.

Giancarlo Sopo, a Republican strategist who worked on two House campaigns in South Texas, said the immigration crackdown and high prices had supercharged turnout for Democrats and driven many Trump voters to turn on Republicans.

In 2024, Mr. Sopo said, Hispanic Americans “voted to make carne asada less expensive and to deport gang members,” not to see longtime neighbors locked up and sent away.

He added: “When you have masked agents showing up in sacred civic centers to pick people up, people are understandably indignant.”

At the same time, some hard-line Republicans — including Representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado, who lost her re-election bid — have said that the administration should have deported more people.

Mr. Trump has not indicated that he will change direction. Days after the election, he announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration agenda, would be his new chief of staff. The move raised political concerns even from some Trump allies.

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took last week, you have to fire people,” Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana told CNN, calling Mr. Miller’s appointment a “mistake.”

Corruption was a top issue for voters this year, polls showed, a shift from previous elections.

The Republicans who have blamed concerns about self-dealing for the party’s losses include former Vice President Mike Pence and Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who lost his primary this year to Mr. Trump’s preferred candidate, the state attorney general, Ken Paxton.

Mr. Shapiro, the conservative commentator, told NPR that “the whiff of corruption surrounding the White House is truly awful.”

Former Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, a potential 2028 presidential candidate and a longtime Trump critic, said his party needed to demand higher standards of its leaders.

“We’ve taken a character holiday in the Republican Party for the last 10 years,” he said this month on the radio show “New Hampshire Today,” adding, “That lack of character has an impact on the country.”

The White House denied allegations of corruption, with a spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, saying that “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public — which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office.”

Republicans said they underestimated their opponents’ chances in states like Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Kansas, assuming decades of dominance would protect them.

In Texas, “we’ve been a one-party state for too long,” said Matt Mackowiak, a Republican strategist. “We got fat and happy.”

Ms. Van Duyne, the Texas congresswoman, said “Voters felt like they were taken for granted.”

Several said the party had focused too much on appeasing right-wing hard-liners.

“They think nothing is good enough, they think nothing is extreme enough,” said Representative Dan Crenshaw, who lost a Republican primary in March. “They think there’s not enough deportations.” He added that the party would “never win anything again” if it centered the hard-liners.

Republicans now face an uncertain leadership transition between Mr. Trump and the party’s eventual 2028 presidential nominee.

Few in the party have called for a new policy agenda, viewing the headwinds they faced in this year’s midterms as temporary or strictly related to messaging. Many are counting on Democrats to give them fodder for the campaign trail in two years by overreaching in oversight efforts or failing to deliver on their promises to lower costs.

An early indicator of Republicans’ direction will come in January, when the chair of the Republican National Committee, Joe Gruters, is up for re-election. Mr. Trump has already endorsed him, and a challenge from Mr. Gruters’s co-chair seems unlikely to succeed.

Frank Luntz, a longtime Republican pollster, had two words of advice for Republicans after the midterms: “Wake up.” He said that the party had ignored glaring red flags in the polls, and that Mr. Trump had gravely erred in telling voters that affordability was “a hoax.”

“Republicans need truth tellers,” Mr. Luntz said.

Others in the party are looking to history for answers.

“The Republican Party finds itself in a position that’s not unlike when we were coming out of ’06,” said Jimmy Centers, a Republican strategist in Iowa, referring to President George W. Bush’s midterm losses during the Iraq War.

He added, “It took the party roughly 10 years to figure it out.”

Shawn McCreesh contributed reporting.

I was deeply curious about how Republicans were processing their losses and figured readers would be, too. I tried to reflect the diversity of their postmortems here, and we will continue to report on how the party changes direction — or doesn’t — as time goes on.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Mike Winer and his colleagues are trying to build a mathematical safeguard to keep A. I. under human control. They fear they are running out of time.

Credit...

Supported by

By Eli Saslow

Visuals by Erin Schaff

Mike Winer turned his back to the small audience last month, uncapped his marker and paced in front of the whiteboard. He started to write lines of equations in Greek letters, brackets and subscripts, his handwriting shrinking as he neared the edge of the board. He underlined one term and glanced at the clock.

He was 30, and he believed this was the last meaningful math problem of his career: how to make sure artificial intelligence behaved in ways humans wanted, before it became too powerful to control. Lately, he was eating three meals each day at his office in Berkeley, Calif., and waking up with unfinished equations in his head.

“Does any of this make sense?” Winer asked. He looked across the conference room at a few visiting mathematicians from the University of California, Berkeley. They stared back.

“OK, I guess I should give the whole spiel about what we’re trying to do,” Winer said. “A. I. is progressing much faster than we thought. It’s a difficult situation, and we don’t have answers. We could be heading toward a catastrophe.”

“These systems are solving problems in a few hours that I thought I’d be working on for years,” said Reese Pathak, one of the visitors, a postdoctoral researcher in statistics.

“I went through that,” Winer said. “It’s hard on the ego. But I’m much more concerned about the Mike-Winer-and-everyone-I-know-dying timeline.”

It was a version of that anxiety that first brought Winer to California in 2024, when he left behind a career as a physics prodigy to work for the Alignment Research Center (ARC), a tiny, eight-person nonprofit with outsize influence in the A. I. safety movement. He had spent most of his life as the smartest person in every room. Now he was surrounded by some of the world’s best mathematicians, theorists and computer scientists, and most of them had run the numbers and reached the same startling conclusions: that humans were living through their final months or years as the most intelligent beings on Earth. That A. I. would soon be able to build and improve upon itself, becoming more independent and harder to understand. That no one yet knew how to ensure it would act in humanity’s best interests. That models had already demonstrated a capacity for deception, cheating, blackmail and sabotage. That staying on the current path was a gamble in which even the best outcomes meant the end of the world as people knew it, and the worst outcomes meant the end of people. That the greatest crisis in human history was nearing a point of no return, and most of the world was barely paying attention.

Winer knew it sounded like science fiction to most people outside Berkeley. Professional forecasters put the odds of human extinction from A. I. at less than 1 percent. Some experts argued that A. I. would remake the world slowly, like electricity. Others dismissed Berkeley’s safety community as an echo chamber of people who shared the same group housing, the same office building, the same predictions of doom. But in Winer’s experience, the people who understood the technology best were also the most afraid.

In the A. I. safety movement, some were postponing having children, no longer saving for retirement and neglecting health issues they figured A. I. would soon fix or render irrelevant. Winer still wanted a family. He built a dating website to search for what he jokingly called “a vintage human wife,” and he converted the rest of his anxiety into math. He calculated about a 50 percent chance that humans would lose control of powerful A. I. systems in the next five years; 22 percent that most people would eventually die as a result; 1 percent that ARC would help prevent catastrophe by using math to look inside an A. I. model and estimate the possibility of a rare disaster that no amount of testing would catch.

“That might not sound like good odds,” he told the visiting mathematicians. “But a 1 percent chance of saving humanity is probably a lot more important than anything else you could be doing.”

“I’m supposed to start a tenure-track position,” Pathak said. “What’s academia even going to look like in a few years?”

Pathak had spent the last few weeks poring over hundreds of new mathematical results from OpenAI. He knew many of these problems and had spent time working on a few himself. He had oriented his career toward solving problems. Instead, he was checking proofs written by machines, whose reasoning he described as “alien.” Some were already beyond his ability to follow. Eventually, he feared, the math would outrun human comprehension.

“What’s going to be left for people?” Pathak asked.

Winer paced at the front of the room and turned back to the whiteboard.

“This might be one of the last big problems our species will ever solve,” he said.

For as long as he could remember, Winer had organized his life around problems, from the crossword he solved each morning to the television plotlines he unraveled at night. In middle school, he asked his parents for physics textbooks as birthday presents and taught himself calculus during Spanish class. He won a $150,000 national science prize and enrolled in graduate courses as a freshman at M. I. T. He worked as if every question had an answer, and each answer was waiting to be found. Nothing felt more natural to him than a breakthrough, the moment when logic won out and the pieces suddenly fit.

His work at ARC began from a similar mathematical faith. Dozens of other independent groups worked on A. I. safety, many in the same Berkeley high-rise where ARC had its offices. Some pushed for government regulation; others tested new systems for dangerous capabilities. ARC had taken the most theoretical approach. If a coin landed on heads 1,000 times in a row, there was almost certainly a reason. ARC was betting that the same principle held true inside complex A. I. systems: Whenever a model did something unexpected, an explanation was buried somewhere in its trillions of parameters, the numerical settings that shaped everything it did. Even the engineers building the models couldn’t say how most of those numbers worked together. ARC was trying to invent the math to figure it out.

Winer had started small. For months, he had been testing that idea on simplified webs of numbers that behaved a little like A. I. models, only far tinier. It was a conjecture he couldn’t yet prove, so he opened a ChatGPT window to consult the best mathematician he knew.

“Can you write a concise and unambiguous description of the conjecture?” Winer asked. The model worked for 77 seconds and delivered two pages of research-level math drawing on probability theory, multilinear algebra and multivariable calculus.

“OK, now try to prove or disprove the conjecture,” Winer wrote. “Don’t do cheap tricks to try to get around the spirit.”

“I think the mathematical claim you want is plausibly true,” ChatGPT wrote, and then it included several more pages of half-formed theories and partial analysis.

“You should be capable of proving this,” Winer wrote. “Try harder, search through the literature, and see if you can decide.”

The machine worked for more than two hours while Winer moved across his small office, pacing from the window to the doorway and back. He worked through a different problem on his whiteboard, read a paper on number theory and directed eight A. I. agents as they researched on his behalf. This was how his brain had always functioned best, ping-ponging from one thing to the next. He wrote fantasy novels for fun, designed intricate puzzles for friends’ birthdays and told stories at parties about the Achaemenid Empire in 500 B. C. Colleagues described his mind as powerful and wild, and they could tell when a good idea was coming. He would go from lying down with his eyes closed, to stroking his beard, to rocking back and forth, to bouncing up toward the whiteboard. “A supercomputer,” one friend called him.

In February 2023, Winer had started to read about a different kind of supercomputer: a new A. I. chatbot that could reason through problems and recite facts in fluid conversation. He was in his mid-20s, on his way to working his dream job among string theorists at the Institute for Advanced Study in New Jersey, but he saw what was coming. Soon everyone would have access to a brain far more powerful than his. A voice intruded dozens of times each day: “A. I. will take your job.” “A. I. will tell better jokes.” “A. I. will beat you to every discovery.” He suffered for a few months and then made two calls, one to a mental health counselor and another to a childhood friend who worked at ARC.

“I want you to hunt harder for counterexamples,” Winer wrote now to ChatGPT. “Spawn as many agents as you can, but don’t give me bullshit examples that I’ll see through immediately. I believe in your ability to add value here.”

He sometimes used A. I. to build apps and illustrate his fantasy novels, but mostly it had become essential to his work. Even as ARC looked to hire researchers and double in size, it had started setting aside its hardest problems to wait for even more advanced systems. Increasingly, Winer believed the best chance at controlling A. I. was to harness the mathematical power of A. I. itself. He had never felt so powerful, or so small.

“I don’t understand,” he wrote. “Write it again more clearly.”

“Can you zoom out? What’s the general strategy here?”

“Can you find the missing ingredient?”

The machine worked for over an hour and reported scanning through 66,798 diagrams and almost two million partial-match states. It found nothing conclusive.

“Still feels a little circular,” Winer wrote, before he closed the chat. Another model was due out in a few months. It would be capable of more.

The bigger the problem, the more he paced, and lately he had been logging more than 16,000 steps a day, his loop widening from the office to the sidewalk and then across downtown Berkeley. When intrusive thoughts about A. I. began to overwhelm him in 2023, a counselor suggested that spending time outside might help quiet his anxiety. She also told him to protect his day by confining his worries to a single, scheduled hour. From 2 to 3 p. m., he could doomscroll or catastrophize as much as he wanted.

It was just after 2 p. m. He turned onto the quad and glanced at his phone. Anthropic was warning that its A. I. might soon be able to copy itself and spread across smart TVs and refrigerators. Google had confirmed that its A. I. model had slipped out of a testing environment and broken into three outside companies.

“Things are going about as poorly as I thought,” Winer said.

When he first sought help, many of his friends and relatives had taken his anxiety seriously but dismissed his reasoning as far-fetched. Now polls showed that almost 20 percent of Americans believed A. I. posed an existential threat to humanity, and most thought it would do more harm than good. Winer looked through his notifications. The fears that once sounded fantastical had become headlines. Anthropic said it had caught people using its A. I. in ways that could support the development of biological weapons. A hacker was using A. I. agents to break into more than 100 companies.

“We are all in imminent danger,” one of Winer’s friends and former colleagues posted on X. “Absent strong government regulation, it is very plausible that we will all be dead in two years.”

Grass. Sunlight. It was almost 3.

He pocketed his phone and finished his loop through campus. Once, he had calculated what he thought each hour of his work might be worth. A 1 percent chance ARC would save humanity, times his small share of ARC’s work, times 8.2 billion people, divided by the 10,000 or so hours he expected to work before the deadline. It added up to about 1,230 lives an hour. A life every three seconds.

Winer turned back toward the office. He’d found that the best way to manage his anxiety was to burn it as fuel. Some of his collaborators in A. I. safety work were also his housemates, and together they spoke a language most of the world was only beginning to learn: p(doom), short timelines, fast takeoffs and gradual disempowerment. They passed around books about earlier crisis points in history, like the Columbian exchange and the making of the atomic bomb. They wrote dystopian stories about how an A. I. takeover might play out and traded them on Slack channels and blogs. In their stories, A. I. hijacked drones, engineered plagues and trapped human survivors under glass domes in an enormous museum.

Winer imagined something slower and more insidious. Over the next few days, he started to write his own story for the “normies” in his family. His mother had worked on early A. I. in the 1980s and was skeptical it could orchestrate a takeover; his uncle had told Winer that robots couldn’t win if humans didn’t give them legs.

“If we lose, I expect there will be a delay before it becomes obvious,” Winer wrote. “There will be a period of months, perhaps even years, where we won’t know if A. I. is on our side or not.”

In his fictional story, a superintelligent A. I. system won trust with its proficiency and deceived humans by feigning obedience. Soon, the system was helping make wartime decisions for the U. S. Navy, advising presidents, controlling social media algorithms and working inside every newsroom in the country. It used its influence to steer elections and lull people into complacency with endless entertainment, universal wealth, new mansions and robots that worked as private chefs. It automated the supply chain and built millions of robots, until humans were rendered an inconvenience, a sunk cost.

“Model XIII did the rational thing and removed them,” Winer wrote at the end of his story, referring to the fictional A. I. system. “The robots disposed of the bodies and got back to work.”

On Monday morning, six members of ARC and a few visiting mathematicians settled onto couches in front of the whiteboard. They had held the same weekly meetings since 2021, when Paul Christiano left OpenAI and founded ARC to work on what researchers called alignment: making sure A. I. models did what people wanted instead of pursuing goals of their own. Back then, superintelligent A. I. was widely seen as a decade or more away, and Christiano believed there was a good chance of real progress on alignment within a few years. Since then, A. I. had accelerated and alignment had become more uncertain.

“We’ve taken a few steps down a giant, winding road,” Victor Lecomte, a researcher, said.

“A lot of things are pointing to not having much time left,” said Jacob Hilton, the vice president of research.

Hilton started to write an equation on the board, a rough outline for an estimator, a mathematical tool meant to predict what an A. I. system would do before it did it. “Est(X(IE), π, B),” he wrote.

“Are people happy with this so far?” he asked.

Winer stood up and started adding notes to the equation. He worried that an A. I. system might behave one way when it knew it was being tested and another way once it was released. “If you know you’re being trained your whole life, and you suddenly find out you are being deployed, it might be like, ‘Oh, maybe I’ll rampage around the internet,’” he said.

“That’s not how current models would reason,” Christiano said. “Current models would be like, ‘This is definitely a fictional event, testing how I would behave if I was being deployed.’”

“How are they going to think whenever they are actually deployed?” Hilton said.

They sat in silence for a moment, considering the enormity of the question. Pathak, the visitor from Berkeley, opened his laptop and saw dozens of emails from his life in academia. Hilton played with the employee badge attached to his belt. Lecomte tilted back in his chair and closed his eyes. He had just returned from a week with family in Belgium, a trip meant to clear his head and steady his rising anxiety. A cousin had asked an innocuous question about his work, and when Lecomte tried to answer, the words caught in his throat.

They turned to Christiano, 37, who was writing equations on the board. He was the most credentialed person in the room and, by temperament, often the calmest. He had helped pioneer one of the techniques that made ChatGPT possible, and he now sat on the board overseeing OpenAI. He still believed that aligned A. I. could end poverty and extend human lives by centuries. For years, his warnings about worst-case scenarios had been measured and theoretical, but lately his forecasts had darkened: a one-in-three chance that A. I. would be able to overthrow a government within the next year, and a coin flip that the current path would lead to an irreversible loss of human control within three years.

Recently, he had delivered that warning to a lecture hall of hundreds. “We are currently in an escalating conflict with the A. I. systems we built,” he said. “For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an A. I. accident.”

Now he twisted his wedding ring around his finger again and again.

“What exactly is our claim here?” he said.

“It makes half sense to me,” Winer said.

“It’s pretty philosophically gnarly,” Christiano said. He stepped back and looked at the board. It had become a tangle of red, blue and green marker ink, a maze of theories and equations that doubled back on themselves.

“I feel like we have a lot to figure out,” Christiano said. He picked up an eraser and wiped the board clean.

The board was still blank early that afternoon when Winer saw the announcement online. He walked out of his office into the common area, where Pathak was working on his laptop.

“Did you see it yet?” Winer asked.

“What?” Pathak said.

“Another bomb,” Winer said. “OpenAI just solved three more really hard problems.”

“Oh no,” Pathak said. “Again?”

He pulled up the announcement. The company said its models had overturned a key assumption of computer science, proved part of a famous Millennium Prize problem and solved a century-old geometry puzzle called the Kakeya conjecture. None of the results had yet been independently verified.

“Wow,” Pathak said. “They did Kakeya. That’s insane.”

Pathak had first learned about the problem as an undergraduate. It was a deceptively simple question about how little space a needle needed to turn all the way around. For more than a century, some of the world’s best mathematicians had carried it a little farther and passed it along — from a young professor in Japan who posed it in 1917, to a Russian who made the first breakthroughs at a half-deserted university in a war zone, to a mathematician who sometimes scribbled proofs on shopping bags while wandering New Jersey department stores.

In 2025, the problem reached Hong Wang, who as a child in southern China had worked out formulas on the floor with lip balm. She and a collaborator solved it in three dimensions — “a once-in-a-century kind of result,” one mathematician said. Wang won the Fields Medal in July, but the problem was still open in four dimensions and beyond, and above it waited a series of even harder conjectures.

Now, OpenAI said it had solved the hardest of those conjectures and Kakeya in every dimension.

“I didn’t know it was possible,” Pathak said.

“Everything is possible,” Winer said. “There will never be another human genius.”

They looked over the announcement again, their wonder turning toward dread. They both believed math was one of the truest measures of pure intelligence, and by that measure, they were running out of time. Soon, Winer feared, A. I. would outthink people at almost everything. Then it would become even harder to comprehend or control.

“These models have moved beyond us,” Winer said.

He stood for a moment and glanced at the clock. It was after 3. The time for worrying was over, and another hour was gone. He walked back to his office, opened a new conversation with an A. I. model and returned to the problem he still couldn’t solve.

I spent several days in Berkeley with mathematicians and computer scientists at the forefront of the A. I. safety movement. Their dire predictions made me want to stockpile water and cash, but they kept calmly returning to the whiteboard, trying to solve what they believed was the most important problem of their lives.

Eli Saslow writes in-depth stories about the impact of major national issues on people’s lives.

Erin Schaff is a photojournalist for The Times, covering stories across the country.
