China’s Spies Set Sights on A. I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

China’s espionage agency has been running a secret campaign to help the country’s companies acquire advanced A. I. chips and to gather intelligence on the sector, officials say.

By Chris Buckley and Julian E. Barnes

When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U. S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman who U. S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.

Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment, and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.

Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.

The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.

The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.

The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.

In April, Mr. Chen unveiled the new mission. “Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a Communist Party journal.

“Focus on tackling the ‘chokeholds’ of critical technologies,” he wrote, and solve the problem of technologies that “cannot be obtained by asking, buying or pleading.”

“Chen is signaling to the party leadership and his own ranks that his agency is elevating A. I. competition with the U. S. as a long-term, top priority,” said Alex Joske, the managing director of security practice at Garnaut Global, a consultancy firm, who studies the Chinese security apparatus. “He is telling his officers to find more ways to wage this struggle.”

The ministry’s campaign is part of a wider push by the ruling Communist Party to overcome Western-imposed restrictions on critical technology. China is determined to close its gap with the United States in the computing capacity needed for progress in artificial intelligence.

At the top, that effort is being coordinated by the Central Science and Technology Commission. The commission is a secretive Communist Party organ that Mr. Xi established in 2023. This was not long after the U. S. Commerce Department, in late 2022, started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.

The party commission is ranked higher than ministries and is led by Ding Xuexiang, one of only seven members of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, its inner circle of power.

“Computing power is a major indicator of overall national power,” Mr. Ding said in May when he visited energy and computing facilities in Beijing and nearby regions that are part of a planned nationwide A. I. computing network, according to Xinhua, China’s official news agency.

Mr. Xi created the commission to better marshal the country’s scientists, institutes and labs across ministries, and companies, for national priorities such as achieving technological self-reliance.

The commission rarely surfaces in Chinese news reports; its budgets and plans are not made public. But it has become an engine of Mr. Xi’s plans for technological pre-eminence, said Christopher K. Johnson, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst focused on China. The director of the commission, Mr. Ding, has long been a close aide to Mr. Xi and is also a vice premier overseeing science and technology policy.

China’s espionage service and other parts of the government have for decades pursued technology and research from abroad, using both open and illicit methods. But under Mr. Xi, that effort assumed greater urgency, with more top-level coordination, including in artificial intelligence, several experts said.

Throughout this year, Mr. Chen, the agency’s chief, has repeatedly said the “anti-blockade struggle” is one of the key duties of China’s Ministry of State Security.

“Certain countries are going to every length to impose a ‘chokehold’ on China in fields of critical technology,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal last year. “Technology competition among the major powers has entered its most intense, most strenuous and most critical phase of close-quarters combat.”

As American companies, followed by Chinese ones, developed successively powerful A. I. models, officials in Beijing have increasingly recognized the potential for artificial intelligence to threaten their power at home and abroad, said Gregory C. Allen, the founder and chief executive of Decision Tree Research, a firm that specializes in A. I. and other advanced technologies.

In September, Mr. Chen himself referred to U. S. tech companies and their A. I. models — like Claude Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber — as examples of new cybersecurity threats, as he described the risks that A. I. posed to the party’s hold on power.

“China’s senior leadership understands that A. I. is critically, strategically essential, and that leadership in A. I. is obviously related to leadership in semiconductors,” said Mr. Allen, a former senior official at the U. S. Department of Defense’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center.

Mr. Chen became the state security minister in late 2022, and just over a year later, the ministry issued a warning that A. I. was “highly likely in the near future to profoundly transform the national security landscape.” In 2024, the ministry said that its officers were scoring successes against the attempts of “the United States and other Western countries to lock us in at the low-end” of technology.

China has sometimes used front organizations or researchers to collect information about foreign A. I. technology, said Mr. Joske, the consultant.

“M. S. S. is very comfortable using business covers,” he said, “and it’s very comfortable running people as assets without directly telling those people that they’re working for the M. S. S.”

Such covers could include organizations ostensibly focused on academic research. In September, MI5, the British security agency, asserted that a Chinese research institute linked to the Chinese spy agency had drawn in British scientists for research that, apparently unbeknown to the scientists, “directly improves M. S. S. technical capability for espionage.”

Companies such as the one Alice Huang founded, Megaspeed, are viewed as another potential vehicle for gathering intelligence.

The precise nature of Alice Huang’s role in the ministry’s chip effort remains unclear. U. S. officials say Ms. Huang, who was having an affair with the Nvidia founder Mr. Huang, passed information to Beijing about him. The U. S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling advanced chips into China.

Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and entered the business of providing high-end computing capacity to Chinese companies. Such services have allowed Chinese businesses to use Nvidia chips at data centers abroad by sidestepping U. S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A. I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

Last week, The Times also reported that Megaspeed was possibly aiding a lab with links to China’s military, through Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant. Alibaba is a customer and financial backer of Megaspeed. Providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military would be a violation of U. S. law.

An Alibaba spokeswoman said: “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose.”

In an effort to address what many in Washington see as a loophole, the Trump administration announced on Monday that it would move ahead with a new rule to prevent China from being able to access advanced semiconductors from Nvidia and other U. S. companies through the use of data centers outside China.

The new restriction will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in countries on a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. It goes into effect in about 90 days.

The restriction could make China’s pursuit of self-reliance more urgent, a goal Mr. Xi has cast as a fight for survival, echoing the party’s revolutionary past.

“Like the Red Army on the Long March, we’re now on a new Long March,” he told technicians, while visiting an A. I. data hub under construction in northern China last month. He was referring to a grueling trek taken by Communist troops in the 1930s that cemented Mao’s leadership of the revolution. “You are an army in the drive for advanced technological self-reliance.”

Chris Buckley, the chief China correspondent for The Times, reports on China and Taiwan from Taipei, focused on politics, social change and security and military issues.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Fact-Checking Stephen Miller, the New White House Chief of Staff

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Fact Check

Mr. Miller has promoted some of the second Trump administration’s most egregious falsehoods about immigration policy, the economy and political opposition.

By Linda Qiu

Reporting from Washington

In ascending to the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, a longtime aide and hard-liner, has displayed messaging that mirrors that of President Trump: bombastic, combative and, at times, unabashedly fact-free.

Mr. Miller, who previously served as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, has promoted some of the second Trump administration’s most egregious falsehoods about immigration policy, the economy and political opposition. His loyalty to Mr. Trump was on show at the president’s news conference on Friday, where he lauded Mr. Trump as having achieved “more than any president has achieved by far in American history,” ticking off a list of the administration’s accomplishments.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, praised Mr. Miller in a statement. “Any good chief of staff reflects the messaging of the president they serve, who was elected by the American people,” she said.

In January, during the administration’s immigration surge in Minnesota, Mr. Miller swiftly called Alex Pretti, the nurse fatally shot by immigration officials, a “domestic terrorist” and accused him of trying to “murder” federal agents — a description at odds with legal reality and video evidence. This summer, Mr. Miller insisted that gas prices had been tamed and inflation had decreased to 2 percent — average gas prices neared $4.20 in August and inflation had risen by 3.4 percent in July. And as the midterm elections neared, Mr. Miller repeatedly and falsely characterized a Democratic Senate candidate as transgender.

Here are four other claims from Mr. Miller, fact-checked.

What Mr. Miller Said

“Let’s go back in history. How do we end up with 60 senators in the first place in 2008 to pass Obamacare? Because Democrats rigged the Alaska election then with a fake case against then-Senator Ted Stevens. So there is a history here where Alaska Democrats have tried corruptly to steal the vote of the Alaskan people and their right to choose their own future.”— in a Fox News interview in October

This is misleading. Senator Ted Stevens, Republican of Alaska, was prosecuted and convicted of corruption in October 2008 by the Justice Department under President George W. Bush. The conviction was thrown out the next year and the case was reviewed and dropped by the Obama administration in 2009. While the Alaska Democratic Party and Senator Mark Begich, Mr. Stevens’s Democratic challenger, attacked Mr. Stevens with accusations of corruption, they were not involved in the handling of the case.

Mr. Stevens was voted out of office in the face of a wide-ranging corruption investigation involving an oil company and its ties to lawmakers in Alaska opened by the Justice Department under Mr. Bush. Federal authorities searched the office of Mr. Stevens’s son, a state legislator, in 2006 and searched Mr. Stevens’s home in 2007. The senator was charged on seven felony counts in July 2008 for failing to disclose gifts from the company and its executive.

That executive, who tended to support Republican candidates, began cooperating with the authorities in the investigation in 2006 and was a key witness in the case against Mr. Stevens. The senator was convicted in October 2008 and lost his re-election bid the next month.

Three months later, in February 2009, an F. B. I. whistle-blower accused prosecutors of concealing evidence from the court and defense lawyers. The Justice Department, under the Obama administration, dropped its case against Mr. Stevens in April and Mr. Stevens’s lawyer said he was “very grateful” to Eric H. Holder Jr., the attorney general, for the decision.

The department and a special investigator appointed by a court released separate reviews of the case in 2012, two years after Mr. Stevens died in a plane crash. Both faulted prosecutors for misconduct and mistakes, but neither attributed those errors to political or partisan motivations. The special investigator told Congress that year that he believed the prosecutors’ desire to win a big case, compounded by tight deadlines, led to the misconduct.

What Mr. Miller Said

“First is we get off of this ridiculous path of having our children get 70 to 90 shots. That is wantonly excessive. Remember, each and every one of these shots produces a profound immunological response. So across any large population, if you give a kid shot after shot after shot, you’re going to have vaccine injuries, you’re going to have immunological issues, you’re going to have potentially neurological issues. Secondly, and so important to you, Mr. President, is the unbundling of the shot. Why do you need to have these shots bundled into these packages? Why can’t you split it into five visits and give this young body, if a parent wants to do a vaccine, one shot at a time? Why is it that in Japan you can get a separate measles shot, a separate mumps shot, a separate rubella shot, but in America it has to all be packaged together?”— in an executive order signing at the White House in August

This is misleading. Mr. Miller overstated the number of vaccines given to American children and offered a contradictory critique of the United States’ vaccine schedule.

The federal government in January tried to reduce the number of recommended vaccines for children to 11 diseases, from 17, but that effort is pending litigation. (In August, Mr. Trump signed an executive order trying the same thing, but it is unclear whether the order has any legal power.)

If children received every recommended dose from birth until they were 18, they would receive 72 doses. That is different from 72 different shots or 72 different vaccines. Annual flu and coronavirus vaccines constitute about half of those doses. (Fewer than half of children obtained a flu vaccine last year, and fewer than 10 percent received a coronavirus shot.) Other vaccines, like hepatitis B and polio, are given in multiple doses. And some vaccines like diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis as well as measles, mumps and rubella are given together.

Japan does offer separate vaccines for mumps, measles and rubella. But it is an outlier, especially among peer nations. In fact, most countries — including the United States, Canada and most European nations — use the combined trivalent shot. Just 15 countries, all low- and middle-income countries in Africa and the Middle East, used a monovalent measles shot. Moreover, Mr. Miller’s suggestion to separate all three vaccines would lead to more shots, not fewer — conflicting with his critique of a high number of doses. Health experts recommend the combined shot for logistical ease and to encourage higher vaccination levels.

What Mr. Miller Said

“So, when you think about, for example, public schools, half of kids in New York public schools can’t speak English properly. Why? Because 40 percent of New York City public or New York State school students are either migrants or the children of migrants. They’re redistributing education from the taxpaying base to newcomers.”— in a Fox News interview in August

This is misleading. Mr. Miller appears to be exaggerating and conflating several different statistics to suggest that New York City schools show how immigrants are taking resources from native-born Americans.

Under a 1982 Supreme Court ruling, public schools cannot bar students from attending based on citizenship, so they generally do not track immigration status. But the Center for Immigration Studies, a research group that supports lower levels of immigration, has estimated, using Census Bureau data, that 47 percent of public school students in the New York City metropolitan area lived in households headed by an immigrant.

A smaller proportion of students, though, “can’t speak English properly,” as Mr. Miller said. About 15.4 percent of students in New York schools were English-language learners in the 2025-26 school year, according to the city. But that does not necessarily mean they were immigrants. Census surveys estimate that some 1.5 million New Yorkers who are native-born citizens and 1.4 million naturalized citizens speak a language other than English at home.

Mr. Miller does have a point that most research shows that immigrant households cost local governments more money than they pay in local taxes. While immigrants have a net positive fiscal effect on the federal budget, they generally have a net negative effect on local and state governments given the cost of education. But that does not mean native-born Americans are being pushed out of public schools; rather, enrollment at New York City schools is declining, fueled by a two-decade decrease in fertility rates and mirroring a trend seen across the country.

What Mr. Miller Said

“The way most welfare works in most states, and most places, is we take your word for it. If you fill out a piece of paper and you say your kids are hungry, you are going to get food stamps. We don’t check as a country if you even have kids.”— at a meeting of the White House fraud task force in May

False. Applicants to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps, undergo eligibility interviews and give proof of identity, residency, income and assets, expenses and other details listed on the application. State agencies must also recertify most SNAP participants every year. (There are exceptions for some low-income seniors in some states, who are recertified every three years.)

Applicants must list the date of birth and Social Security number of each household member and, contrary to Mr. Miller’s claim, state SNAP agencies then verify this information with the Social Security Administration. Similarly, agencies and workers rely on a variety of government databases and private companies to check residency, immigration status, income, assets, disability status and employment history.

The Government Accountability Office, in a 2024 review of the SNAP program, found that about 11.7 percent of payments in the 2023 fiscal year were improper (which is not the same thing as fraud), stemming from a variety of errors including state agencies’ not always verifying household size. The watchdog office did not estimate how widespread that oversight was.

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

Andrew Scott Plays a Dying Actor Playing Hamlet: ‘I’m Not Scared of Sadness’

The New York Times November 22, 2026

Scott is the subject of Oscar chatter for his performance recreating the last months of Ian Charleson for the biopic “Elsinore.”

“My job is to try and reflect what it’s like to be a human being,” Scott said. Credit...

Supported by

By Alexis Soloski

Visuals by Sela Shiloni

Of all the parts the actor Andrew Scott has played, Hamlet is the greatest. “Because it’s so multifaceted,” Scott said in a recent video interview. “He’s so delicate and fragile and vulnerable. He’s also an orator, a prince, a soldier, a lover, a grieving son. He’s got 5,000 lines and you do it eight times a week and then you have a sword fight in the third hour. You go off and you think, ‘I’m going to go mad.’”

Scott, 50, first attempted the role onstage in 2017. (He didn’t go mad.) Now in the biopic “Elsinore,” opening Friday, he is playing a version of Hamlet again. He plays Ian Charleson, an acclaimed stage actor and a star of “Chariots of Fire.” Charleson died in 1990, of complications from AIDS, just weeks after taking on the role of Hamlet at the National Theater in London.

To play Charleson, Scott had to unlearn his own Hamlet. And he had to imagine himself in the mind and body of an artist risking his health to answer his calling. “I had to embrace Ian while he was being embraced by the part, if that doesn’t sound too weird,” he said. That double embrace has already made Scott a serious contender for an Oscar nomination for best actor in addition to being a critics’ favorite.

“Scott is one of the most mesmerizing actors working today, and even by his standards he’s splendid in this role,” The Times’s Alissa Wilkinson wrote in her critic’s pick review of “Elsinore.”

On a video call from Los Angeles, Scott, in a tight black T-shirt with a shockingly blue Erewhon smoothie by his side, discussed being, not being and why he doesn’t think he has a gift for tragedy. These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

Before you read Stephen Beresford’s script, how much did you know about Ian Charleson?

The Ian Charleson Awards, for young actors who have done really well in classical roles, are very well known in London. And I knew about “Chariots of Fire,” but to be honest not a lot.

What were his gifts as an actor?

He had great lightness. He had a great sense of humor. He had a beautiful singing voice. And he had a kind of dignity about him.

You had his screen roles as a reference. How else did you prepare?

Obviously, there’s accent work and a physicality about the way the illness was taking hold. But actually, I felt pretty free. I didn’t feel like, “Oh my God, am I sounding like him every day?” I was quite nervous when we showed the movie to his family and friends. Because you want them to see somebody they loved so much represented and have some degree of, “Oh, there he is.” I won’t say what they said, but it was it was extraordinarily gratifying and the most celebratory day for me of this whole experience because I owed that to them.

What was the physical transformation like?

There was a degree of weight loss. Frankly. I’m hesitant to talk about that because it is absolutely nothing in comparison to what Ian went through.

But because of the constraints of our budget, you’re doing things where you’re very healthy in the morning and then extremely ill by the end of the day. Simon Stone, our director, said, “We have a choice here. We could get Johnny Flynn for five days, Olivia Colman for six, Juliet Stevenson for three.” I was happy to prioritize getting these incredible actors, in this film that is a love letter to actors, rather than making it so that I could go through in chronological order the decline of Ian’s health.

What was it like to play someone from a previous generation of gay men, a generation that was decimated?

It affects me deeply. What must have been so frightening is the absolute lack of support and the absolute lack of knowledge of how do we even contract this. I feel enormous compassion for them and an enormous gratitude because they fought the fight.

You played Hamlet in 2017. How would you describe your Hamlet?

I have always been fixated on the idea that Shakespeare could be conversational, that actually you could speak it in some way that would make it understandable for an audience. That’s what I focused on.

He’s also a really funny character. People talk about Hamlet as the grieving prince in the inky black cloak. But his father died two months ago, and his mum has married his uncle. You’d be wearing a black cloak as well! What’s more interesting is who was he before the grief. We all go a bit mad with grief. Who was he before that? A really, really funny student prince. He had the whole world at his feet.

What was Ian’s Hamlet like?

When people said, “Oh I saw Ian’s Hamlet,” I would be grasping them by the shoulders and going, “OK, tell me what your experience was.” Most people’s experience was that he was very, very funny. And when he did “to be or not to be,” he was just at ease. He was very near that undiscovered country and so it had an authenticity where he could sort of do away with acting.

Simon Stone began his career as a theater director. Did that make the rehearsal scenes more realistic?

Without a doubt. It’s this very practical nature of what rehearsal rooms are actually like. They’re not swathed in velvet curtains and all comfort. They’re usually quite cold, basic rooms with bad lighting in which you create magic, and I love that. Extraordinary things happen in places that aren’t immediately beautiful.

You’ve been described as having a gift for tragedy. You don’t agree with that?

No, I dispute that. Because what person is without sadness in their life? If there’s anything that I possess in life, it’s lightness. But my job is to try and reflect what it’s like to be a human being. So I’m not scared of the sadness.

We always come back to these sad plays. We’re always doing “Hamlet.” We’re always doing “Lear.” Why are we drawn to tragedy?

Because it doesn’t end well for any of us. This idea that we want a happy ending? Great. Wonderful. But if there is going to be an ending, it’s going to be sad a little bit for the people in your life.

Best case! If not, then you’re a monster.

Exactly. Tragedy is in some ways how you get to enjoy your life. We need it to give us perspective. We’re all getting on with our lives and making plans for summer holidays and hoping we might fall in love in the full knowledge that that’s going to end at some point. Tragedy reflects that. You go, yeah, that’s where it’s going and then you keep calm and carry on.

Is “Elsinore” a tragedy? Ian dies at the end. And so young. Yet he does the thing he sets out to do. He lives with purpose.

It’s heartbreaking that we didn’t get more of him, and it’s awful that it was so incredibly difficult to be alive at that time, with the fear-mongering and prejudice and hatred both personally and professionally. But he was not a victim. He was looking forward all the time. At the end of his life, he was still talking about doing Benedick in “Much Ado About Nothing.”

I would hate for people to think of Ian as a tragic figure, because what more can we do on earth than to have a passion for something and engage with people that you adore and who adore you and spend your life pursuing that passion? It’s the quality of his life that I hope we remember and not the number of years.

Alexis Soloski has written for The Times since 2006. As a culture reporter, she covers television, theater, movies, podcasts and new media.

Easy Thanksgiving Recipes That Take Up Absolutely No Oven Space

The New York Times November 20, 2026

Dishes for the stovetop, the slow-cooker, the air fryer, the Instant Pot and more.

By Sharon Attia

Published Nov. 19, 2026 Updated Nov. 20, 2026

Oven space is famously precious on Thanksgiving. Below are 17 recipes that skip the game of Tetris entirely. Some are cooked on the stovetop, others in a slow-cooker, an instant pot or an air fryer. A few require no heat whatsoever.

Don’t let the casserole dish fool you — this recipe never touches the oven! Dan Pelosi likes to spread a thick layer of creamy, cheesy mashed potatoes into a 9-by-13 pan and top them with potato chips. But not just any potato chips; ones that have been sautéed in melted butter, toasted garlic and herbs.

Recipe: Potato Chip Mashed Potatoes

Sheelah Prakash’s tabbouleh-inspired salad swaps the usual parsley and tomatoes for shaved brussels sprouts, scallions, mint, pomegranate seeds and roasted pistachios. Making the bulgur is the only cooking the recipe calls for. It’s perfect for potlucks or planners, as it can be assembled ahead of time and served at room temperature.

Recipe: Brussels Sprout Salad With Pomegranate and Pistachios

Sarah DiGregorio’s tender turkey meatballs and gravy are a great cost-saving alternative for anyone who doesn’t feel the need for a whole bird on Thanksgiving. The meatballs are seared in a skillet before moving to the slow cooker, where they hold on warm for several hours.

Recipe: Slow-Cooker Turkey Meatballs and Gravy

This is Kay Chun’s lighter, quicker alternative to the classic green bean casserole. Green beans are blanched and tossed in a vinaigrette made of white miso, lemon juice, minced shallot and finely chopped walnuts. Fresh dill is added before serving.

Recipe: Green Beans in Walnut Vinaigrette

Vegan? Lactose intolerant? Corn lover? This recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon is for you. She uses coconut milk, instead of dairy, which brings out corn’s natural sweetness and cooks down beautifully with the grated kernels to create a creamy, porridge-like side dish.

Recipe: Coconut Creamed Corn

This no-cook cranberry sauce from Daniel Humm, the chef of Eleven Madison Park in New York, is bright, tart and oh-so-easy to make. Toss cranberries, sugar and orange zest into a stand mixer with a paddle attachment (a food processor won’t work), turn it on the lowest setting and come back in an hour to a glorious, ruby red, macerated chutney.

Recipe: No-Cook Cranberry Chutney

Genevieve Ko’s simple stovetop mac and cheese is creamy, silky and ready in 35 minutes. This recipe calls for a standard white sauce (butter, flour and milk) and grated, sharp yellow Cheddar — but it will work with any blend of cheeses. If you’ve got some random nubs in the fridge, grate ‘em up and chuck ‘em in!

Recipe: Stovetop Mac and Cheese

Be like Kay Chun and blanch your broccoli. While it’s still warm, toss it with a vibrant dressing of scallions, oil, lemon juice, ginger and miso to help the vegetable soak up all of that flavor. One reader said the 20-minute recipe was “even better the next day.”

Recipe: Ginger Scallion Broccoli Salad

Yossy Arefi’s pumpkin cheesecake looks down its nose at your oven. Her no-bake dessert is delightfully autumnal: It has a buttery Biscoff cookie crust, a fluffy and lightly spiced pumpkin filling and a cinnamon whipped cream topping. If you’ve got the fridge space, it can be made up to four days in advance.

Recipe: No-Bake Pumpkin Cheesecake

Inspired by a Cantonese dish that translates to “flavorful rice,” this dish from Genevieve Ko lives up to the name. In her recipe, chewy sticky rice (sometimes labeled sushi rice) is studded with bacon, mushrooms and crispy ginger. It’s a wonderful gluten-free and dairy-free alternative to buttery bread stuffing.

Recipe: Crispy Ginger Sticky Rice

Melissa Clark’s Instant Pot mash is ready in 20 minutes. Twenty minutes! Her recipe yields extra creamy potatoes (thanks to both butter and sour cream), which are then topped with a little Parmesan and fresh chives. (If you don’t have an Instant Pot, see Melissa’s guide to making the best mashed potatoes.)

Recipe: Instant Pot Mashed Potatoes With Sour Cream and Chives

Yewande Komolafe’s warming, 35-minute soup is an adaptation of a long-simmered stew common to much of West Africa. In her recipe, peanut butter, coconut milk and canned pumpkin temper the heat from the habanero or bird’s eye chile.

Recipe: Spicy Peanut and Pumpkin Soup

If there was ever a time to make the case for air-fryer supremacy, it may be on Thanksgiving with brussels sprouts. It achieves that ideal of a crunchy exterior and a tender interior. Melissa Clark throws in slivers of garlic, which crisp up, and then dresses the sprouts in a glossy mixture of lime juice, soy sauce and balsamic vinegar that’s been simmered until thickened.

Recipe: Air-Fryer Brussels Sprouts With Garlic, Balsamic and Soy

Yossy Arefi’s cheese ball is the ultimate make-ahead party trick: It’s easy to make, looks fun and will keep your hungry guests at bay as you finish up dinner. Her recipe features sharp Cheddar, dried cranberries, toasted walnuts or pecans, scallions, onion powder and Worcestershire sauce. Serve with crackers, chips or crudités (or all three!).

Recipe: Cranberry Walnut Cheese Ball

Sarah DiGregorio’s recipe proves you don’t have to make your mashed potatoes immediately before serving. This Cheddar mash can be held on the warm setting for up to three hours before eating, saving you from the last-minute stress of getting the required side dish on the table in time.

Recipe: Slow-Cooker Cheddar Mashed Potatoes

Pierre Franey’s 15-minute recipe is a French classic. The dish is dead-simple: Cook carrots with some sugar, water, lemon juice and butter until they are tender and glazed with the melted sugar. C’est magnifique!

Recipe: Glazed Parsley Carrots

This potato recipe from Mark Bittman’s skips peeling, boiling and mashing and opts for braising potatoes in onions, garlic and a sprig of thyme or rosemary. As one reader commented: “Huge favorite! I’ve tried various potatoes. Yukon Gold are ideal for this, both in terms of flavor and structural integrity.”

Recipe: Simple Braised Potatoes

The Best Travel Adapters for Power On the Go

Wired November 22, 2026

Shop

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon (UK)

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

Ceptics

Shop

Amazon

There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

For all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

Epicka

Amazon

Perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

When I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any issues with the UK prongs.

Ceptics

Amazon

Shop

This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

One Beat

Amazon (UK)

Amazon (Europe)

Amazon (2-Pack for Japan)

What I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

On the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

Mukiya

Amazon

Shop

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a new brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

Ceptics

Amazon (Set of 5)

Amazon (Set of 12)

Shop (Set of 5)

Universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

Ceptics

Amazon

Shop

This kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

There is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

Mophie

Shop (Mophie)

Amazon

This cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

It’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:

Input: 100–220V 50/60Hz

That should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

What About Wattage?

Travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

Some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

How I Test Travel Adapters

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that shows you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

Statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

Arsmel VisaPro

Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

Satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

Baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

Anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

EZQuest WorldTravel

EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

The Gifts Moms Actually Want, Picked by Moms

Wired November 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is now upon us, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

If you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.

Therabody

Amazon

Shop

Nuuly ($38 Off First Month)

Therabody

Therabody

Amazon

Shop

The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. Therabody's TheraFace Mask Glo has a range of treatments with both red and blue light, a unique vibration therapy feature, and removable eye shields if you don't want the light in your eyes.

Yardsale

Yardsale (30L)

Alex Mill

Shop

Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

The Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a colorful personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

If your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

Skylight

Amazon

Skylight (With Plus Plan)

My latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can quickly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.

Nuuly

Nuuly ($38 Off First Month)

To me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely new closet.

I've been loving renting from Nuuly this pregnancy because the brand has an entire maternity section that lets me find pieces to fit me in this short—but very different size—season of my life. My older mother also loves having a clothing subscription because she gets bored of her outfit options to wear into the office, and I loved it for the same reason when I had my first clothing subscription right out of college. If Mom has been talking about wanting some new looks but feels overwhelmed about what she wants to invest in, these rental services are a fun way to get a lot of new clothes in your life without having to store them or spend as much as you would have (some of my favorite maternity clothes I've gotten through Nuuly would have cost me $200 apiece!) The service costs $98 a month, but your first month is discounted to just $60. There's one piece I miss already that might drive me to pick up a second subscription, which would genuinely be cheaper than buying the piece I want brand new.

For years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.)

I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($50) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($68). If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.

This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands, but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons.

I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight's Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

The graduation from diaper-bag-carrying mom to tote-full-of-snacks-and-clothes-changes mom to an adult who only needs to carry their own stuff is a parenting milestone that deserves celebration. This is my favorite grown-up mom bag, which holds only the essentials: water (because no matter how old your kids are, someone is going to get thirsty), cards, phone, and keys. The thick strap makes it comfortable to carry, and there’s a color, material, or theme for just about anyone’s vibe, including a new line of clear stadium versions. Once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($499) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the new console, and now my husband and I are completely hooked on the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake that came out a few weeks ago. It's also quickly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he was been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but now he's dubbed Ocarina of Time as “Big Little Link” and is obsessed with using the grappling hook and using up all of our arrows.

If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another big update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam users and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games, especially if she already got herself the new gadget as I did.

I'm currently grounded from drinking any cocktails while I'm pregnant, but moms (and people in general) can have all kinds of reasons to want to explore unique, interesting drinks that are sans alcohol. I really liked this set for how many cool drinks it exposed me to, from bottles of nonalcoholic wine to knockoff cocktails. If you're looking to spend a little less, my favorites so far have been the Château del Ish Non-Alcoholic Sparkling Espumante ($20) and Lapo's Non-Alcoholic Melograno Mule ($20 for four).

Look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck (or maybe she just wants an e-reader that isn't a Kindle), the answer is actually a Kobo. My favorite is the Kobo Libra Colour. It's cheaper than the Kindle Colorsoft and can also double as a digital notebook if you add on the $70 stylus. I also prefer Kobo's annotating options: You can write right on the pages instead of in weird pop-up margins and boxes only on Kindle. Kobo also has a page-turner remote ($34), which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. I gave a similar pillow stand to my mom, and now I can spot her last reading spot easily because that pillow is resting there.

You could also gift her one of the new Kindles if she's a Kindle addict. Many of my friends are drooling over the new purple Ube color of the 12th-gen Kindle ($150), but my personal favorite is the Kindle Aluminum (I just wish it were cheaper!). There's also finally Kindle page-turn remote, the Kindle Click ($35).

If the mom you know is into LED red-light therapy, she probably already knows about face masks and hair growth devices like the one we recommend above, but there’s one area she’s probably neglecting: her hands. With aging comes loss of collagen, subcutaneous fat, and cumulative effects of UV exposure. I spent the first 26 years of my life living in California, where I rarely remembered to put sunscreen on the tops of my hands. Twenty years later, it shows—they’re wrinkly and have age spots and look like they belong to someone 15 years my senior. Trust me; no mom wants this. I’ve been using Omnilux’s FDA-cleared red-light glove for the past few months to try to mitigate some of the damage, and while I haven’t seen any changes yet (Omnilux says changes happen in four to six weeks, but in my experience with red-light masks, it typically takes much longer to see results), I very much enjoy using this device on its own. The soft silicone glove is comfortable to wear and warms as it heats up, so it feels good and works to reduce joint pain. It’s easy to do while I’m reading or watching TV—just three 10-minute sessions per week—and the rechargeable battery (USB-C) lasts a little over a week. If your giftee already spends 10 minutes at the end of the day relaxing in an LED face mask, she’ll know exactly what to do here. —Kat Merck

I love a backpack when I'm on the move with my 4-year-old, but one thing that annoys me is that things are hard to find inside, because packs are typically so deep. That's why I adore the Mina Baie Emmy Diaper Bag: It's a wide, shallow bag instead of a long one, making it easy to open and see most of what I store in it without digging around. I'm not toting diapers at the moment, but I've used it to pack a ton of snacks, toys, and spare clothing for my kid.

I'm intrigued to see how using it with two kids goes—I chose the Emmy Midi, which is the midsize bag, but if you're a pumping parent or need to carry a ton of bottles with formula, you might want to try the larger Emmy Full. If Mom loves entertaining—or just being festive—but doesn’t want to have to store a million different dishes, Nora Fleming’s modular serving-tray system is for her. First, pick a base—there are trays, baking dishes, utensil crocks, and even salt and pepper shakers. Then, pick one of dozens of hand-painted “Minis,” or ceramic accents (sold separately). Best part is that if Mom likes this setup, you’ll be set on gifts for the foreseeable future, provided you can keep finding new Minis you think she’ll like. —Kat Merck

I'm expecting again, and this time I'm on a mission to find a good pregnancy pillow. I tried a large body pillow on the advice of another site for my first pregnancy, and it was honestly an awful experience—the pillow was too large and firm for me to comfortably use, let alone have room for both it and my growing midsection in my bed. Plus, it was heavy, which is annoying when your body already feels too cumbersome to move around.

So far, using the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow has been the opposite. It's slim and light with just enough squish to add a little support under or around my belly without being difficult to get comfortable. It’s beautiful and easy to maneuver around. Wildbird also suggests it for other support positions postpartum, and I'm curious if those will work for me. But it makes for a beautiful gift for any expecting mom and will be one she's excited to put on her bed and curl up with at night.

Weddell

Amazon

Weddell

For most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification.

Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25 each, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck
